ASRS:1772532.n: I have been having severe headaches after flying lately. Being masked on an airplane and duty day that are now on average 10-15 hours a day. I had a deadhead recently and wore an oxygen sensor from start to finish. My oxygen in the hotel was 99/98 on the pulse oximeter. During the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 I wore it the whole time. My oxygen was between 89 and 94 the whole way until landing. It then was back up to 98, 20 minutes after landing. It is a fact that extra oxygen is pumped into hospital rooms during long surgeries because the doctors are masked. I feel this shows that lack of oxygen, just on 1 flight is proving how I'm getting my headaches, let alone being masked as well. I have never felt more unsafe flying than I have since having to wear masks.
ASRS:1772532.s: A crew member reported severe headaches and low oxygen saturation (89-94%) while masked during a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. The reporter attributes these symptoms to hypoxia caused by mask usage and long duty days, stating they feel unsafe flying under current conditions.

ASRS:1772562.n: On a 1.5 mile final for ILS XX at ZZZ Aircraft Y turned to base right in front of us even though we had just made a radio call and he knew we were on a short final. This caused the instructor to grab the controls and full throttle to go missed. Had we not done this we would have been within a hundred feet of Aircraft Y. He knew where we were and disregarded our radio calls and cut us off.
ASRS:1772562.s: Aircraft Y turned to base right in front of the reporting aircraft on a 1.5-mile ILS final at ZZZ, disregarding radio calls. The instructor executed a missed approach with full throttle to avoid a collision within 100 feet.

ASRS:1772563.n: Operation in violation of Certificate of Waiver issued for UAS flights of multiple aircraft. I was issued a part 107 waiver to operate multiple aircraft with one remote pilot. One of my waiver provisions is to issue a NOTAM 24 hrs in advance of my operation. I flew yesterday without a NOTAM issued. We had issued a NOTAM to close the runway at airport ZZZ in which our operations are taking place. I thought this NOTAM was sufficient to satisfy our requirements. When reading the operational waiver again today I took note that provision X of my waiver was not satisfied by the issuance of a closed runway NOTAM [as follows]:Not less than 24 hours prior to conducting operations that are the subject of this waiver, a Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) must be filed. The NOTAM must include location, altitude, and/or operating area, time and nature of the activity, and number of sUA flying in the operating area, To correct my mistake I called to issue a NOTAM as soon as I discovered my error.
ASRS:1772563.s: The remote pilot operated multiple UAS at airport ZZZ without the required 24-hour advance NOTAM, mistakenly believing a runway closure notice satisfied the waiver. The pilot corrected the violation by filing the proper NOTAM immediately after discovering the error.

ASRS:1772564.n: Catastrophic engine failure at 8500 ft. MSL. Uneventful landing at ZZZ.
ASRS:1772564.s: The pilot reported a catastrophic engine failure at 8,500 ft MSL. The aircraft subsequently made an uneventful landing at ZZZ.

ASRS:1772584.n: While conducting a IFR training flight with a student, we were on an IFR flight plan and on initial climb vectors from ATC when we noticed the Oil Pressure indication slowly, but consistently, dropping. It triggered a CAS caution message for Low Oil Pressure, then the pressure reading slowly recovered. As we discussed the potential causes of this indication change, the Oil Pressure reading decreased again causing another CAS message. At this point we both decided to return to the departure airport ZZZ. The student informed ATC of the issue and asked to return to the airport. We were given vectors back to ZZZ and confirmed with ATC that we [would like priority handling] We ran the appropriate checklists as a crew. We were then cleared for a visual approach and landed uneventfully at ZZZ. This event was a great learning experience for the student and myself. Always leaning towards caution and returning to the airport was the right move. It would have been easy to convince ourselves that the oil pressure indication was a sensor error and continue to our destination, but this would have been very poor ADM. While on an IFR flight plan and on initial climb vectors from ATC, we noticed the oil pressure indication slowly, but consistently dropping. It triggered a CAS message for low oil pressure, then the pressure reading slowly recovered. As we discussed potential causes of this indication change, the oil pressure reading decreased again causing another CAS message. At this point we both decided to return to the departure airport ZZZ. I informed ATC of the issue and asked to return to the airport. We were given vectors back to ZZZ and confirmed with ATC that I would [request priority handling]. We ran the appropriate checklists. This likely could have been a sensor issue, but I always prefer to be more safe than sorry.
ASRS:1772584.s: During an IFR training flight on initial climb, the instructor and student observed fluctuating low oil pressure CAS messages. They elected to return to departure airport ZZZ, received vectors and priority handling from ATC, and landed uneventfully after running checklists.

ASRS:1772585.n: After landing, during taxi to ramp in movement area, the airplane's front landing gear failed and collapsed resulting in the propeller striking the ground. The mechanic on site indicated that the top of the front gear strut is prone to failing and sheering off. He also said that inspection of the strut and specifically the top portion should be inspected as part of a normal annual inspection because stress cracks can occur over time in the part. He suggested that failure in the top part of the front gear strut was responsible for the collapsed gear. I am not qualified to determine the accuracy of the mechanic's diagnosis however it seemed plausible.
ASRS:1772585.s: After landing and during taxi to the ramp, the aircraft's front landing gear collapsed, causing the propeller to strike the ground. An on-site mechanic attributed the failure to a sheared top strut, suggesting stress cracks in that area were the cause.

ASRS:1772587.n: I was transiting from ZZZ1 to ZZZ, VFR, beneath Class B at 1000 ft and circumventing ZZZ2 [military] Class D airspace to the southeast, when I got a traffic alert. I spotted a C130 to my right, about 500 feet above and 2000-3000 feet horizontally. In watching him and turning out of his path, I inadvertently climbed to 1260 feet, into the Class B airspace. I immediately descended back into unrestricted airspace.
ASRS:1772587.s: A VFR pilot transiting beneath Class B at 1000 ft received a traffic alert for a C130 and inadvertently climbed to 1260 ft into Class B airspace while maneuvering. The pilot immediately descended back into unrestricted airspace.

ASRS:1772589.n: HNL ATIS [is] so long no one actually listens to it. For the last several years I have listened to HNL ATIS thousands of times. It is the worst and longest ATIS I have ever heard and the ultra-long, droning voice with redundant, useless information creates conditions under which a pilot can't listen to and understand the whole thing even if he tried. I have timed the ATIS broadcast several times and it's always over 2 minutes in length. This represents about 5 NM traveled in a small aircraft, and probably double that in an airliner. Additionally, most of the information is useless or suffers from poor quality control.Examples:-Listing all lighting inoperative for a runway that is closed, in the middle of the day.-Way too much time spent on taxiways out of service.-Duplication of information like 'LAHSO in effect' spoken twice.-'taxiway Relative Humidity out of service' referring to taxiway RH.-'men and equipment working all taxiways and runways' has always been on the ATIS.-'increased bird strike hazard all runways' has always been on the ATIS.Nobody listens to this. I have tried to pay attention to the whole thing and it's damn difficult even on the ground. Last year when there were more runway closures there were events where aircraft overran closed sections of runway and I believe ATIS was primarily to blame.Ideas to make this better:-Get a faster talking robot, or make a human record it (that will eliminate some errors).-Move information that's always on there (like the bird strike thing) to the chart supplement.-Consolidate groups of information, like 'Taxiways closed: B, D, F, RH, RB'.-Maybe make a separate frequency with a 'long ATIS' for out of towners who want to hear about how bad the bird strike hazard is getting.We have a 20 min leg from ZZZ. This ensures that 10% of the flight will be spent listening to HNL's ATIS. Please make the FAA fix this.
ASRS:1772589.s: A pilot reported that the Honolulu (HNL) ATIS broadcast is excessively long, containing redundant and useless information that prevents pilots from understanding critical details. The reporter attributed runway overruns to this poor quality control and requested the FAA to shorten the broadcast by removing static data and consolidating taxiway closures.

ASRS:1772594.n: While troubleshooting an audio squeal at the Captain's cockpit station, ZZZ AMT discovered the AMU in the E/E was overheated. After removing the unit and allowing it to cool off, the AMTs found the rack cooling plugs were filled with a rubber plug. Given that this aircraft was less than 2 weeks old, it was believed that the rack cooling holes were inadvertently left plugged. The ZZZ AMTs misread the plug configuration placard on the rack, and my department did as well. As the [Maintenance] Manager, I allowed the aircraft to depart with the plugs removed. Boeing confirmed on the following day that the plugs should have been installed. The aircraft operated one leg out of configuration before corrective actions were taken.
ASRS:1772594.s: ZZZ maintenance technicians discovered an overheated Audio Management Unit caused by inadvertently left-in rubber cooling plugs on a new aircraft. The aircraft operated one leg out of configuration after the team misread the placard and removed the plugs, which Boeing later confirmed should have been installed.

ASRS:1772596.n: I was working Position X with numerous runway restrictions. Due to taxiway and runway closures we were running 4-8 MIT (Mile in Trail) to our runways we utilize except for Runway XXL which was normal. Due to these restrictions, over feeding an arrival controller happens quickly unless you build space by vectoring and speed reductions. Although this is necessary almost every push now, you begin to get backed up and run out of airspace. ZZZ [TRACON] already does not have much airspace and when you vector almost an entire base leg that is entering the metroplex airspace it becomes congested rather quickly. I was utilizing Runway YYR for as many aircraft that I could from the ZZZ1 Center, Position Y sector. We have had issues getting our spacing from this sector so we have to start taking aircraft off of the arrivals and slow them to make it work. I had assigned Aircraft X, Runway XXC because he was too close to the proceeding aircraft to land Runway YYR. The Controller working Runway XXC was already turning a 25 mile final so I vectored Aircraft X 130 [heading] down the Runway YYR final descending to 5,000 to put them in the downwind. I was also feeding ZZZ2 downwind aircraft to Runway YYR if I had gaps. Aircraft Y was one of these aircraft and turned to a 310 descending to 060 for right downwind to Runway YYR. I kept working and noticed the CA on both aircraft and immediately intervened by climbing and turning away Aircraft X. Aircraft Y also got a descent to 4,000. Closest proximity was 500 FT and 1.7 miles. I was in my airspace the entire time but the controller working YYR was so busy that he did not see my aircraft descending to 5,000. Aircraft X was not in a good place to begin with. I usually stop these vectored aircraft at 7,000 so I assume the other Controller was just not expecting anyone there at 5,000. We have an incredible amount of traffic with very little staffing. We should certainly keep the staffing the way it is for COVID-19 for the safety of the facility personnel. The issue is the amount of concrete we have at ZZZ available to us. We are constantly doing things out of the norm that could potentially cause an error. I could have handled this better by stopping at 7,000 or 8,000.
ASRS:1772596.s: An arrival controller vectored Aircraft X to 5,000 feet while feeding Aircraft Y to Runway YYR, resulting in a 500-foot vertical and 1.7-mile horizontal separation. The controller attributed the conflict to high traffic volume, limited airspace, and the landing controller's failure to notice the descent due to workload.

ASRS:1772597.n: I was working Ground Control and Controller in Charge position. I was over seeing the operation when I noticed the Cessna on landing roll when the RV was almost over the threshold on the same runway. I ordered the Local Controller to send the landing RV around. The Local Controller refused. I again ordered the Local Controller to send the RV around because there was not 3,000 feet between the Cessna on landing roll and the landing RV. Again the Local Controller refused. Runway separation was lost and a runway incursion occurred.This is a controller judgment issue not a system issue. This controller continuously puts aircraft under his control and other controllers aircraft in danger on a daily basis. Nothing is being done about it. I recommend decertification.
ASRS:1772597.s: The Controller in Charge reported a runway incursion when a Local Controller refused orders to send an RV around a Cessna on landing roll due to insufficient 3,000-foot separation. The reporter attributed the incident to the Local Controller's poor judgment and recommended decertification.

ASRS:1772599.n: I was working all positions combined in RADAR. Traffic started to pick up far more than what we have had over the past few months due to COVID. Aircraft Y was level at 10k westbound and Aircraft X was east, inbound ZZZ out of 11 for 2500. I saw the traffic and turned Aircraft X 15 degrees left to maintain separation from Aircraft Y. I thought the turn would have been enough for 3 miles and degrees of divergence but ended up not being so. At the closest point I had 2.87 laterally and 800 ft. We went from a slow COVID season to busier than normal with a lot of crossing traffic.
ASRS:1772599.s: An air traffic controller managing combined radar positions issued a 15-degree left turn to Aircraft X to maintain separation from westbound Aircraft Y at 10,000 feet. The maneuver failed to provide adequate spacing, resulting in a minimum separation of 2.87 miles laterally and 800 feet vertically due to increased crossing traffic.

ASRS:1772614.n: I was operating flight to ZZZ. The weather was good and after detecting inadequate fuel planning and requesting additional fuel we departed on time and flew the filed flight plan. We were clear direct to ZZZZZ. Our ATIS was showing that we were expecting to land on Runway XX left.Knowing it was early in the morning we did anticipate a possible runway opening of either XX right or XY. When we were about three minutes from ZZZZZ, We were given the instructions to depart ZZZZZ on a heading to intercept the XY localizer. Although we had planned for the possibility of XY, this was a fairly abrupt and last-minute instruction from ATC. As briefed, this falls under the 'slam dunk' which was is always a threat, as I briefed for departure.We departed ZZZZZ on the assigned heading and began to set up for the intercept of the XY localizer. We were given a descent to 9000, then very quickly a decent to 6000, then a speed reduction to 170 and then briefly after that another speed reduction to 160 (until 5 out). All of this seem to happen in [a] very quick sequence. I was set up to intercept, set up to descend and began to slow down According to our instructions.We established our self on the ILS [Runway] XY without incident but when I realized that we needed to slow down, I called for flaps 22 'out of sequence.' (Typically flaps 22 is called with 'Gear Down'). I had already called for flaps nine, and just naturally called for flaps 22 knowing I needed to slow down.My First Officer (FO) followed the command and put in flaps 22. I naturally look down and scanned my instruments as I always do after a change command and I immediately realized that we were above the 200 knot threshold. I immediately took action - I pressed in the TCS (Control Steering) button, pitched up and began to slow down. As quickly and as safely as I could I brought the aircraft under the 200 knot limitation and completed the rest of the flight without incident.Upon landing I called my dispatcher, explained what happened, maintenance came out, they completed a full inspection and downloaded the information from the airplanes computer. We swapped airplanes so that the inspection could be completed and by the time we landed in ZZZ1, I had heard back from the maintenance supervisor. He told me that the inspection was completed no defects were found and the airplane was returned to service.I detected the problem. I always do a brief scan during critical phases of flight to confirm that the command and input was followed. So I did my scan after calling for Flaps 22 and immediately realized the error. I did not alert FO, as it was not necessary and I simply made the adjustments to the pitch and speed by using the TCS button. I feel there were 2 factors contributing cause to this event. The first was the additional time we had to spend on considering our planned fuel situation. This was definitely an added concern that both FO and I collaborated on before we even left the gate. Then, as Runway XY was opened and we received the 'Slam Dunk' vectors onto the ILS XY, was a second major contributor to this situation. My suggestion as to how to avoid this situation is to simply avoid the 'slam dunk' vectors. Had I asked for better vectors, I'm certain that this situation could and would have been avoided.
ASRS:1772614.s: The flight crew operating a flight to ZZZZZ received abrupt "slam dunk" vectors to intercept the XY localizer, leading to an out-of-sequence flaps 22 command above the 200-knot limit. The captain immediately corrected the speed using the TCS button, and a subsequent maintenance inspection found no defects.

ASRS:1772615.n: The flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ was dispatched under our new fuel management program. The 1 hour and 25 minute flight was dispatched with planned fuel of 5830 lbs. The FO and I both noticed and mentioned that the landing fuel numbers were very low for our standard operation. The NAV Log section of the release showed 1,829 lbs. which is planned fuel minus taxi and fuel burn. But the fuel calculation section showed 1,660 lbs. This concerned both the FO and I, as such a long flight with very little fuel to be landing with. We both discussed that the airplane was [under] fueled by at least 200 lbs. Therefore we both felt landing with 2,000 lbs. or worst case scenario 1,800 lbs. was low but a safer and acceptable number. The performance manual shows around 1,700 lbs. at 5,000 ft. is around 45 minutes of fuel. Knowing our fuel was tight, we did what we could to help conserve fuel by delaying the second engine start as long as possible, and we attempted a Flight Level Change climb by several and normal intermediate level off altitudes with only 7 miles in the opposite direction. We continued to monitor our fuel burn. Upon our initial descent, we noticed we had burned more than planned, but we had received a shortcut and still calculated landing with around 1,800 lbs. On a few turns before final, the right fuel gauge began to flash amber at us then continued to flash in and out as fuel moved around throughout the final approach. Upon landing, we had around 1,800 lbs. of fuel. I feel this margin of safety is extremely low for a safety conscious airline and program. The fuel management program should be providing us with more fuel not less fuel. We were [under] fueled and received no undue delays and were proactive in managing and conserving fuel. Our end result was landing with 1,800 lbs. of fuel. In a medium case scenario, if the airport shuts down for an aircraft emergency or anything else, a go around diversion to the closest company destination (ZZZ2 is 78 miles away), say 25 to 30 minutes at 8,000 ft. (1,100 lbs.), would have me landing with 400 lbs. of fuel and I would have had to make that decision immediately. ZZZ3 is the next closest at 117 miles. That is also if those stations both have personnel staffed to service the aircraft. While legal, and probably acceptable, this practice seems to create an unreasonable reduced margin of safety standards with the trade-off being cost savings. In addition, as a Check Airmen and experienced pilot, I have more wherewithal to be neurotically monitoring developing situations, and weather. I can see an average pilot easily being forced into a no-win situation or very unsafe situation with dire outcome.[We] detected and attempted to manage [the issue] upon review of the release and even with proactive measures, the aircraft still landed with an uncomfortable amount of fuel. [We] took proactive fuel burn reductions with no changes in landing fuel. The airline's new fuel management program and a lack of safety margins created by the program [were contributing factors].I suggest changing the standard practice of providing 45 minutes of cruise fuel from flight level altitudes and provide the crew with an accurate and manageable 45 minutes of fuel near 10,000 ft. which is where most people will need that extra fuel in the case of holding, delays, reroutes and diversions which more likely occur below the flight levels. Add fuel and increase the amount of minimum fuel required to be on the airplane for dispatch.
ASRS:1772615.s: The Captain and First Officer reported that a new fuel management program under-fueled their ZZZ1 to ZZZ flight, resulting in a landing with only 1,800 lbs of fuel. They attributed this low safety margin to the program's calculation errors and inadequate reserve requirements for potential diversions.

ASRS:1772628.n: Approximately 3 hours into flight a group of 3 passengers would not comply with the Flight Attendant instructions regarding wearing their face masks. She notified us and we told Dispatch of the situation and their seat location. Shortly after, they became belligerent to the flight attendants and continued [with] non-compliance. Now they were using foul language and disrupting other passengers. The Captain asked one of the foreign language speaking flight attendants to go try and deescalate the situation but that only made things worse. We looked in the Flight Operations manual and technically this was a threat level 1. We discussed whether should we notify Dispatch and we agreed by the definition it was, but we did not really think this was anything other than a couple of intoxicated passengers. The Captain got on the PA and addressed the cabin of the importance of wearing the mask. After this announcement we had no further trouble with these passengers. They apologized to the Flight Attendant as they exited the plane in ZZZ.Mask requirements in cabin, possible intoxication, lack of respect for airline rules. As soon as the Captain made the announcement this problem went away. Maybe we should have tried that sooner.
ASRS:1772628.s: Three intoxicated passengers refused to wear masks and became belligerent during cruise, escalating after a flight attendant attempted de-escalation. The Captain addressed the cabin via PA, which resolved the issue, leading to the passengers apologizing upon exit.

ASRS:1772633.n: On approach into ZZZ Runway XXR, the Captain called for Flaps 1. The slats extended as expected. Shortly thereafter Captain called for Flaps 2. An ECAM message appeared and flaps had not moved at all. We followed ECAM procedures to no avail. Several miles out, we went around to diagnose the problem with the aircraft and requested priority handling. We ran the ECAM [procedure] and landing data as required then flew a zero-flap approach to an uneventful landing and roll out. The Captain notified Operations and filled out the logbook as required. Two weeks later I received a call from the gatekeeper looking for information on the event. I turns out Maintenance said they could not find a problem and signed off the logbook. The next day the following crew had the same issue flying into ZZZ1 according to the gatekeeper.
ASRS:1772633.s: During approach to ZZZ Runway XXR, the crew encountered a flap failure after selecting Flaps 2, triggering an ECAM message. They executed a go-around and landed safely with zero flaps, but maintenance failed to identify the cause, and the issue recurred for the next crew.

ASRS:1772669.n: After getting on the aircraft to fly, I did all my pre-flight duties including putting my personal luggage away and doing my safety checks. Just before we were ready to board, the flight crew including myself, was notified that someone had tested positive for COVID-19 from the inbound flight. We were later told that it was a passenger who tested positive for COVID-19. After waiting and many phone calls by the ground management as well as the pilots, it was decided ground personnel would clean the area where the customer had sat more thoroughly than just the tray table areas. The passenger was said to have been sitting in row X that tested positive. The cleaning personnel who wipe down the areas cleaned row X and the surrounding 6 rows behind it as a precaution. They then did it again because the cleaning solution being used says on the directions that it must sit for at least XX minutes on the surfaces being cleaned to properly be effective. Once the cleaning process was finished and completed, we boarded the flight and went on our way.The safety concern here is that there is no protocol for this exact situation and possible exposure. Our whole working crew and whatever ground personnel who entered the plane post flight are possibly exposed to this virus. I personally work in the affected area of the row. I sat in the row waiting for answers as to the protocols on what we were to do next. I touched all overhead bins around row X, the bathroom, bulkhead working station, and all surrounding areas that all could have been affected by this customer who tested positive. It's also not known if this customer had affected any other parts of the cabin and if this virus is on surfaces of the plane in more than just row X and the area of the aircraft that all the crew had to walk on to get on the aircraft.
ASRS:1772669.s: Cabin crew reported potential COVID-19 exposure after a passenger on the inbound flight tested positive, requiring extensive cleaning of row X and surrounding areas before departure. The reporter highlighted a lack of specific protocols for such events, noting that crew members touched potentially contaminated surfaces like overhead bins and the bulkhead while awaiting instructions.

ASRS:1772679.n: I did not remove my mask to during demo to show oxygen mask use because passenger in X1, was eating and I cannot socially distance while he was not wearing a mask. I did not feel safe removing my mask because of risk of COVID exposure. He wasn't wearing a mask while I was in close proximity to him.I recommend not removing face mask during oxygen demo. We touch shared safety cards in the seat back for the demo and then directly touch our masks to remove to demo the oxygen mask. There is no opportunity to sanitize in between touching dirty, shared items before touching our masks which are supposed to be done with clean hands. This is unsafe during a pandemic and can spread COVID.
ASRS:1772679.s: A cabin crew member did not remove their mask during the oxygen demonstration due to a passenger in seat X1 eating without a mask, creating a perceived COVID exposure risk. The reporter recommends keeping masks on during the demo to avoid touching shared safety cards and then their face without sanitizing.

ASRS:1772689.n: Engine oil pressure maxed out during flight. Requested ATC to direct me to nearest airport. ATC sent me to ZZZ1. I landed safely. In light of this event, I believe the FAA should not exempt club aircraft from the same maintenance schedules required by training/school aircraft. A law should be implemented that aircraft for rent, for example, through a club, should require the exact same maintenance requirements as training/school aircraft. In talking with the owner of the plane, owner and his son both knew there was an engine oil pressure [gauge] issue, but allowed me to rent his plane and fly it. I noticed [gauge] was slightly high during run-up. The needle went full deflection after reaching cruise. I believe this situation could have been avoided if the [club] came down harder on aircraft owners to maintain their planes. It should be mandated to impose stricter maintenance schedules on club planes for rent. The airplane owners in the club have very little incentive to spend the money to keep the planes properly maintained, beyond the annual inspections. Pilots suffer due to owner thriftiness.
ASRS:1772689.s: The pilot reported engine oil pressure maxing out during cruise in a club aircraft, despite the owner knowing of a gauge issue. The pilot diverted to ZZZ1 and landed safely, attributing the event to inadequate maintenance enforcement for rental aircraft.

ASRS:1772698.n: I was planning to fly from the ZZZ airport to my home on the lake a distance of approximately 5 NM. I was solo, and did a weight and balance and determined I needed 45 pounds of ballast in the nose anchor compartment, and confirmed it was there. The winds were very light out of the south and I took off on Runway XX and turned towards my home. I went to do a 'splash and dash' on the lake before going to the house so after climbing to about 500 ft. I reduced power and did my pre-water landing checklist. On touchdown I immediately did a water loop with no injury to me or any other property, and minor damage to the plane. I must have let the nose get too low, and possibly was hit by an unnoticed boat wake. Since I had lake specific recurrency training on [Date] and [Date1], have done [Number] water landings, [Number1] in the last year and [Number2] in the last 90 days I do not know what else I should have done.I did notify the tower that I had a problem and was heading back on the water to the seaplane ramp. They called the fire department and asked them to launch a boat to assist if needed. When I got to the seaplane ramp their launch vehicle, trailer, and boat were on the left side of the ramp. I tried to call the tower to ask them to have the equipment moved, but could not raise them. I then tried to get up the right side of the ramp, and the right main gear went off the ramp and was damaged. I feel personnel should not block runways, taxiways, or seaplane ramps when trying to help.
ASRS:1772698.s: A solo pilot flying a seaplane from ZZZ airport to a lake suffered minor aircraft damage during a water landing, likely due to a low nose attitude or boat wake. Further damage occurred when the right main gear went off the seaplane ramp while avoiding emergency response equipment blocking the area.

ASRS:1772704.n: At ZZZ, an uncontrolled airport, my student and I had just landed. We cleared the runway and taxied to Runway XX for another lap in the pattern. Making appropriate radio calls, we searched for traffic and then lined up on Runway XX. To our surprise, there was an aircraft on the runway at the other end. It was too late to move by the time we realized the aircraft, some type of business jet, was taking off. We heard no radio calls from this aircraft either before or after the event. We knew that we were on the correct frequency because we heard comments from the other aircraft also waiting to depart Runway XX. The departing aircraft flew directly over us as we sat in position at the numbers XX.
ASRS:1772704.s: A pilot and student lined up on Runway XX at uncontrolled airport ZZZ while a business jet took off from the opposite end without radio calls. The jet flew directly over the stationary aircraft, which had cleared the previous runway and was waiting for departure.

ASRS:1772718.n: Departed FCM on a VFR climb to the south. Climbing through 2,300 [feet] we saw an object (looked like and aircraft) we assumed an aircraft potentially on downwind for Runway 28L at FCM. We adjusted our flight path to pass to the right of the object. No indications on ADS-B. As we got closer we were able to identify the object as a large drone with 4 rotors. The drone was stationary as we flew pithing 2,000 feet horizontally. We immediately reported this to the FCM Tower.
ASRS:1772718.s: A VFR pilot departing FCM encountered a stationary four-rotor drone at 2,300 feet while climbing south. The pilot adjusted course to pass the object, which lacked ADS-B indications, and immediately reported the incident to FCM Tower.

ASRS:1772737.n: I signed in to work, and went to get the person out of positions at Sector X. The CPC who was working had just gotten someone else out 5 minutes earlier, which added to the confusion in my opinion. During all of this, I was not wearing my eyeglasses because they fog up badly when I wear a mask for COVID. I received a quick briefing, and during the briefing, I vaguely heard Sector Y tell the Controller who was working to 'start the Aircraft X down to FL310.' Then I recall hearing a straight descent to FL310. I was unable to really scan accurately because I could not see any data blocks. Anyways, the briefing completes, and I sit down and put my glasses on and start working and scanning. I answer a landline call or two, issue a few clearances, then look at Aircraft X who was now FL390 for FL310. I notice that it looks like it will be close with an aircraft level at FL350, so I call Sector Y and asked them what they want me to do with the two planes and that I had just sat down. After some back and forth, they told me to stop the guy at FL360.Well, the first Controller at Sector X should have never given a pilot's discretion clearance to FL250. Secondly, we're supposed to comply with the SOP with ZZZ Center Sector Y, which would have the Aircraft X crossing the boundary AOB FL310, this was never done.I believe all of the relief briefings had a part to play with the lack of communication in this scenario. Another aspect which compounded this all is that I wasn't able to wear my glasses due to the fogging up issue. I wasn't able to properly scan before I really sat down because I trust the members on my crew.
ASRS:1772737.s: An Air Traffic Controller at Sector X reported a potential conflict between Aircraft X and another aircraft at FL350 due to a relief briefing error and the Controller's inability to scan data blocks while fogged glasses prevented vision. The incident resulted from an improper pilot's discretion clearance and failure to follow SOPs for crossing the boundary at FL310.

ASRS:1772739.n: This is a general safety concern. We landed and departed during a time of limited visibility which, for us, was a period of approximately 3 hours. First off, the Tower controllers did an excellent job but it was obvious they were task-saturated. A single Controller was working Tower/Ground/Clearance frequencies with an inability to visually see aircraft on approach and while taxiing. The weather conditions were simply too overwhelming for one Controller to safely keep track of arriving/departing aircraft as well deconflicting taxiing aircraft. Again, phenomenal job by the controllers, however, was the risk necessary to continue the single Controller operation of the airport? In my opinion, no, and it would be unfair to blame the Controller if an incident had occurred.Forecasted poor weather should mean extra manning of ATC facilities. One Controller [was] working Tower/Ground/Clearance during low visibility operations.
ASRS:1772739.s: A pilot reported that during low visibility operations, a single air traffic controller managed Tower, Ground, and Clearance frequencies while unable to visually track aircraft. The reporter concluded that this staffing level created an unsafe risk due to controller task saturation and recommended extra manning for such weather conditions.

ASRS:1772743.n: Climbing out of ZZZ, at approximately 18,500 feet, we heard a muffled bang and felt yaw. The engine instruments indicated the number two engine EGT was near zero, and it was no longer producing thrust. I asked the FO to tell ATC we required a level off at FL190, and requested priority handling. I then directed the FO to read the QRH Engine Failure or Shutdown checklist.We asked ATC for return vectors to ZZZ. The landing runway was Runway XX, and strong, gusty winds favored this choice. We relayed number of souls onboard and fuel remaining to ATC.After the Engine Failure checklist was complete and the engine was secured, I spoke with the FAs, immediately followed by a brief PA to the passengers. I told them the number two engine has failed, we're returning to ZZZ, and we should be on the ground in 10 to 15 minutes.The remaining 'clean-up' checklists went well, and to my knowledge all steps were completed. We were a bit rushed due to our proximity to ZZZ. In hindsight we should have asked for slightly extended vectors to give us more time, as the approach brief was glossed over. Although it was clear VMC and we were familiar with the airport, it would have been best to do a standard brief. Also, I should have considered restarting the engine, as there was no abnormal vibration, but just occasional slight buffet. We made an uneventful, under max weight, Flaps 15 landing.The rescue trucks met us with one on Taxiway 1, north of the far end of Runway XX, and another group, I believe on the Apron near the fire station. We easily exited the runway on Taxiway 2X, and we told them we did not need any assistance, but to follow us to the gate. ATC and Crash Rescue were flawless. They were helpful, did not interfere, and followed up where necessary.Other agencies also contacted us in a professional manner, and we spoke to them in turn: Dispatch, Maintenance, Operations team, Chief Pilot, and [other] Management. Preflight and takeoff were without incident until climb through 18,000 feet. As the aircraft was climbing through 18,000 feet. I felt an abnormal airframe vibration along with thumping sound that seemed to come from the right side of the airplane (lasting a few seconds). Within a few seconds the #2 Eng Fail indication appeared accompanied with a roll back and aircraft yaw. Almost immediately the 'A' Flight Attendant called up and inquired if everything was okay. I informed her we lost the #2 engine, and we would call her back. The Captain told me to call ATC [and advise them] and get vectors back to ZZZ. We accomplished the Engine Fire or Engine Severe Damage or Separation Checklist as we began our descent back into ZZZ. The Captain briefed the Flight Attendants and informed the Passengers about our situation. During our descent, we encountered occasional airframe vibrations. We also completed the One Engine Inoperative Landing Checklist on the way into ZZZ. The Captain flew a visual approach backed up with the ILS to Runway XX. After landing we taxied to the gate (IAW Brake Cooling).
ASRS:1772743.s: The crew experienced a number two engine failure with yaw and vibration at 18,000 feet while climbing from ZZZ. They returned for an uneventful landing on Runway XX after securing the engine and completing checklists, noting they should have requested extended vectors for a better approach brief.

ASRS:1772744.n: 150,000 pounds at pushback. Pushed straight back off Gate XX. Started both engines. Did checklist and released brakes for taxi. Plane wouldn't move. Added power, no movement. Increased N1 to 40%, plane would not move. Figured we were chocked or brake stuck. Had Ramp Agents come out and check if we were chocked. They believed mains were below the lip of ramp. They suggested to add more power. I shut both motors down and had them go get a Tug. They discovered both mains were in storm drains. We pushed plane back 10 more feet. Started up and taxied out.Suggestion - Have ramp in ZZZ be aware of storm drains.
ASRS:1772744.s: The flight crew attempted to taxi a 150,000-pound aircraft from Gate XX but found the main landing gear stuck in storm drains. Ramp agents confirmed the gear position, and the aircraft was successfully pushed back 10 feet by a tug to clear the drains before taxiing out.

ASRS:1772747.n: BNA is in desperate need of a Ramp Controller. On this flight, we had four airplanes pushback simultaneously, unnecessarily crowding the alleyway. I wish I had paid closer attention to which gates had pushed, but we pushed, in essence, tail 'NW at a 45' from Gate XX, another aircraft pushed from the opposite side of the alley effectively blocking us in, and then two aircraft pushed off the end of the terminal effectively blocking the both of us in. All this while there was an aircraft waiting on the south side of the terminal trying to get into the alleyway. We are setting ourselves up for failure (late pushes, delayed departures) or worse yet, an incident or accident. And this was day VMC. Add a few additive conditions and we are in trouble.
ASRS:1772747.s: The pilot reported that four aircraft pushed back simultaneously at BNA without a Ramp Controller, causing the alleyway to become blocked and trapping their aircraft. This uncoordinated activity in day VMC created a risk of late departures or a potential ground incident.

ASRS:1772750.n: Arrived at appropriate report time. Flight planned and then proceeded to COVID test site. Test extremely unpleasant. Results took XX minutes. Had to call Operations and delay the flight, fortunately a cargo flight today, so no passenger connection issues. Departure was XY minutes late. This could result in crews rushing in the future. Please have someone review testing procedures and timeliness of receiving results. Forward as you see fit.
ASRS:1772750.s: A crew member reported a delayed cargo departure caused by an unpleasant COVID test and slow result turnaround. The pilot requested a review of testing procedures to prevent future crew rushing due to such delays.

ASRS:1772753.n: After I aligned the aircraft with the gate, I noticed the chocks were in position. I then transferred my attention to the Marshaller providing positive guidance. Smoothly and slowly approaching the Marshaller's stop signal, I felt a slight bump - after that the Marshaller gave me abrupt opposite direction guidance and then simply the stop guidance, and shook his head. I spoke to the Gate Agent in the jetbridge who concurred with my description of the event and informed me that he saw the right portion of my nose gear hit the chocks. FO inspected the nose gear and did not notice any damage, I called Maintenance Control to report a precautionary discrepancy (because I could not enter it myself at the point). I described to them what happened.
ASRS:1772753.s: The pilot reported that while aligning with the gate, the aircraft's nose gear struck chocks, causing a bump and prompting the marshaller to signal a stop. A First Officer inspection found no damage, but the pilot reported a precautionary discrepancy to Maintenance Control.

ASRS:1772754.n: We are supposed to run our [specific equipment] to reduce COVID exposure, yet I was flight planned with [specific equipment] inoperative. When I queried the Dispatcher why it was dispatched that way, his response was 'I don't know.' I refused the aircraft.After refusing the airplane the Dispatcher stated [I] was to speak to Flight Operations. The Dispatcher also had me talk to Maintenance to confirm I 'understood the nature of the MEL.' This sounds a lot like pilot pushing to me.
ASRS:1772754.s: The pilot refused an aircraft dispatched with specific equipment inoperative, despite a requirement to use it for COVID exposure reduction. The pilot attributed the situation to pilot pushing after the Dispatcher claimed ignorance and required the pilot to consult Maintenance regarding the MEL.

ASRS:1772766.n: During my third flight back after a 7 month absence (first flight back into ZZZ), I forgot to call the ramp prior to parking at Gate XXX, one of the exterior gates. I believe ground control cleared us 'taxi to the gate' or a similar clearance, and I simply forgot that I was supposed to call Ramp Tower. Taxed into gate without ramp clearance. The self park was green with wing walkers. It is a short taxi from Runway XXR.
ASRS:1772766.s: The pilot, returning after a seven-month absence, taxied to exterior Gate XXX without calling Ramp Tower despite believing Ground Control cleared them to the gate. The aircraft entered the gate without ramp clearance, though the self-park light was green and wing walkers were present.

ASRS:1772774.n: Climbing out of ZZZ on the ZZZZZ2 RNAV Departure. The departure lists the fix ZZZZZ as cross at or below. As monitoring pilot I was waiting for the hand off from Tower to Departure. Tower was busy handling other aircraft, and sometimes they hang on to you a little longer than normal. My mind was fixed on listening for the hand off, and wondering why we didn't get it. Not to mention I am brand new to the aircraft and have not flown much in the last several months. I finally decided to switch to Departure on my own and about that time I noticed the autothrottles retarding. I realized what had happened, the flying pilot had overlooked the level off and we crossed the fix 600-700 feet high. I contacted Departure and we continued the flight without further incident.
ASRS:1772774.s: The monitoring pilot reported that while climbing on the ZZZZZ2 RNAV departure, the flying pilot overlooked a level-off restriction at fix ZZZZZ, causing the aircraft to cross 600–700 feet high. The crew contacted Departure after the autothrottles retarded, and the flight continued without further incident.

ASRS:1772790.n: Currently in ZZZ COVID-19 is spiking. Employees in breakrooms and offices are breathing unfiltered/unclean air. Installing HEPA filters in all employee breakrooms and offices will clean up the air and mitigate exposure to our employees.
ASRS:1772790.s: The reporter states that employees in ZZZ breakrooms and offices are breathing unfiltered air during a COVID-19 spike. Installing HEPA filters in these areas is proposed to clean the air and mitigate employee exposure.

ASRS:1772792.n: On [date] two ramp employees came into the breakroom, neither had a mask on...they both stood close to me.
ASRS:1772792.s: Two unmasked ramp employees entered the breakroom and stood close to the reporter. The narrative describes this proximity as a potential exposure risk but does not state any specific outcome or cause beyond the lack of masks.

ASRS:1772793.n: There is no social distancing being enforced at ZZZ lobby and people are at risk of contracting COVID-19 and most importantly our employees are being exposed day in and day out. The company is not doing enough to protect us from contracting this virus.
ASRS:1772793.s: Cabin crew reported that no social distancing was enforced in the ZZZ lobby, exposing employees to COVID-19 risk. The reporter stated the company is not doing enough to protect staff from contracting the virus.

ASRS:1772801.n: Aircraft X apparently hit a set of stairs on pushback with their right wing tip unbeknownst to the crew or Marshaller. A ground crew member saw it and called it in to his supervisor, who called it in to the Ops (Airport Operations). The plane at this point was on takeoff roll and wasn't in contact with Ops via radio anymore. After getting airborne, Ops took it into their own hands and called Tower and told them to have the flight return to field. I received an message from the crew asking why the return to field, which is when I started to make calls. This happened while the crew was at 3,000 feet and turning around. Crew landed uneventfully and the plane was taken out of service with visible damage to the right wingtip. No request was issued for a return to field as I felt in the short time frame, and with how busy the crew would have been setting up an unexpected approach, that it would have been unsafe to add more to their workload. Operations staff need to be fully aware of their limitations in regards to operational control of flights. Perhaps there needs to be a rapid communication procedure for the ground personnel, as they had to make several calls to get the information to someone who could have made a difference quicker. After we took off and checked on with ZZZ Departure Control we were advised by the controller that Company wanted us to return to the airport. Upon questioning, the controller did not know the reason. I sent an ACARS message to our Dispatcher advising of an air turn back and asked why. His response was that he didn't know but would find out. We set up for the return to ZZZ and landed uneventfully and taxied to parking. Upon aircraft shutdown and secure a ZZZ maintenance representative met us inside the cockpit to advise us that the right wingtip possibly came into contact with a set of crew stairs during block out. We took a look at the wing and there was some minor damage to the right outboard leading edge slat just inside the right navigation light. At all times during the block out we were under the guidance and direction of the marshaller. Appropriate logbook entry made and reports submitted by both myself and First Officer. Reflecting upon blocking out, after engine start we cleared the mechanic and ascertained immediate area left and right were clear, I signaled the marshaller across the ramp and on the nose that we were ready to taxi out. We were marshaled straight out into the alley and given the signal for a left turn into the alley followed by a wave-off and salute. During the initial block out taxi roll, the First Officer mentioned the crew stairs seemed close, but from my position the stairs did not appear to be encroaching on the taxi lane and I continued to follow the marshaller's instructions. All marshaling signals were consistent with the aircraft being clear of any obstacles, and at no time did the marshaller give us a stop signal during the taxi out, nor did we feel any bump from the right wingtip possibly making contact with the crew stairs. I do not know if there was a wing-walker on the right wing due proximity of ground equipment between our aircraft and the aircraft to our right. I do recall a white ramp vehicle was encroached in the clear area to our right as we were blocking out, but the vehicle backed up out of the way. Recommendations: wing-walkers, all ground equipment clear, equipment safe boxes painted on the ground around the aircraft like in ZZZ1.
ASRS:1772801.s: During pushback, Aircraft X's right wingtip struck crew stairs unnoticed by the crew or marshaller, causing minor slat damage. Airport Operations ordered a return to the field after the aircraft was airborne, leading to an uneventful landing and removal from service.

ASRS:1772846.n: We got our IFR clearance from ZZZ Tower about 30 minutes prior to departure. We were surprised that ZZZ Tower closed shortly after getting our clearance, at XB:00 p.m. we taxied to the runway and made position announcements on the CTAF. After takeoff we contacted ZZZ Approach at about 1,500 feet AGL. Approach informed us that we should have gotten an IFR release from them on the ground. We need to remember to get an IFR release for departure from Approach Control if the Tower closes after issuing our clearance. In ZZZ, I called ZZZ Clearance and received our IFR clearance to ZZZ1 at approximately XA:30 p.m. local time. After a slight ramp delay, we pushed back around XB:10 p.m. The Tower at ZZZ closes at XB:00. We made all our CTAF calls and took off in clear VFR conditions. I checked in with departure at 1,400 feet. At that time Departure let us know we did not get our IFR release on the ground.I recommend once a Tower closes, even with a clearance received prior to closing, always contact Departure on the ground prior to departing and pick up your IFR release to destination. The cause was some confusion with already receiving the clearance and picking up the release after the Tower closed. Lesson learned is as described above, once Tower closes you need to pick up your clearance from Departure prior to taking off.
ASRS:1772846.s: The pilot received an IFR clearance from ZZZ Tower before it closed, then took off and contacted Departure at 1,400 feet. Departure informed the crew they lacked a required ground IFR release, causing confusion because the Tower had closed after issuing the initial clearance.

ASRS:1772848.n: During climb after departing ZZZ, we experienced light clear icing, which began around 12,000 ft and ended around 20,000 ft. During this time, we noted STALL PROT ICE SPEED status message displayed, as well as the WING and both ENG BLEED VALVE OPEN advisory messages displayed. Roughly around 24,000 feet and still climbing, we experienced a master warning EICAS message (A-I WING 1 LEAK). The FO was flying, so I asked him to maintain control of the airplane, and to handle the radios while I ran the QRH checklist. The checklist drove us to press the wing ice protection button out, which we did. Almost immediately the EICAS message disappeared from view. I brought up the ice protection schematic on my MFD, and verified the wing valves were closed. We continued and completed the checklist.We exited icing conditions around 20,000 feet, and it appeared that clear skies were ahead and above us. We decided to continue the flight and landed safely at ZZZ1.We decided that icing conditions were not forecast or reported on our WSI app along our route of flight. We also could not see any apparent icing conditions ahead. With this in mind, ultimately I decided that we could continue the flight safely to ZZZ1. I also did not feel that this warranted an in-flight call to Dispatch and Maintenance, however, I did call maintenance control after we reached the gate at ZZZ1. I informed the controller what we experienced, and we both agreed that a discrepancy no longer existed and therefore did not make an AML entry. At the end of our day, I made the next Captain aware of our event verbally when we got to ZZZ2.I wish that I had taken a picture after the wing valves were closed on the ice protection schematic on my MFD. I think we handled the situation well as a crew, and we both agreed that we could continue the flight safely.
ASRS:1772848.s: During climb after departing ZZZ, the crew encountered unforecast clear icing between 12,000 and 20,000 feet, triggering an A-I WING 1 LEAK warning. Following the QRH, they deactivated wing ice protection, which cleared the message, allowing them to land safely at ZZZ1 without filing an AML.

ASRS:1772850.n: Applied full power for takeoff on [Runway] X, engine static RPM went to 2250 but then dropped 300 rpm and went back up. Engine abnormality. Crew made decision to abort takeoff and exit [Taxiway] X1 on taxiway 2. Wrote up the aircraft.Monitor engine instrument during all critical phases of flight.
ASRS:1772850.s: The flight crew aborted takeoff on Runway X after engine static RPM dropped 300 rpm during full power application. They exited via Taxiway X1 to Taxiway 2, grounded the aircraft, and recommended monitoring engine instruments during critical phases.

ASRS:1772856.n: Upon arriving at MSO airport on [Date] at approximately XA:00 the winds were not favorable to execute the ILS to RWY (Runway) 12. The weather conditions to perform the RNAV GPS D were alternating between ceiling and visibility going below minimum conditions. We were communicating with Dispatch along the way and were discussing diverting to our first alternate, which [was] Billings (BIL). The ceiling and visibility at MSO was above minimums at time of arrival. We started the RNAV approach with a circle to land on RWY 30. After crossing the final approach fix at 6,800 ft., and descending to our MDA of 4,700 ft., we started to have some ground contact. The FO (First Officer) said that he saw the PAPI lights to the right of us. The approach did not allow for us to circle to land northeast of RWY 12/30. The only way to commence the circle was to fly over the airport and circle around to the west. We briefly discussed circling to the west and quickly decided that it would be unsafe to circle around the airport at night in low visibility with LLWS (Low Level Wind Shear) conditions in mountainous terrain. During the decision making phase I had inadvertently disconnected the auto throttle. We continued to the missed approach point. As we went around I had realized that the MAP fix was not in the box. As we looked at the approach plate and quickly made a climbing left turn on a heading of about 340. We asked ATC for a heading while we headed in the proper direction. Once WENKE was back in the box we realized we were right on course.At approximately 8,000 ft. we were back in radar contact and was giving a vector off the final approach course. ATC asked us if we wanted to commence another approach or divert to a different airport. After discussing the conditions that we saw and weather forecast to be deteriorating, we unanimously decided that it would be unsafe to conduct a circle to land night approach based on the current weather and forecasted conditions.We then told ATC that we were going to divert to BIL. We sent ACARS message to Dispatch telling them we were diverting as well. After landing at BIL, Dispatch told us that we were to refuel and proceed back to MSO. Dispatch then said the weather was not good enough to go back and was delaying our departure. After waiting about an hour Dispatch said the winds were improving and we should be able to do the ILS RWY 12 back into MSO. We departed BIL for MSO with BIL as our alternate if we could not get in. We executed the ILS to RWY 12. While in Billings we contacted ATC and they told us at that time that they did not have radar until about 8,000 ft. The controller said that he was not working at that time but discussed with the previous controller that we were right where we were supposed to be and we said we just were at a high work load and wanted to verify with them that we were on course.High workload with low ceilings, LLWS, at night in mountainous terrain. Having to circle with visibility below what was projected and inadvertently disconnected auto throttles to land.I feel like this approach is not a safe approach to do at night. I spoke with several carriers that land at this airport and this approach is not authorized.
ASRS:1772856.s: The crew diverted from MSO to BIL after deciding a night RNAV circle-to-land was unsafe due to low ceilings, LLWS, and mountainous terrain. High workload led to inadvertent auto-throttle disconnection and a missed approach, prompting the diversion despite Dispatch's initial request to return.

ASRS:1772861.n: Please read MEL 24-XX-XX and apply (O) action #2. This morning on a first flight of the day at XA15 we received paper work for Flight XXXX ZZZ to ZZZ1. I reviewed the paper work and noted 2 MELs. One for the coffee pot and the other for a TRU (Transformer Rectifier Unit). I reviewed the log book and noted that everything had MCNs and appeared correct. I then proceeded with the acceptance inspection. Once the acceptance was complete I looked up the MELs to familiarize my self with them. The coffee pot MEL was complied with correctly. The TRU MEL was complied with correctly as well. After reviewing the MEL with my First Officer we then proceeded with the rest of the gate work, checklist, and departed. While en route I decided to re-read the MEL and learn a bit more about the write in the log book. I came to the conclusion that the MEL did not apply to the write up. The write up said 'DC Service Bus still shows powered when no power is applied to the aircraft. Nav Lights are still on, Placarded and Placed on MEL.' The MEL (24-XX-XX) was applied and the service TRU was MEL'd. When the (O) action #2 was applied per the MEL however the Essential Tie is closed manually and DC Service Bus was re-energized via the Essential TRU2. This did not solve the problem stated in the write up. Once we landed in ZZZ1, I contacted Dispatch and Maintenance and we all agreed that the MEL was inappropriate for the discrepancy in the log book and the aircraft was taken out of service. The complexity of the electrical system and the rarity of MELs used on it played a factor in missing this at the gate as well as the early morning and pressure to get out on time.
ASRS:1772861.s: A pilot and First Officer departed with an MEL for a TRU, but later determined the MEL was inappropriate for the DC Service Bus discrepancy. The aircraft was taken out of service after landing because the MEL action failed to resolve the issue, attributed to system complexity and departure pressure.

ASRS:1772869.n: First flight in Aircraft X. We programmed the FMS with the intended runway for departure. Upon taxi clearance, we had a runway change of [Runway] XX. When we changed the runway the FMS deleted our fixes in between our departure and arrival. We proceeded to program the FMS again with all fixes and found no further issues. Next issue was our following flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2. We programmed landing into ZZZ RNAV Y XXL. Instead of showing the landing runway on FMS and MFD, it showed the missed approach point of ZZZZZ. Once reaching that point, two EICAS messages displayed. Vertical mode off and lateral mode off appeared with no FMA modes active. We also lost guidance from ZZZZZZ to the runway. We are unsure if in a missed approach guidance would be active if needed. Once we landed the EICAS messages went away and no further issue. Programming the FMS [for the next flight], performance data showed us landing with 4,100 lbs of fuel. Once we started engine 2, we received a message to check fuel reserve with indicated landing fuel of 2,500 lbs. We stopped at hold short line of Runway XXL to further diagnose. We found the climb page showing us climbing at a speed of 138 knots (V2) to TOC (top of climb). This showed us taking a total of 43 minutes to TOC, which should have been 20 minutes. We tried to program the climb speed and switch to manual to see if it would recalculate but it did not work. We were above our planned fuel and calculated our fuel burn manually to find we would be safe to begin the flight. Once we advanced our power, it recalculated our landing fuel to our projected 4,100 lbs. No other issues came of this flight.
ASRS:1772869.s: The flight crew experienced FMS failures on Aircraft X during taxi, approach, and pre-flight phases, causing lost fixes, mode disengagement, and incorrect fuel calculations. These issues were resolved by reprogramming the FMS, manually verifying fuel, and advancing engine power to trigger correct performance data.

ASRS:1772882.n: Near top of climb we had an intermittent ENG 1 OIL LO PR Amber Caution message which became a steady RED Warning message. I performed the ECAM (Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor) actions and follow up for the message which included shutting down the engine. The Captain [advised ATC]. We landed without further incident.I don't know what caused the indication but we had multiple indications which led us to believe it was not an erroneous indication and resulted ultimately in the engine shutdown per the ECAM.I believe it was a mechanical issue but I was unable to find a clear procedure for what to do for an intermittent (or even steady) ENG 1 OIL LO PR Amber Caution message with other supporting indications. Having a discussion in training about unusual/non standard situations would be helpful insight. ATC was very accommodating and we found it helpful to have ATC provide us a separate frequency to communicate with Tower and ARFF (Aircraft Rescue Fire Fighting) simultaneously. ARFF was very responsive and communication was excellent. It was a seamless process on final approach with our requests.
ASRS:1772882.s: The crew experienced an intermittent then steady ENG 1 OIL LO PR warning during climb, leading to an Engine 1 shutdown per ECAM procedures. They attributed the event to a likely mechanical issue and landed safely with support from ATC and ARFF.

ASRS:1772902.n: Crew was descending into ZZZ Airport at about [night] time. Weather revealed winds 350 with good visibility and MVFR conditions. With the higher winds out of the north, the crew elected to fly the RNP Approach which requires the PAPI to be operational to fly the approach. A review of the NOTAMs revealed this would not be an issue, though the REIL was out of service to this runway. Icing conditions on the approach prompted to crew to conduct a flap full landing with ice numbers. Additionally, Tower mentioned that they would be closing just prior to our arrival. The Captain, myself, briefed the autothrottles would be disconnected on the arrival, with the autopilot off once established inbound. I disconnected the autothrottles and left the autopilot on as briefed. We continued to configure through the landing checklist and saw the runway on the approach. Once we rounded out on final, I disconnected the autopilot and began slowing to our approach speed when the lights at the airport clicked off. I briefly shallowed the descent anticipating the possibility of a go-around and had my First Officer turn the lights to high which failed to bring the PAPI back online. Being VMC and within required company parameters for a safe approach, I inquired to my First Officer if he was comfortable with continuing under the conditions which he was. I corrected descent angle and the flight landed without any further incident.This was the flight crew's first time flying this approach, my first RNP approach in a while, and my fourth night landing in about 2.5 months. This RNP Approach requires the PAPI to be operational to use. With there being no PAPI NOTAM, it was determined that it would be appropriate to fly it. After we had landed we found that the Tower, attempting to enable the pilot controlled lighting, had inadvertently switched all lights off. This was corrected with my First Officer turning the lights back on but the action failed to turn the PAPI on. The ATIS had called for gusty winds out of the north but, once we were established on final, I noticed we had a quartering tailwind at 15 kt. which caused me some confusion. The light issue and shifting winds prompted me to shallow out the approach due to the possibility of a go-around. However, with the airport lights on minus the PAPI and in VMC conditions, I figured the safest course of action was to continue given the fact that we were within parameters required to continue the approach and land. My thinking was a go-around late at night, in mountainous terrain and icing conditions with a possible changing weather pattern, may not be the best idea given we were still within tailwind parameters and touchdown requirements for landing. To me, this incident illustrates how important it is to appropriately manage [non-forecasted] distractions, especially during high workload phases. Additionally, it's imperative that we strive to remain current even during prolonged periods of stagnation.When weather is in vicinity, ensure [that] the most accurate weather is obtained from Tower if necessary. Relay concerns of airport issues to ATC or go-around. Be wary of Tower closures near arrivals to airports. A reminder that higher elevation airports present unique challenges which must be reviewed and briefed prior to flying into them. A reminder to chair fly approaches to destination airports, especially if the approaches you intend to follow are unfamiliar. The importance of maintaining appropriate approach currency. Speed management and adequate monitoring during all flight phases. A reminder to fly the airplane first and, if mounting distractions cause confusion, go-around. I briefed the descent and approach with Captain, Captain as pilot flying. Reviewed FMS approach briefing card. Verified all NOTAMs and approach requirements per the chart and current ATIS. Both First Officer and Captain acknowledged Runway End Identifier Lights were inoperative, [but was not] not required for approach clearance. Received approach clearance from Approach. Tower closed while just outside the FAF with acknowledgment from Tower on Tower frequency of no traffic in the area on frequency and no issues to report from the last reported ATIS. Broke out from IMC to VMC conditions before the FAF. Acknowledged 'runway' by First Officer and 'landing' by Captain. Clicked the CTAF frequency 5 times by [the] First Officer to assure lights would remain illuminated while on final, [as] requested by [the] Captain. Runway lights removed from view while just past the FAF.Then, [the] First Officer clicked 5 times on CTAF frequency again, after [the] Captain asked about the runway lights turning off, both runway lights illuminated again. Moments later we both acknowledged that we didn't see the PAPI to the left. CA (Captain) asked if I found the circumstances to land safe versus a missed approach late at night and snow in the forecast. [We] agreed it would be safe to land given the real time circumstances. Upon landing with no issue, Tower Controller got on CTAF frequency to apologize that they configured the runway lighting incorrectly, which is why it turned off momentarily. The First Officer reported the PAPI was also not working when lights returned. [The] ATC Controller reported on CTAF, 'That is weird;' and would be reporting it to airport operations. Great example in how reality and goal for safety require pilot judgment.
ASRS:1772902.s: The flight crew descended into ZZZ Airport at night in icing conditions when Tower inadvertently switched off all lights, including the PAPI, while attempting to enable pilot-controlled lighting. Despite the light failure and shifting winds, the crew continued the RNP approach in VMC and landed safely after confirming the situation was within operational parameters.

ASRS:1772914.n: We were navigating between coordinates at FL410 and M.80 assigned. We received a CPDLC clearance that said, 'Resume normal speed'. We reviewed the Europe Jeppesen Airway Manual section entitled 'Operations Without an Assigned Speed' to review this relatively new procedure. After agreeing on what it meant we accelerated to M.83 and advised ATC at XA:03z via CPDLC 'Present speed .83'. ATC responded at XA:13z with 'Do you want M.83'. We responded, 'Received normal speed CLNC and advising our speed is .83'. At XA:17z ATC sent, 'You may want to read up on that. Resume normal speed means plus or minus mach .01 from cleared mach.' We immediately changed speed to Mach .81 and replied, 'Roger speed now is .81 requesting M.83' (XA:18z). At XA:19z ATC sent 'Maintain .83M'. All communications were done via CPDLC. The rest of the flight was uneventful. We disagree with the controller's interpretation of the 'Resume normal speed' clearance and request clarification from the company. Page 668 of the Jeppesen Airway Manual (Europe) says, 'If the aircraft then receives RESUME NORMAL SPEED (via CPDLC or Voice), the flight crew no longer needs to comply with a previously issued Mach. However, the flight crew shall advise ATC if, as the result of the RESUME NORMAL SPEED message, they intend to adjust their speed by plus or minus Mach 0.02 or more from their last assigned speed.' Furthermore, in the operational example given on page 688 it says, '...message RESUME NORMAL SPEED will be sent. The flight crew no longer needs to comply with a previously issued Mach. However, the flight crew shall advise ATC if, as the result of the RESUME NORMAL SPEED message, they intend to adjust their speed by plus or minus Mach 0.02 or more from their last assigned speed. In this case, with a previously assigned speed of .81, they must inform ATC if the flight either slows to M.79 or less or speeds up to M.83 or more.' Finally, in the North America Jeppesen Airway Manual it says, ' When adherence to an assigned 'MACH' setting is no longer required, pilots will receive a controller-pilot data link communications (CPDLC) message to 'RESUME NORMAL SPEED;' at which point the flight crew can continue at their cost index. Refer to aeronautical information circular (AIC) 1/20 Operations Without an Assigned Fixed Speed (OWAFS) in the North Atlantic for more details.' In looking at the ICAO NAT OPS Bulletin (2019_001), the text mimics what is published in the Jeppesen Airway Manual. In conclusion, I believe we were in full compliance with the 'Resume normal speed' clearance when we accelerated to M.83 and advised ATC but since the controller has a different understanding of the situation I would like to get clarification from the company.
ASRS:1772914.s: Flight crew at FL410 accelerated to M.83 after receiving a CPDLC "Resume normal speed" clearance, citing Jeppesen manuals. ATC disputed this interpretation, claiming the clearance required staying within ±M.01 of the assigned speed, leading to a speed reduction to M.81 before ATC later authorized M.83.

ASRS:1772916.n: While performing the Before Takeoff checklist the Master Caution sounded and the EICAS message W/S 1 HEAT FAIL appeared. Flight crew completed QRH. Captain contacted company Dispatch and Maintenance and attempted to troubleshoot the issue, but the message remained. Flight returned to gate.
ASRS:1772916.s: The flight crew encountered a W/S 1 HEAT FAIL EICAS message during the Before Takeoff checklist. After troubleshooting failed, the aircraft returned to the gate.

ASRS:1772922.n: I was Pilot Flying for a normal departure from ZZZ. Takeoff was normal, but just after the Pilot Monitoring called acceleration altitude we received the EICAS: BAGGAGE DOOR OPEN. We finished the climb flow, contacted ATC for delay vectors, and then I took over the radios as the Pilot Monitoring began the QRH. As we accomplished the QRH we noted the cabin altitude was climbing rapidly and determined we would return to ZZZ. We accomplished our remaining checklists and set up for an uneventful approach and landing. After we returned to the gate one of the ramp crew informed us he had seen that the baggage door 'didn't look right' and he had cycled the latch and closed the door again. We called Maintenance who found no defects. When Maintenance was finished, we continued our flight uneventfully. It may be beneficial to train ramp crews not to touch or interfere with a door until instructed in a return to gate or return to field scenario. After talking with Maintenance we both agreed it would have been much easier to determine the cause if Maintenance would have been able to see the door before it was cycled.
ASRS:1772922.s: The Pilot Flying reported a baggage door open warning after departure from ZZZ, causing a rapid cabin altitude increase and a return to the gate. Ramp crew subsequently cycled the latch before Maintenance inspection, preventing defect identification, though the flight later continued uneventfully.

ASRS:1772925.n: It was the Captain's leg on a return flight from ZZZ when we were given the ZZZZZ3 SID. We were given a standard take off clearance from Runway XXL (no heading, altitude, or fix to fly) and I, as the pilot monitoring, engaged the autopilot modes as directed. When I engaged the NAV mode, it did not arm FMS but instead HDG mode. After double-checking I correctly engaged NAV mode, we were still in HDG with the only white needle navigation being from ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1 and then on the rest of the departure. Since we were still in HDG mode with what I remember was runway heading bugged, we were heading directly for the terrain off of the departure end of XXL. We received hasty instructions from ATC to turn left immediately to get away from the terrain, which we complied with. We were in VMC and could clearly see the terrain, which we had already climbed above when the instructions from ATC came through to start the immediate turn. We never received a GPWS terrain alert. Once established heading back to ZZZZZ on the departure, the Captain had disengaged and reengaged the NAV button to finally arm FMS mode. ATC then advised us to resume the departure and continue our assigned climb altitude to 17,000 feet. No further communications between us and ATC about what had happened. The rest of the flight went on normally and without incident. Really make sure on RNAV departures that when you select the NAV button that the FMS mode activates and if needed spin the heading bug to the headings provided on the charts to avoid conflicts like this.
ASRS:1772925.s: During departure from Runway XXL on a return flight, the crew inadvertently flew in HDG mode toward terrain because the NAV mode failed to arm the FMS. ATC issued immediate left turn instructions to avoid the terrain, after which the crew successfully re-engaged FMS and resumed the climb to 17,000 feet.

ASRS:1772928.n: We were following a heavy 787 on departure from NRT on 34L, and were quite heavy ourselves (405,000 lbs or more). Vref 30+40 was 215 KIAS and Vref 30+80 was 255 KIAS, so we had to use the airspeed tape F bug to retract Flaps 1, approximately 241 KIAS. Turbulence from the 787's wake struck as we retracted Flaps 1, causing the airspeed to increase faster than the AP (autopilot) could compensate, and because of the small margin between 241 KIAS and the 250 max for Flaps 1, I disengaged the AP to gently pitch up in order to not exceed 250 KIAS until the flaps were up. The clacker went off for less than a second before the flaps fully retracted and we continued with a high-speed climb out of 265-270 KIAS (we had requested and were approved for high-speed by ATC when we retracted Flaps 5 to 1) and flew normally down to ZZZZ. I wrote up the flap overspeed, which lasted less than a second and did not appear to exceed 252 KIAS until the flaps had fully retracted, and informed maintenance after landing.
ASRS:1772928.s: A heavy aircraft departing NRT on 34L encountered wake turbulence from a preceding 787 while retracting Flaps 1 at 241 KIAS. The pilot disengaged the autopilot to prevent exceeding the 250 KIAS limit, resulting in a brief flap overspeed warning before continuing a high-speed climb.

ASRS:1772931.n: The crew departed ZZZ on time after calling maintenance to reset a Rudder Trim Limiter ECAM malfunction. Pushback, start, taxi, takeoff and climb out were uneventful. Passing FL260 for a cruise altitude of FL270 the First Officer (Pilot Monitoring) identified a flashing oil quantity advisory reading and a low oil pressure indication on the #1 engine system display. Due to the aircraft's momentum and vertical rate of climb the Captain (Pilot Flying) elected to level off at FL270 as planned. Initially the zero oil quantity and low 60 PSI pressure indication were not accompanied by an ECAM message and system status indicated normal. Within a couple of minutes a series of intermittent ECAM cautions and warnings occurred leading to an engine shutdown condition. The amber ENG 1 OIL LO PR Caution illuminated first on the ECAM display. The crew responded by initiating the company non-normal checklist strategy.
