The Captain announced 'my aircraft' then the First Officer verified that the ECAM was not a Quick Action or ECAM exception item. The Captain elected to remain flying and also took control of the radio. It was a crew awareness only caution so the FO (First Officer) then checked the QRH for follow up items. This Caution does not direct the crew to adjust thrust settings. During this process the caution [message] cleared itself without any inputs from the crew but the zero oil quantity and 60 PSI indications remained. At this point the ECAM display was clear and system status indicated normal. Shortly thereafter the red ENG 1 LO PR warning illuminated on the ECAM display. This occurred intermittently 3 times and then cleared itself each time resulting in a normal system status display on the ECAM. Oil quantity remained at zero and pressure was now steady at 40 PSI on the system display. These intermittent ECAM warnings lasted for approximately 2-3 seconds and then cleared to a normal status for roughly the same amount of time. The next time the ECAM warning illuminated it remained steady and the crew followed the ENG 1 LO PR warning procedures and shutdown the engine. The crew notified Center and requested a radar vector descent to final for the engine out approach at ZZZ1. The non-normal indications initially occurred just prior to the ETP (equal time point) between ZZZ and ZZZ1. However by the time the ECAM directed engine shutdown the flight had progressed passed the ETP and was at a normal descent point for ZZZ1. Dispatch was called using the iPad crew phone and notified of the nature of the emergency and decision to land at ZZZ1. The flight attendants and passengers were briefed about the Precautionary Landing at ZZZ1 and the possibility of airport fire vehicles near the aircraft. After shutting down the engine and notifying ATC, the crew requested and was given a vector and descent direct to a left 10 NM base at ZZZ1. Descent and approach were very stable and normal. The Captain flew the descent and approach with both the autopilot and auto thrust on. Crew requested ARFF (airport rescue fire department) for the landing and cleared the runway for a brief inspection of the engine. On request of the crew the fire department followed the aircraft to the gate. Shutdown at the gate and passenger deplaning were normal. Note: ATC handling by ZZZ Center, ZZZ1 Approach and Tower were outstanding. Handoff from Tower to ARFF at ZZZ1 was seamless and well coordinated. Flight Attendant performance was also outstanding and the passengers remained well informed throughout the emergency. Although oil fault indications were somewhat intermittent and erratic the fact that multiple independent sensors indicated a problem caused the crew to shutdown the #1 engine when directed by the ENG LO PR Warning ECAM. After the flight, maintenance personnel initially reported normal engine oil quantity on a sight gauge even though the engine instrument remained at zero. Initially crew suspects a partial blockage or pump failure in the system without oil loss. The engine oil quantity and pressure indications were initially both alarming and confusing. As the adrenaline level increased for the crew due to the perception there would be an engine shutdown there was also a level of doubt that the indications were accurate. Low oil pressure on the engine instrument should be accompanied by a Low Pressure ECAM Caution or Warning. Why did the pressure remain steady in the amber range with zero on the quantity? This is an uncomfortable situation because our training does not address multiple oil failures without ECAM warnings. It puts the flight crew into one of those gray areas where a Captain is expected to make a decision based on the information he has on hand in a situation not covered in training. The natural instinct of a pilot is to shutdown an engine before complete oil loss to prevent a catastrophic failure. In this occurrence engine indications identified a problem well in advance of ECAM warnings. Yet crew training and aircraft procedures generally do not address engine shutdown without ECAM warning checklist direction. Should crews be given shutdown discretion in the absence of ECAM warnings and checklist? In this situation the Captain elected to continue as the Pilot Flying while the crew worked through the non-normal checklist strategy. Even though most aspects of company's non-normal strategy were performed correctly the overall pace and structure were hampered by the Captain continuing to fly. In this case the checklist strategy would have been better managed if the Captain had delegated flying to the FO. For example, when the ECAM directed the 'Engine Master Switch-Off' both pilots confirmed it was the #1 engine but the Captain positioned it to off. Procedure dictates that the non-flying pilot position the switch to off.
ASRS:1772931.s: The crew of a flight departing ZZZ experienced intermittent #1 engine oil quantity and pressure indications that eventually triggered an ENG 1 LO PR warning, leading to an engine shutdown and precautionary landing at ZZZ1. The reporter attributes the event to sensor discrepancies and notes that the Captain's decision to continue flying hampered checklist management during the emergency.

ASRS:1772963.n: Passenger X was removed for testing positive for COVID virus. Plane was not deplaned and sprayed. Passenger was on board 20 minutes with face covering not covering nose.
ASRS:1772963.s: A passenger tested positive for COVID-19 and was removed from the aircraft after 20 minutes on board wearing a face covering that did not cover their nose. The aircraft was not deplaned or sprayed following the incident.

ASRS:1772967.n: Captain came out to brief FAs. Told us [the] FO was not going to wear [a] mask in cockpit, anyone [have] a problem. I said I did. And would prefer to have him wearing [one] when we [are] in the cockpit. Captain continued to look for another FA to go in the cockpit.My take: If there is no courtesy to me or any of my flight attendants, why should we have to go in the cockpit? When I said I had a problem, he should have backed off. Yet, now he was telling us, he had no problem wearing a mask, but the FO had. Then, later, [the] FO comes out of cockpit not wearing a mask, and proceeds to talk (very close) to a FA standing near him, with no mask on. I reminded him, to go out, he had to wear a mask. He put his mask on.I have a problem with a pilot who does not care about our well being. Our health, our ability to work and stay healthy to support our families, and all that comes with us exposing ourselves. It is not acceptable and it should not be tolerated to continue to ask for a FA to go inside the cockpit when the FO was not going to wear a mask.Today, we had an XX:59 minutes duty day + hour before and hour after wearing a mask. The least he could do is wearing a mask for 5 minutes when one of us goes inside to relieve them. It's intimidating, it's a disregard of others and disrespectful to all FA group, as if we do not matter.This is not company policy and someone should speak with him about caring for his coworkers, or anyone for that matter. Because I bet he is not wearing a mask where he goes. Just unacceptable. I have a problem with a pilot refusing to wear a mask when a FA goes in the cockpit, and whoever is reading this, should too.
ASRS:1772967.s: A flight attendant reported that the Captain and First Officer refused to wear masks while the attendant entered the cockpit, despite company policy requiring it. The First Officer later spoke closely to an unmasked attendant before complying when reminded, creating an intimidating environment and disregarding crew health.

ASRS:1772981.n: During thrust reverser cycling #2 eng inadvertently started causing over temp to 821.5 to 28 seconds. As per MM 71-00-00-800-804-f00, [it] will require boroscope due to temp going into area C of chart. I did not notice that the APU bleed was left on and I did not pull ignition circuit breakers. [I] had 2 techs clearing around engine.
ASRS:1772981.s: A mechanic inadvertently started engine #2 during thrust reverser cycling, causing an overtemperature to 821.5°C for 28 seconds. The incident occurred because the APU bleed was left on and ignition circuit breakers were not pulled, requiring a boroscope inspection.

ASRS:1772982.n: Social distance cannot be adhered to due to lack of spacing. Nothing is setup in the bus to promote social distancing.
ASRS:1772982.s: Cabin crew reported that social distancing could not be maintained on the bus due to a lack of spacing and the absence of any setup to promote it.

ASRS:1772984.n: With the COVID-19 pandemic, technicians are concerned about proper safety with the removal and disposal of HEPA filters. The procedures are consistent with all of company fleet types, including both Manufacturer X and Manufacturer Y aircraft types. All of the AMM procedures include a list of the necessary PPE as well as Disposal requirements.DescriptionSTD-XXXX Coveralls - Hooded STD-XXXY Goggles - Safety, Non Vented STD-XXXZ Respirator - Particulate, meets NIOSH 42 CFR 84 Class N95, N99, N100 The question here is, what qualifications (if any) are needed and where can we find the company policy. The main item is the use of the respirator Class N95 as is called out for in the AMM procedures [for several aircraft types].The second question concerns proper disposal of used HEPA filters and used PPE. Obey the airline policy, local health department and law enforcement regulations when you discard this material. Obey these instructions to prevent injuries to personnel.
ASRS:1772984.s: Technicians expressed concern regarding safety procedures for removing and disposing of HEPA filters on Manufacturer X and Y aircraft during the pandemic. The report questions specific respirator qualifications and disposal policies while noting that AMM procedures mandate N95 respirators and adherence to local regulations to prevent personnel injury.

ASRS:1772985.n: During bus transportation, from the employee parking lot to airport. Social distancing is not being addressed or enforced. Employees are not 6 feet apart and the bus is completely full [to] the point where employees are holding onto the railings. Due to the current spike of COVID-19 in ZZZ, we need to enforce social distancing in the bus area and parking lot.
ASRS:1772985.s: Employees reported that social distancing was not enforced on the full bus transporting staff from the parking lot to the airport in ZZZ. The reporter stated that passengers were holding railings and not maintaining six feet of separation due to the current COVID-19 spike.

ASRS:1773000.n: I was working enroute Center for two hours and 20 minutes with heavy to moderate traffic without the help of a D side. Sector XX. Normally this would not be a problem but during the coronavirus situation there is a skeleton crew of controllers in the area and we are short staffed. Training in the area was also underway. Also, we had no management in the area acting as a Supervisor. We had a Controller-in-Charge position staffed by one of the FPLs in the area. After working 2 hours of heavy traffic I began to tire and was transposing callsigns and missing check-ins.I asked one of the controllers working another less busy sector to swap positions with me. I just could not work that volume of traffic anymore. The Controller was kind enough to swap with me. I was mentally drained. The culture does not generally allow for complaints of this type. After my break (which I am on right now) I will do it all over again. If this continues the risk grows of a Controller contributing to error within the airspace. This is normally not necessary. This is a very busy time of the year and it is unbelievable that the FAA would allow this lack of staffing and allow the normal flow of traffic. This situation routinely happens at ZZZ (Center) in Area X, I am not sure about the other areas, but I have heard similar things from other controllers.
ASRS:1773000.s: An enroute air traffic controller in Sector XX reported mental fatigue, transposing callsigns, and missing check-ins due to heavy traffic, skeleton staffing, and lack of supervision during the coronavirus situation. The controller swapped positions with a colleague to mitigate the risk of contributing to an error in the airspace.

ASRS:1773017.n: Our aircraft had just landed at ZZZ when a single-seat aerobatic biplane began to do low-level aerobatics (hammerheads and rolls) opposite normal traffic in the pattern. A Cessna 150 entered left downwind Runway XX, well spaced from the biplane, which was in a modified right downwind/base, when the biplane crossed the field and entered a midfield left crosswind-to-downwind behind the 150. The 150 continued downwind, turned base then final, when the biplane banked hard from downwind directly to final abeam the 150 and approximately 25 feet above. The 150 initiated a go-around and the biplane did the same, nearly colliding which each other. The 150 eventually landed on a second go-around while the biplane continued to execute high speed low passes over the runway at about 50 feet AGL. The problem likely arose because the biplane, which was NORDO, was engaged in a low level acrobatics display for a group of onlookers in the tiedown area and was not scanning for conflicting traffic. The 150 likely saw the biplane traffic near the airport, but the biplane's erratic behavior and rapid altitude and direction changes would have complicated efforts to maintain separation. The conflict could have been resolved if the biplane pilot refrained from low-level aerobatics in the vicinity of the traffic pattern, was visually scanning for traffic, and vacated the traffic pattern area when other traffic was inbound to land.
ASRS:1773017.s: A NORDO aerobatic biplane performing low-level maneuvers near ZZZ nearly collided with a Cessna 150 on final approach. The conflict occurred because the biplane pilot was not scanning for traffic while executing erratic turns and low passes, forcing the Cessna to initiate a go-around.

ASRS:1773033.n: During a Medevac flight to ZZZ1 from ZZZ I initiated an approach with less than the required RVR to do so. Our return flight had been delayed by 4 hours because the patient was very difficult to stabilize. I had checked the weather before departing ZZZ and it was above the minimums that were required for the approach. While enroute to ZZZ1, I acquired the ATIS and found that visibility had decreased to 1/8 mile. The situation at the two nearest options that would allow me to get the hospital was the same. I chose to go to ZZZ2 because it was near enough that we could get the patient to ZZZ1 and the automated weather was well above minimums for the approach. After two attempts at landing in ZZZ2, I realized that the weather was worse than reported there. While I had been maneuvering I was monitoring the conditions at ZZZ1 and they seemed to vary minute by minute. I decided to divert to ZZZ3 since the medic told me we had no time to waste with another approach as he was running low on medication for the patient. When I requested the change to ZZZ3, the controller asked me if I wanted to attempt an approach to ZZZ1. After two go around and working on my fifth backup plan, I was desperate to get the plane on the ground and the patient to the hospital. I accepted the clearance and started the approach. I saw the runway lights at 400 ft AGL and the runway at 200 ft AGL. I decided to land. As I was rolling out I noticed that ground visibility was very low and I realized I had landed with less than the required 2400 RVR that I was supposed to have. Contributing factors: I had the weather and forecast from when I left ZZZ1 6 hours prior printed out. I should have reviewed the forecast more thoroughly rather than just checking present conditions before returning to ZZZ1. I did not realize that night that I was getting sick. During the climb out I was queasy and I attributed this to a lack of horizon at night. The next day I had full flu like symptoms that precluded me from working. What I would do differently: I should have asked the medical team where they wanted to go if ZZZ1 did not work out. If I had that we could have all been prepared to go to a different hospital if the ZZZ1 airport did not work.
ASRS:1773033.s: The pilot of a Medevac flight landed at ZZZ1 with less than the required 2400 RVR after multiple diversions and go-arounds. The incident was caused by the pilot's failure to review updated forecasts, deteriorating weather, and undiagnosed illness that impaired decision-making.

ASRS:1773034.n: VFR instrument currency flight at ZZZ on RNAV GPS Runway XX with safety pilot. When outbound to ZZZZZ IAF at 3,300 MSL and entering the course reversal saw airspace indicated on GNS 530. I realized the floor of ZZZ C airspace was 2;X00 MSL and penetrated airspace. I Immediately descended to 2;Y00 MSL and continued the course reversal at that elevation and completed the practice approach. Traffic display from ADS-B did not show any traffic conflict while at 3,300 in ZZZ C airspace. Lack of flying in past 6 months due to COVID limits contributed to reduced situational awareness and unfamiliar with this area and airspace. Flying more and better use of EFB charts would have corrected this situation.
ASRS:1773034.s: A pilot conducting a VFR instrument currency flight with a safety pilot penetrated ZZZ Class C airspace at 3,300 MSL due to reduced situational awareness from inactivity. The pilot immediately descended to 2,900 MSL to comply with the airspace floor and completed the approach without traffic conflict.

ASRS:1773038.n: ZZZ Tower was closed due to mandatory cleaning when a Controller tested positive. The airport was operating under CTAF frequency. We got the ATIS after pattern work at ZZZ1, then decided to shoot the RNAV XX, with the winds reporting 300 @ 12 knots. We contacted approach and got vectors for the RNAV XX. After being switched over to the CTAF frequency from Approach, we heard multiple aircraft utilizing Runway XYR. With the traffic using Runway XYR we decided it would be best to circle to Runway XYR, since a circle to Runway XYL is NA per the approach plate. When reaching circling minimums and within the circling radius we began to circle east of the field on a left base to Runway XYR. This required us [to] cross over the extended centerline of [Runway] XYL. We flew the rest of the pattern and landed with no incident or traffic conflict. Additionally, no traffic was in the pattern for [Runway] XYL at the time and no traffic was affected by this decision.I believe that the other traffic using Runway XYR instead of Runway XX (based on what the wind was calling) was a huge factor. My student and I were concerned on entering right traffic for Runway XYR and overflying the field roughly 1,480 MSL/600 AGL feet above and potentially creating a traffic conflict for those operating on [Runway] XYR. This is what drove us to make left traffic for Runway XYR. I was flying the RNAV XX into ZZZ with CFI (Certified Flight Instructor). ZZZ Tower was closed early due to mandatory cleaning after Controller tested positive for COVID-19. Airport was operating under CTAF frequency. After checking ZZZ ATIS after pattern work at ZZZ1, the decision was made to shoot the RNAV XX into ZZZ as winds were 300@12. Contacted Approach, who granted us the approach clearance. Upon switching to ZZZ CTAF, it became clear that traffic was using [Runway] XYR/L despite the winds favoring Runway XX. We made the decision to break off the approach at CAT B circling minimums and circle to [Runway] XYR as a circle to [Runway] XYL from RNAV XX is NA per the approach plate. This required us to cross over the extended centerline of [Runway] XYL. We circled east of the field and entered a left base for Runway XYR and proceeded to fly a normal pattern with no incident or traffic conflict.If we were to fly right traffic instead for Runway XYR that would have required us to cross midfield at 1,480 MSL (approximately 600 FT AGL), which could create a potential conflict for traffic on go-around/missed. Rather, we elected to essentially perform a circle [Runway] XYL with a sidestep to [Runway] XYR (as the circle to land [Runway] XYL from [Runway] XX is NA). Additionally, no traffic was affected by this decision.
ASRS:1773038.s: A pilot and student flying an RNAV XX approach at ZZZ Airport, where the tower was closed due to COVID-19, broke off the approach to circle to Runway XYR. They crossed Runway XYL's extended centerline to avoid potential conflicts with traffic on Runway XYR, landing safely with no incidents.

ASRS:1773053.n: I am a contract pilot and an on-call simulator instructor on the various Falcon EASy airplanes. The PIC is an experienced large airplane pilot. His current experiences are on numerous types of Boeings, etc. He became the manager/pilot of the subject -900EASy and has roughly 6 flights with this aircraft, most with me. His type training was about 3 months ago and he did not fly the airplane until roughly 1.5-2.0 months after his check ride (guesstimate). I have been providing SIC support (until the other full-time pilot can accomplish his type training) as well as IOE on the airplane and especially on the EASy avionics. The pilot's 'airliner avionics' background has generated system misunderstandings that I have corrected. This includes incorrect use of Flight Guidance selection choices. While arriving on the STAR into ZZZ we were advised to 'descend via the STAR'. The Captain highly prefers to use VNAV for virtually all climbs and descents and as he was selecting such I was reprogramming our waypoints for altitude crossings. The Captain then questioned me as to 'how best to set up the VNAV function'. I explained various ways to do so, i.e. VNAV versus minimum altitude to select, using the vertical profile 'laser pointer' to start the descent or to use for constant descent without stair-stepping through crossing altitudes, how to change the descent angle utilized on the FMS avionics page, etc. However, after some time I noticed that the VNAV was not capturing and that the 'laser pointer' was moving away from the target setting, i.e. waypoint selected for crossing. This happened a few times. I even showed him how to do a 'Direct Vertical Descend To' but it also did not work. The Captain was complaining about the EASy system compared to the Boeings he flies and couldn't understand why it was not capturing. During this time I was acquiring the ATIS and setting up for the approach to be utilized. However, when I once again noted that we were still not descending correctly I stopped doing my functions and spent more time analyzing the situation. That is when I noticed that the airplane was west of the intended course (I would guess about 4-5 miles). I then informed him that somehow he had lost LNAV guidance. As such, the VNAV would not be correct. Although he asked me to now give him direct to the waypoint I told him he instead needed to rejoin the arrival and advised him to use HDG (heading) or TRCK (track) to perform a turn back to rejoin. He said he understood but I noticed his confusion and delay in doing so. I again advised him that he needed to get back on course and almost simultaneously ATC noticed our discrepancy. Because of our course deviation we did not descend accordingly. As such, ATC gave us a direct to ZZZZZ and cross at 10,000. I performed the 'direct to' and advised the Captain to start an immediate descent which he slowly did, however, the eventual angle was high and as such the airspeed increased. He complained about the increasing speed and I told him that he needs full airbrakes to check the speed increase (twice). He looked confused and delayed the extension of the airbrakes until the speed had already climbed, i.e. he now had to reduce the speed he had allowed to increase during the initial descend maneuver. Therefore, we exceeded the 250 knots below 10,000 feet for roughly 600-700 feet (I think we were back at 250 before 9,300 ft.) The remainder of the flight was uneventful. I should note that during a post debrief the Captain was noting how only one person should be touching the guidance panel. He was, in my opinion, somewhat deflecting responsibility for the loss of the LNAV function (after I asked him if he knew how we lost LNAV guidance). However, I did not manipulate the panel. I pointed to what and where he needed to go for his choice of modes. This is especially true during the initial mistake. Although I cannot guarantee my thought I think that the Captain inadvertently disconnected LNAV after passingZZZZZ1 while we were setting up for the descent. He has previously chosen the wrong button before, e.g. he once switched guidance to the non-flying pilot during his attempt at setting-up another choice. At that time I saw his action and corrected him immediately (that time I did change the setting myself). It was in a very high workload moment and I did not have the time then to explain to him what he had done. In that situation I needed to get the guidance back to the pilot flying which necessitated a minimum of three button selections. After a little time, and after I had completed what I was doing as the SIC, I attempted to explain what he had done but prior to such he said he understood his mistake so I did not delve deeper into it. Since aircraft traffic in the ZZZ area was light there was no deviations and ATC did not 'appear upset'. However, I felt it important to write this ASRS Report. This Captain is very confident of his methods (he is very experienced) and strives to be as efficient as possible. He chooses to carry the minimum fuel required for a trip, always flies at Long Range Cruise power setting, requests as many short cuts as possible, and wishes to start the airplane moving as quickly as possible after engine starts. As such, he has often questioned me in relation to after start tests that need to be performed for each flight versus those that only need to be performed once a day, or maybe even once a week. He does not like sitting with engines running. Therefore, we are sometimes somewhat in a hurry. Being the SIC and as a contract pilot I have acquiesced to his overall style as it is not illegal or unsafe, although it is not the method I prefer. For a pilot new to an airplane I would recommend that the pilot 'go slow' and diligently learn the process of the new airplane but a pilot's prior experiences can alter that process. This is especially true when the pilot has a vast (many years) experience flying numerous large airplanes worldwide. I have suggested that this Captain fly as the SIC for a bit to truly learn the airplane but he noted that during his training he only got experience in the left seat. His comment was that he wants to become familiar with the left seat before trying the right seat. As the SIC can be busy it is hard for an experienced pilot (in a particular airplane) in that role to provide guidance to an inexperienced pilot (in a particular airplane) while doing both instruction, IOE overview, and normal duties simultaneously. My recommendation is that regardless of experience that a pilot 'to a new airplane' be limited to the SIC duties for a minimum of 5 flights (segments, not hours) before transitioning to the left seat. What is required is the 'muscle and mental memory' performing the numerous tasks associated with the various sections of a flight.
ASRS:1773053.s: A contract SIC reported that an experienced Captain new to the Falcon 900EASy inadvertently lost LNAV guidance during a STAR arrival, causing a course deviation and speed exceedance below 10,000 feet. The incident resulted from the Captain's unfamiliarity with the aircraft's avionics and his preference for VNAV, requiring ATC to issue a direct clearance and the crew to manage excessive airspeed.

ASRS:1773083.n: I was conducting right base to new private airport level at approximately 500' AGL in order to evaluate appropriate traffic flow for the landing site. ZZZ is awaiting final activation in the ADIP (Airport Data and Information Portal) portal system. While in my right turn, a local property owner was conducting legal drone operations. There was not a collision hazard, but the potential for such an event was identified by the drone operator. After engagement with the operator, I agreed to adjust pattern corridor to avoid overflight of the area of concern at low altitude. Prior to further low altitude flight operation in the immediate vicinity of ZZZ I will await final FAA activation of the landing site. I will also engage the immediate community to inform them of flight operations and solicite any additional safety concerns. It was a good learning experience on community engagement and to be more proactive in risk identification/mitigation.
ASRS:1773083.s: A pilot conducting a low-altitude evaluation at 500' AGL near the unactivated ZZZ airport encountered a legal drone operation during a right turn. Although no collision occurred, the pilot adjusted the flight path to avoid the area and will await FAA activation before resuming low-altitude operations.

ASRS:1773101.n: Alternator went out and had radio/communications failure. Guard came on and [asked] if there was an emergency. I informed 'no emergency and we are on short final for Runway X'. Flaps were already down. Landed safely. Called ZZZ Approach to inform that we are safe.
ASRS:1773101.s: The pilot reported an alternator failure causing radio loss during short final for Runway X with flaps down. After confirming no emergency on the guard frequency, the aircraft landed safely and the crew contacted ZZZ Approach.

ASRS:1773121.n: The planned flight was VFR from ZZZ to ZZZ1 via ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 at XA:00 on November [date] 2020 in Aircraft X (Cessna 150) rented from Company. I was PIC, Person Y was the only passenger. We had previously flown Aircraft X on July [date] 2020 from ZZZ, ZZZ4, ZZZ3 and had noted that the passenger door was not closing properly -- a small gap in the upper-left corner of the window frame allowed wind to enter the cabin. The owner of the plane investigated the issue then and found that the upper window frame was bent. I assumed that the issue was fixed by an A&P mechanic after the investigation. The plane has been regularly flown by other pilots since July.On November [date] 2020, I noticed no irregularities during pre-flight. During run-up, I noticed that the gap in the passenger door was still present and was a bit bigger than I remembered it from July. I thought that the slight wind in the cabin would be unpleasant but not otherwise an issue and continued with the flight. During the take-off roll just after rotation, the passenger door swung open. Once we were stabilized on the downwind, I shut the door and reassured my passenger. However the passenger door swung open again -- the wind through the upper-left gap torqued the entire door outward and that overpowered the door latch. So I requested landing clearance from ZZZ Tower and executed a precautionary landing without any incident. I taxied back to parking, shut off the engine and investigated the passenger door. The upper window frame was flexing slightly and could be bent to snap into the correct position. I pushed the frame into the correct position, verified that the frame was now snug against all the door frame inserts and that no wind was leaking into the cabin.I took off from ZZZ around XB:00 and noted no issues this time. As we were transitioning ZZZ3 Class D airspace, my passenger noted that she heard some sound from her door. I verified that the gap in the window frame was not present and that the door was shut properly. Shortly after we flew through the Class D, my passenger also reported that she could feel cold air from near the lower-right part of her door. As we flew past the marina, the door again swung open. This time the door shook violently which caused the window also to be flung open. I requested landing clearance from ZZZ3 was given priority and then I clarified my situation. I noted that reducing the throttle helped remove the violent door shaking. I reached over to shut the door, then pulled the upper window frame back into the door inserts and then closed the window. The ATC alerted me with a low altitude warning, so I decided to ignore the door and climb 300 ft. to intercept the glide slope and fly the plane first. As I increased RPM, the door again flung open. The door was twisting and wobbling around the hinge like a sheet of paper with the hinge as a paper-clip, and either wind or resonant frequency was increasing the severity of the wobbles. My passenger held the door to dampen its shaking. The landing at ZZZ3 was without any incident, and I taxied to a maintenance shop on the field. An A&P mechanic diagnosed that the passenger door needs to be replaced entirely and that the plane was not airworthy. We drove back to ZZZ after ensuring that the owner of Aircraft X knew what had happened and where to find the plane's key.In follow-up communication with the owner, I do not believe that the plane door was inspected and fixed by an A&P mechanic in July. The owner mentioned that he adjusted the door latches and attempted to bend the window frame back into place. This 'fix' ensured that the 'door shut properly 90% of the time'. He mentioned that he drove up to ZZZ3 with a spare C150 door and replaced it -- I do not know that he is qualified to make such repairs. His name does not show up in the airmen registry as holding an A&P license. The owner also mentioned that he was checking the door occasionally and that it had clearly worsened in the lastcouple of weeks and that there is no strength left in the window frame.Based on our conversations, I believe that the owner fixed the discrepancies that pilots reported using methods that are not by the book.(1) Normalization of deviance. I should have canceled the flight after landing at ZZZ after the initial trouble with the door.(2) Normalization of deviance. Owner should have replaced the door in July, rather than waiting for the door condition to get worse and create an [issue].(3) Crew management. I should have briefed my passenger during/after the [event]. She thankfully did all the right things (e.g. dampen the door vibrations) purely on instinct.(4) Aviate & Declare. I did not use 'emergency' or 'mayday' in my communications, despite that, the ATC at ZZZ and ZZZ3 both realized that something was up and gave me priority. Kudos to them. When diverting to ZZZ3, I flew very close to the prohibited airspace near marina to minimize my flight path to the runway.(5) Pre-flight Airworthiness Check. I should have insisted on viewing the maintenance records of the airplane to verify that my previous squawks were satisfactorily addressed.
ASRS:1773121.s: The PIC and passenger flew a Cessna 150 where a bent passenger door frame caused the door to swing open twice during flight due to wind torque overpowering the latch. The pilot executed precautionary landings at ZZZ and ZZZ3, after which an A&P mechanic grounded the aircraft for door replacement, citing improper prior repairs by the unlicensed owner.

ASRS:1773128.n: Maintenance Controller reported miscommunication over an MEL that allowed an aircraft to fly in a non-airworthy status.[Maintenance] in ZZZ called about Aircraft X had a 24 ELEC FAULT GEN INOP message. Several attempted resets with no help. A MEL was mentioned. Initial read through of the MEL and procedures appeared to be able to defer left generator. RTM was not generating any faults related to aircraft for chapter 24 at the time message was present on aircraft. I got dispatch approval and deferred Left generator with [Maintenance] reference log number XXXXXXX. After engine start noticed that RTM had generated a fault for Left Generator 24 ELEC FAULT GEN INOP with a no dispatch under the reference column. Reread the MEL and found an exception for INFO Message 24 ELEC FAULT GEN INOP making it a non-dispatchable MEL with this message. Immediately attempted to contact ZZZ maintenance and the flight crew of the aircraft to prevent Take off. The aircraft had already departed for ZZZ1. Contacted ZZZ1 maintenance about MEL not being dispatchable and that it would have to be fixed prior to departure from ZZZ1. Applied a CAR to lock down aircraft in ZZZ1 on arrival. ZZZ1 maintenance worked the item and was able to repair per A220 FIM and clear log item. To prevent future occurrences a highlight or bullet point in the section of the MEL for not being able to dispatch with that Message. Making it easier to identify message.
ASRS:1773128.s: A Maintenance Controller misinterpreted an MEL exception, allowing an A220 to depart with a non-dispatchable generator fault. The aircraft was locked down at the destination for repairs after the error was identified, prompting a recommendation to improve MEL clarity.

ASRS:1773173.n: Runway 22 in MMPR has a 4 bar PAPI. The trees on final have grown too tall to safely use 1 white 3 red on the PAPI when transitioning to land. This can be seen on approach and also watching landing aircraft. Request MMPR airport operations to trim or remove the trees closest to Runway 22. Add notes to the 10-7 mentioning to fly the 2 white 2 red PAPI to touchdown due to obstructions.
ASRS:1773173.s: A pilot reported that trees on final approach to Runway 22 at MMPR obstruct the 1 white 3 red PAPI indication, making it unsafe for landing. The reporter requested tree removal and noted that pilots should fly the 2 white 2 red PAPI setting to touchdown due to these obstructions.

ASRS:1773176.n: Upon arrival in ZZZZ, we experienced some health and safety concerns. Everyone that interacted with us was in full PPE but the most concerning part was we were followed by a guy that sprayed some chemical into the air around us. Some type of fogging machine - no idea what the chemicals were. They even had another person spray a liquid chemical onto the floor after we walked through customs. (That was the only point where we were actually inside a building). They transported us in an airport bus that also had a strong chlorine smell to it.Arrival at the hotel was like a scene from the movie Outbreak. The entire inside of the hotel is drenched in a white powder substance (probably from fogging) and carpets/floors haven't been cleaned or vacuumed in weeks. Room floors were covered in dust, lint, and other crumbs. Trash bags were all over the hotel hallways. To add to the chemical list, we were even given chlorine tablets to drop in the toilet prior to defecation.Food was delivered to the room as you were not allowed to leave your room during the entire stay. Although we were supposed to have set times for food drop-off, it was never consistent. Coordinating your international sleep around their food delivery was impossible. Some people like to sleep upon arrival at XA:00 pm to catch some of your previous WOCL - in that case your dinner sits outside and potentially spoils.I'm writing this report a couple days later as I still have a slight sore throat that developed during the layover. The Captain has had similar symptoms along with congestion. It's unlikely we contracted COVID as we all tested negative the morning of that trip but do think it could be related to all the chemical/cleaning agents they used around us.
ASRS:1773176.s: The crew reported health concerns during a layover in ZZZZ after exposure to unknown chemicals sprayed by ground staff and chlorine-smelling transport. The reporter attributes subsequent sore throat and congestion symptoms to these cleaning agents rather than COVID-19.

ASRS:1773187.n: I have spent this pandemic sitting reserve and trying to minimize my risk of catching COVID by minimizing my flying. I have family members in my household that have respiratory issues so we all work hard to stay as safe as we reasonably can and we have made many sacrifices this year as a family. Of course on occasion I will get called out to fly, and when I do, I am as cautious as I can be. But I am getting increasingly frustrated showing up in the flight deck with pilots with no regard for the mask wearing recommendations. Also troubling, is learning they are frequenting bars and regularly visiting others. I know individual choice is just that. But I do not understand why we as a company and union have not made it a norm to require a mask, at all times at work, not just for show in front of the passengers. I have a right to feel as safe as I can on the flight deck too. I understand at this point mask wearing is a choice on the flight deck, and it is one that I made. But it should be a requirement. As for arguments about communications issues and oxygen use, I have worn a variety of masks including those provided by the company and have not had any internal or external communications issues and removing an over the ear mask is no more problematic than sunglasses or a headset. They are non-issues that can be managed easily by a professional crew.As the infection rate goes up and we try to spread out the flying among more pilots, this conflict will become more of an issue. It is best to err on the side of caution and safety and just wear a mask at work. All the time. Nurses and doctors wear them all day long and are able to communicate just fine. There is no reason why we shouldn't too.
ASRS:1773187.s: A reserve pilot reported frustration regarding fellow flight deck crew members who ignore mask recommendations and socialize in high-risk environments. The pilot argued that masks should be mandatory at all times during work, stating that communication and oxygen concerns are easily managed by professional crews.

ASRS:1773190.n: I was Captain [on] Flight ABC ZZZ to ZZZ1. We flew the inbound in the same aircraft from ZZZ1, both flights were completely full. In between the flights, I did my setup for departure, and then went to walk the terminal for a moment. What I saw as I left the jetway into ZZZ terminal was a little shocking in today's safety and COVID environment. The end of the terminal had about four flights all trying to load or unload at the same time. The area isn't large but there was at least 1,000 people crammed into the jet way area. No one had room to social distance. Everyone did have a mask on, but it was very uncomfortable. I navigated as well as I could past the crowd as quickly as I could and went much further into the terminal to find an open area. I kept an eye on the loading area from afar but it took a long time to empty the crowd as they boarded. I didn't go back near the gate until about 10 minutes to departure. It was still crowded on my flight and the other boarding planes had crowds around. The jet bridge backed up and our airplane didn't get loaded until just before departure time. I know the agents were trying as best they could, but when that many planes are set to depart at the same time it was difficult. I asked about it and was told that also [another aircraft] had a mechanical and had to de-board all of its passengers into the same crowd as it was awaiting parts.An agent asked our passengers who were at a standstill on the jetway to please get seated quickly, so we didn't have to delay the flight. One passenger said there isn't anywhere to go as the line was just stopped. I feel the management of this boarding process was not well thought out. If flights are departing that close in time they should be spaced in gates down the concourse apart from each other. If this is the operation each day of the week, it should be looked at to see if there is a better way.
ASRS:1773190.s: The Captain of Flight ABC reported severe crowding at the ZZZ terminal jetway where four flights loaded simultaneously, exacerbated by a mechanical issue on another aircraft that forced deplaning passengers into the same area. This congestion caused boarding delays and prevented social distancing, leading the pilot to criticize the gate assignment and boarding management.

ASRS:1773201.n: Captain did not conduct pre-flight briefings per Standard Operating Procedures. Even after advising of the threat that [are] due to COVID, I have not flown regularly at all, and may need a little bit more time or to be watched closely, Captain still skipped virtually all briefing elements. I missed that we did not login to CPDLC and get our departure clearance, which I absolutely would have caught with a proper briefing. When contacting Ground Control, ATC stated it didn't look like we had our clearance. I logged into CPDLC and received our clearance and verified all the elements before departure.
ASRS:1773201.s: The First Officer reported that the Captain skipped pre-flight briefings, causing a missed CPDLC login and departure clearance. The crew contacted Ground Control, logged into CPDLC to receive the clearance, and verified all elements before departure.

ASRS:1773213.n: We as employees are very concerned on the conduct and unsafe work environment that is going on at the ZZZ facility with the COVID precautions. With many of our employees getting sick and even passing away, we have noticed the lack of safety regarding the management of COVID-19. There has been a couple of outbreaks and the company never identified the outbreak area, no Investigation on the outbreak and especially no contact tracing efforts or warnings of contact exposure. The weather is getting colder, the breakrooms are packed with no social distancing and no improvement in the ventilation. This is giving us high stress and anxiety in this work environment.
ASRS:1773213.s: Employees at the ZZZ facility reported an unsafe work environment due to inadequate COVID-19 precautions, including packed breakrooms, poor ventilation, and a lack of outbreak investigation or contact tracing. These conditions caused high stress and anxiety among staff as multiple employees became ill or died.

ASRS:1773222.n: The reason for this report is in regard to the air filters that we have at work. I am looking to see if we can have HEPA filters in the workplace because of the spike in COVID-19 that we are having in ZZZ. These filters will help out a lot with this virus. If the aircrafts have them I believe it's just right to have the airport with them, as well as break rooms and offices. We still have many people at work that don't wear their mask, sneeze out in the open and cough. I witnessed this in the office environment I'm currently in.
ASRS:1773222.s: A ground employee reported a request to install HEPA filters in airport facilities, break rooms, and offices due to a local COVID-19 spike and observed non-compliance with mask-wearing and hygiene protocols. The reporter noted that while aircraft may have these filters, the workplace currently lacks them to mitigate virus transmission.

ASRS:1773249.n: On a flight from ZZZ-ZZZ1, we were cleared on the standard route. Having not flown as much as usual during the COVID-19 pandemic, I tried my best to stay ahead of the airplane where possible. We began performing the brief for the ZZZZZX arrival before performing the climb checklist, and also briefed our eventual landing on [Runway] XXL at ZZZ1. During this time, we reached our cruising altitude of FL220, but did not realize that we had missed the completion of the climb checklist.ATC notified our aircraft that our altitude readout was between 250-300 feet higher than it should have been. This was because we did not reset the altimeter through FL180.The decision to brief the arrival and approach earlier than expected caused a routine checklist to not be performed at the normal time. Altimeters were reset, the checklist was performed, and altitude was corrected. Although staying ahead of the airplane is generally a good idea, don't allow the neglect of standard procedures to be what breaks the barrier to safety.
ASRS:1773249.s: Pilots on a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 missed the climb checklist while briefing the arrival early, causing the altimeter to remain unreset above FL180. ATC reported the aircraft was 250–300 feet high, prompting the crew to reset altimeters, complete the checklist, and correct the altitude.

ASRS:1773317.n: On short final to land Runway XXR we heard a 'too low, flaps' audible warning. As the PM, I saw we were at flaps 25 with a planned flaps 30. I called this out to the First Officer who was the flying pilot as I selected flaps 25 and performed the landing check which we had apparently missed on approach. We made a normal landing. This was our second day in a row of very early flights with wake up calls and 3 time zone changes. While I didn't feel fatigued, I suspect I was more tired than I realized. We had just flown a nearly 5 hour cross country flight with a breakfast of a couple spoonfuls of granola, a couple spoonfuls of yogurt, and a few grapes. This was our company provided meal for the flight. While I normally take responsibility for providing my own food, this is not always possible in the current COVID environment. I believe this was a significant contributing factor. In hindsight, the proper response would have been to perform a go around and set up for another approach. While I don't feel my handling of the situation was unsafe, it was not consistent with company procedures. With reasonable sleep and nutrition I'd like to think I would have made a different decision.
ASRS:1773317.s: During short final to Runway XXR, the Pilot Monitoring triggered a "too low, flaps" warning due to missed flaps 30 configuration and an incomplete landing check. The crew attributed the procedural deviation to fatigue and inadequate nutrition from early flights and time zone changes, though they completed a normal landing.

ASRS:1773320.n: On descent into ZZZ, we momentarily exceeded Vmo by approximately 1 knot for less than 3 seconds. I later completed an AML entry and notified Maintenance Control. There was no operational impact. I was the CA and PF. While on descent into ZZZ, ATC halted our descent at FL240. This put us behind our VPATH solution. When we were next cleared to descend, I elected to go into Vertical Speed Mode, selecting 2000 FPM in order to recapture the VPATH. The task saturation over the next few seconds took my scan away from our airspeed, and we surpassed and we surpassed XXX knots, our 'barber pole' airspeed. I immediately disconnected the AP, overrode the autothrottles and raised the nose of the aircraft. The max airspeed reached [was] XXY knots for a second or two, before returning to green numbers. There appeared to be no adverse effect on the aircraft or passengers. I later completed an AML entry and notified Maintenance Control. I had not flown in 3 weeks, due to my inactivity on reserve status. I now know that I must be more diligent on my scan, especially when I have not flown in a while. On descent, I must be more cognizant of airspeed when using the VS mode. In this case, using Green FLCH would have been a better choice. It was an excellent learning opportunity.
ASRS:1773320.s: The Captain, acting as Pilot Flying, momentarily exceeded Vmo by approximately 1 knot during descent into ZZZ after selecting Vertical Speed Mode to recapture VPATH. Task saturation caused the airspeed excursion, which was immediately corrected by disconnecting the autopilot, resulting in no operational impact or adverse effects.

ASRS:1773341.n: Aircraft X was at ZZZ to change the Emergency/Parking Brake cable. I was on the crew that finished installing and adjusted the cable, working the adjustment of the cable. I had safe tied the two lower jam nuts below the bracket on the handle end of the cable to each other, then over the bracket to the jam nut on top of the bracket. I used the safety cable kit for this task. The brake cable being installed does not have the locking support tab to facilitate easier safety of jam nuts. On my way to work the next day as I was driving. It occurred to me that that safety cable would cut through the bracket over time due to movement of the cable as the handle is actuated. When I arrived at work I notified the supervisor of my mistake and the plane was removed from service. The manual is not very clear about how to safety this this jam nut for this location. I was using Emb-170 AMM task 32-XX-XX for my reference. [The figure] shows the technique for a nut and jam nut at location X which is not where I was working. I corrected the safety procedure of my location to illustration X and returned the aircraft to service. The task 20-XX-XX Typical safetying methods, does not cover this situation with the jam nut. It was getting close to the end of my 12hr shift and I should have thought this thru more carefully. I also think that the Embraer manuals should be more explicit when it comes to different types of safetying situations.
ASRS:1773341.s: A mechanic on an Embraer 170 incorrectly safetied the emergency/parking brake cable jam nuts, fearing the cable would cut the bracket. The aircraft was removed from service until the mechanic corrected the procedure using a different manual illustration and returned it to service.

ASRS:1773349.n: I have noticed that while wearing the face mask for prolonged periods, I feel my self gasping for air and sweating. Also, I see myself having a dry nose which leads to a runny nose while on the aircraft. Once off the aircraft, the symptoms pass. The hyperventilating is my main concern, I can't catch my breath like normal and it's a grave concern at this point.
ASRS:1773349.s: A crew member reported experiencing hyperventilation, sweating, and nasal issues while wearing a face mask for prolonged periods on an aircraft. Symptoms resolved after leaving the aircraft, but the crew member expressed grave concern regarding the inability to catch their breath normally.

ASRS:1773352.n: On landing, I was the A Flight Attendant. I landed in the X jump seat as opposed to the Y jump seat. (This is the correct jumpseat position pre-COVID). This is a new procedure due to COVID because of social distancing. The C Flight Attendant sits in the X row and I land in the X jump seat.
ASRS:1773352.s: The A Flight Attendant landed in the X jump seat instead of the Y jump seat during the landing phase. This deviation followed a new COVID-19 social distancing procedure requiring the C Flight Attendant to sit in the X row.

ASRS:1773357.n: I was briefing the over-wing window exit as the C Flight Attendant with my safety information card in hand. When I asked the gentleman in the two-seater if he was willing and able to sit in the exit row and ask for a verbal confirmation he asked for water.I told him no sir I was asking him if he was willing and able to sit in the exit row he said yeah. He said do you want me to move? I said no you're fine I just wanna make sure that you're aware that you're in the exit row. And that was it.I don't know if you could not hear me because of the mask. Or I was speaking too fast. Or not clearly enough for him. I will need to work on that.
ASRS:1773357.s: A C Flight Attendant briefed an exit row passenger on over-wing exit duties but received a request for water instead of a direct confirmation. The crew member attributed the communication breakdown to potential issues with mask interference, speaking speed, or clarity, and noted a need to improve their briefing technique.

ASRS:1773377.n: During boarding, the passenger originally seated in X2 moved herself to exit row XYA. I was in the back, waiting for the aisle to clear so I could close the overhead bins and brief exit rows. I noticed the customer was in the galley speaking with the forward FA. I wasn't sure what her seat was, so I waited for her to go to her seat before I started walking forward and closing the bins. She grabbed her bag from row X and then sat in XYA, the exit row. I just assumed that was her assigned seat at the time. I closed the bins all the way to the front. I noticed a pilot commuting in row Z who had his mask around his chin and wasn't eating. I requested he put his mask back up and he did. The man behind him in X4 had his mask completely off, so I asked him to put it on and he did. When I asked that guy to put his on, another customer across also pulled theirs up, so I didn't have to ask that third person. I don't recall where the third person was sitting, I only remember they sat in [the area] on the left side of the aircraft. They put their mask up before I asked, so I didn't think much of that.I was quite annoyed that I had to remind so many customers to put their masks up. I briefed the exits like normal. After the door was closed and I did my compliance checks, other flight attendant motioned me toward her before the safety demo. She said that the woman who moved to the exit row was originally seated in [in a different area], and that many customers had their masks off in that area, so she requested to move else where, and that's why she moved. I told other Flight Attendant that I did notice a lot more than usual with their masks off or down, especially in those first few rows of [that area]. Especially the [commuting] pilot and the guy behind him. Other flight attendant said the woman said something about a crew member not wearing a mask. There were a few flight attendants commuting, too, but they all had their masks on that I knew of. Later, inflight I spoke to the woman who moved, and I apologized and told her that it was not okay that they weren't wearing their masks, and that I did tell them to put them on and they did. She said she was especially appalled that a pilot wasn't wearing one, and said she was traveling to see a family member and was stressed enough. I gave her [a voucher] and offered her wine or beer, which she would have gotten in her [original] seat anyway. She seemed calmer and thanked me a lot.Later, I spoke with the [commuting] pilot and reminded him the importance of wearing masks around customers, and that one did move herself back because he wasn't wearing his. After I told him the first time (before door was closed) to put it back on, he kept it on except when eating or drinking. The man behind him, however, I told twice more (three times total including before door was closed) to put his mask on. Once inflight when I was collecting trash and he was sleeping. He had his mask all the way below his chin, near the collar of his shirt so that it didn't even look like he had one there. And another before landing, when I was doing my final compliance check. There was another guy in main cabin who fell asleep twice and I had to shake him awake and remind him to put his mask up, but his was covering his mouth, it just wasn't over his nose. I checked on the customer in XYA again and told her I spoke with that pilot again, and he has complied with mask requirement since the door was closed. Hopefully he just forgot and takes the mask requirement seriously. I only told him once, so I'm not sure how long he had it off or if he was eating before and just forgot to put it back on. I spoke with flight deck before I spoke with that commuter because our paper work and guest service tool app did not say there was a non-rev seated in Z4. So I asked FD if maybe he was listed as jumpseater, which didn't make sense because there were enough seats for all the non-revs to get on and he had higher priority. So I told FD about the customer complaint about that commuting pilot. When I spoke with him, he said he asked gate agent for a seat without the bulkhead, since he was originally given seat A3. So it seemed the woman who was seated in Z3, was swapped to A3. And the pilot was moved to Z4. I'm not sure exactly.
ASRS:1773377.s: A flight attendant reported that a passenger moved to an exit row due to crew members not wearing masks, specifically a commuting pilot and another passenger. The attendant corrected the mask violations, apologized to the passenger, and confirmed the pilot complied with requirements for the remainder of the flight.

ASRS:1773378.n: Customers in XX1 and 2 didn't know each other and asked me if they can move because they didn't think they could be seated next to each other. I told them once we're finished boarding we can see if there's empty seats or you can talk to the gate agent if not. One of them sits across in XX4 for time being. Customer Service Agent (CSA) comes on and says someone else is assigned that seat. He goes back to see who should be in that seat, comes back and finds him sitting in row XY next to someone, I guess they knew each other. So the other customer stays in XX4.The customer in Y2 was also seated next to a stranger, and asked about moving up to row 1. I said unfortunately because we have seating caps, first class is at its max up there. I said once CSA comes back you can talk to him. I go to get a trash bag to collect the purell wipes, and he's right behind me when I turn around. I was confused why he was there all of a sudden. He said he would go talk to the gate agent. I told him to make sure he has all his bags if he's stepping off, but didn't understand why he didn't just wait for GA to come back. Because he had to come back to sort out the customers in row XX. And he asked why he had to take his things, thinking that meant he'd miss the flight. I asked why not just wait in your seat until the gate agent comes back, and he calmed down and nodded, saying that's a better idea. I guess he didn't hear me when I initially told him to wait for CSA to come back. Then CSA comes on and finishes sorting [out] XX12. Then he talks to Y2 and says exactly what I told him about seat caps, maybe he told him something more I'm not sure. Y2 kept complaining about the whole row 1 being open, and why can't he sit there, as if nobody explained the covid seating caps to him (both me and CSA did).Then, I finish collecting wipes and notice XX2 has a lace mask. Like lacey dress or underwear material, super thin with holes in it. And I ask if she has a regular mask without holes, or we can give one to her. And she has a startled/insulted look on her face, and says how she needs the holes because 'I can only breathe out of my left nostril.' I told her if it's a medical concern, it's not showing up on our end, and we weren't informed of any passengers with medical exceptions. So we would need to talk to the CSA and get that on your booking, so you can get an exception. And then she says how she flew with that mask from ZZZ, and it was fine. I told her it was possible nobody noticed on those flights, and unfortunately it's not allowed. Even if nobody else noticed before, that doesn't mean I can ignore it when I notice.So I go back up and flag down the CSA as he's closing the jetbridge doors. And I ask him about any medical exceptions, and he said nobody was approved for that and that he didn't notice anyone with a lace mask. So he says he'll be back with a mask. We have masks onboard but it was better he did that because she was already giving me attitude about it. He comes back and asks who it was and I said XX2, one of the ones we were talking with earlier. He goes back and gives her the mask and comes back saying how she told him that she wore that mask from ZZZ and I that he told her that it doesn't matter what happened on previous flights. Basically the same stuff from when I spoke to her.She got past him during boarding, then the other FA up front, then me in back during the whole seat issue, and then the GA again when he helped with the seat issue. And it wasn't until near departure time that I even noticed. So I think there's a good chance that on her other flights, those CSAs and FAs didn't notice either.Also, it was obvious she didn't have a medical exemption because she told me she needs a hole-y mask since she can only breathe out of 1 nostril. What I did not tell her was that she was speaking to a FA who hasn't been able to breathe out of either nostril in years because of a medical issue, and I was wearing a regular mask just fine. Iwould feel blessed if I could breathe out of even just one nostril. Somehow she didn't think that breathing out of one's mouth alone is possible in a mask. And I know I'm not the only FA with a similar sinus issue, too, and we all wear regular masks.
ASRS:1773378.s: A flight attendant reported a passenger in seat XX2 wearing a non-compliant lace mask during boarding, claiming a medical need to breathe through one nostril. The crew enforced mask policy after confirming no medical exemption existed, and the passenger eventually accepted a standard mask provided by the Customer Service Agent.

ASRS:1773379.n: Passenger in [seat] X4 was told twice by myself and co-worker to fix her mask properly. I told her that her mask should be over her nose and mouth. She told me that she was drinking her water. I stood there while doing my safety demo and not once did I see her take a sip of water. She got upset when I told her that she needs to wear her mask properly.
ASRS:1773379.s: A cabin crew member reported that a passenger in seat X4 refused to wear her mask over her nose and mouth despite two verbal instructions. The passenger claimed she was drinking water, but the crew member observed no drinking and noted the passenger became upset when reminded of the requirement.

ASRS:1773391.n: I was flying in cruise and realized the radio had been quiet for too long. I tried to talk to Center, it may have been Fort Worth center at the time, I have forgotten which, but received no answer. I noticed my volts were not where they should have been. The volts were slowly decreasing and the amp meter read discharging. I assumed the volts were not powerful enough for me to transmit radio so I started trying multiple frequencies and trouble shooting. It was a beautiful flying day so as long as I didn't smell burning I wasn't concerned with the electrical enough for me to drastically change my current situation with nearby unfamiliar fields and inability to speak to anyone. I knew I could trouble shoot and be on the ground at an unpolished airport in 30 minutes, only slightly longer than any other quicker choice may have presented, but with more confidence in my plan and less time spent researching nearer options. Once I discovered the problem I descended to lowest safe altitude and landed without incident. I called [Flight Service] and told them that I had lost contact while under flight following with Center. The problem and issue were resolved and I continued on the next day.
ASRS:1773391.s: The pilot experienced radio silence and electrical discharge during cruise, suspecting low voltage prevented transmission. After troubleshooting, the pilot descended to the lowest safe altitude and landed without incident at an unpolished airport, resolving the issue the next day.

ASRS:1773403.n: Intended flight was from my home base at ZZZ, to ZZZ1. Flight time was calculated to be about 20 minutes. Approximately 4 miles from ZZZ1 the engine power suddenly rolled back. I immediately looked for a landing field while at the same time trying to adjust the mixture and the throttle to regain power.As I was setting up to land on a field, the engine power came back up again. I deducted that the partial power failure was due to either water on the fuel tank or a clog in the fuel line. I decided to abandon the forced landing and try to land at the airport, which was only about 3 miles away. I lowered the landing gear, execute my Before Landing Checklist and set to land. The engine quit shortly after that. I had to quickly pick another forced landing spot because there were trees all around. The aircraft impacted hard, 1.2 SM from the airport. I sustained injuries.
ASRS:1773403.s: A pilot flying a single-engine aircraft experienced a partial power loss 4 miles from the destination, suspected to be caused by water in the fuel or a clogged line. After power briefly returned, the engine quit again during the approach, forcing a hard impact landing 1.2 SM from the airport and resulting in pilot injuries.

ASRS:1773413.n: I'm writing to report the challenging nature/difficulty in making visual approaches in a jet to Runways 35L/R at Henderson Exec Airport (HND), where terrain is a prominent factor as close as a 3-mile final approach. Compliance with ATC spacing instructions can leave the pilot and airplane in a position where neither of the options for trying to land straight-in are particularly good options: Maneuver in proximity to high terrain, knowing in advance that you will be facing the prospect of repeated GPWS warnings as you try to visually get into a position to make the final approach as stable as possible, or, remain high until well clear of the foothills, but face the prospect of a 'chop and drop' close-in final approach, which is neither stable nor desirable.Our afternoon arrival was in excellent VMC conditions. HND was landing 35L and 35R. I have been into HND a few times, and from several years ago I remembered the terrain issues to the south, so I made it a special point of emphasis prior to top-of-descent to brief the SIC that I intended to maintain visual separation with the terrain and expected we would be dealing with the GPWS while maneuvering to get the airplane in a position to fly a stable final segment.We did not fully fly our filed STAR, but instead we were vectored SW of LAS and eventually turned inbound on an E-NE vector on what looked like a 10-15 mile left base leg. This initial vector looked promising, as I thought it might allow for a close-in base to final, which I considered preferable to having to navigate the mountains to the south of the airport. However, as we got inside of 10 miles, approach control instructed us that Tower wanted us to 'widen out more to the east, and square the base turn to final...cleared visual approach 35L.' This instruction basically put us in the position of having to navigate the mountainous terrain on our left base, with a turn to final at approximately 5-6 miles. I set the autopilot to descend for 5,000 MSL (approximately 2,500 AGL above touchdown elevation), but I knew that I would have to get the airplane down to a lower altitude before rolling out on final, or else be faced with either a 'chop and drop' situation or needing to ask for a circling approach over the airport in VMC.I opted to hand fly the airplane and visually maneuvered between the saddles of some higher peaks as I transitioned from left base to final. I was able to gradually descend another few hundred feet as I was flying this portion of the approach, but the GPWS had become active with constant terrain cautions, as expected. I was able to keep the terrain in sight at all times while maneuvering, maintaining a 500-700 foot margin on the radar altimeter over the path I was flying. Beyond dealing with the GPWS audio until we cleared the highest points, I did get the airplane into position to fly a stable final segment and land. Everything transpired pretty much how I thought it might, starting from the descent briefing all the way to touchdown. But I walked away from the airplane not feeling satisfied, thinking there has to be some better way to set up and coordinate visual approaches to 35L/R. Of course, the pilot always has full responsibility to maintain terrain avoidance on visual approaches, but where difficult topography exists, such as south of HND, some extra assistance from ATC in the form of additional vectoring and/or coordination with the local tower could go a long way in helping to better manage visual approaches to 35L/R at this airport.When we were instructed to contact the tower, the approach controller was appreciative of our cooperation in squaring the base as instructed, but I am left wondering if he realized that making me deal with the high terrain on extended final made flying the visual approach that much tougher.I've already decided that if I am put into a similar situation at this airport in the future, I am not going to consider either of the two aforementioned solutions to try and make it straight-in on a visual approach. Going forward I will opt to negotiate a circling approach in the traffic pattern with the controller(s) instead of battling issues with terrain or excessively steep final approach considerations. It may make things a bit more complicated for the controllers and traffic flow, but I think this course of action is really the safest alternative of the lot.
ASRS:1773413.s: A jet pilot reported difficulty executing a visual approach to Runways 35L/R at Henderson Executive Airport due to high terrain and ATC vectoring that forced a left base turn near mountains. The pilot managed constant GPWS warnings by hand-flying between peaks to achieve a stable landing but concluded that requesting a circling approach is the safer alternative for future operations.

ASRS:1773417.n: We were on arrival into ZZZ and on vectors with Approach Control. Prior to switching over to Approach Control ATC advised us that we could expect moderate turbulence, I believe from 9,000 to 12,000 feet, on descent. We were higher up on our descent when they notified us that we could expect the moderate turbulence in the lower altitude structure. We were switched over to approach control. I remarked to approach that we were picking up moderate turbulence, again I believe we were at or above 6,000 feet to give them a heads up. We were given a left northerly turn to 010 degrees and a descent to 5,000 feet. The Autopilot was engaged. It was very turbulent. We received an Alts Cap which is a normal indication on the FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) that the autopilot is now armed to capture the selected altitude. We were getting bumped around pretty good by now, full continuous moderate turbulence. It was at that moment when the autopilot was capturing the altitude that the upset occurred. The aircraft was rocked to a 45 to 50 degree left bank and a sinking drop occurred similar to what you would receive in an airliner if you ever have hit an air pocket. This exceeded the limits of the autopilot and it kicked off. I took over manually to right the airplane and that is when we received what I would call a severe bump which led to the second upset that did the same thing, left bank to 45 to 50 degrees and a pitch downward. I was already in the process of advancing power from the first upset but this time I went to full thrust, TOGA power if you will, to initiate the unusual attitude recovery. I was aggressive in the recovery, put some G on the aircraft, airspeed bled down from 250 to about 180 or 190 at that moment which is still a safe flying airspeed in our type aircraft, well above stall. I traded airspeed for altitude to expedite the recovery. We recovered to altitude shortly after.This all happened so quickly. Severe turbulence upset coupled with automation exceedance were contributing factors. Lessons learned are significant. Turbulence is always a threat.Constance vigilance is always required. Secondly we stress at our company to never fully rely on automation and that it will not always work in all situations. We also stress that situations can happen to anyone regardless of experience. An Incident/Hazard Report has been filled out as part of our Safety Management System (SMS) program and submitted to the Director of Safety at our company. We train for upset situations every X months as part of our X month continuation qualification and training. I've flown many types of aircraft as well as fighter type aircraft and have never experienced a situation such as the one described above.
ASRS:1773417.s: During arrival into ZZZ, the crew encountered severe turbulence while descending to 5,000 feet with the autopilot engaged. The turbulence caused two upsets exceeding autopilot limits, forcing a manual recovery using TOGA power and trading airspeed for altitude to regain control.

ASRS:1773419.n: I own a Cessna 172N that I lease to a flying club here. The club president and I agreed we would comply with 100hr inspections for reasons of safety due to the amount of flying the aircraft did. We did not think the 100hr was a requirement and did get clarification from the FSDO about this but still had them accomplished but with the thought that they were not required. This led to 2 overfly events for AD Date. I did not keep the logbook nor did I pour over it until just recently. It was kept in a locked closet where the club operates. I have changed a main ship's battery and a tire and some oil changes prior to Year but overall I wanted an Inspection Authority to work on the aircraft and wanted to stay out of the maintenance side. I had always thought it's better to get an unaffiliated outside person to perform the maintenance and annuals instead of someone that actively flys the plane and is the owner and club member. I think that the focus was on completing the 100hrs as an added safety measure but we did not notice that the seat rail AD was a 100hr requirement. Because of this if the Inspection Authority was not available or we were unable to move the aircraft for some reason it kept flying. I really did not know much of what was going on with the day to day schedule especially at the end of Year and on into Year/Year until now. I could not obtain my Class 3 MED due to a [medical issue] and quit flying all together for over X years. I kind of left it up to the club. Just recently I've taken advantage of Basic MED and am flying again. I had installed a broken piece of plastic on the elevator and while signing it off went back through the book. This is where I found the errors. On 2 occasions we flew past the seat rail AD once by 53hr and once by 11.6hr. The seat rail has now current with 6 hours remaining, we have scheduled the AD to be accomplished this week and will be well within the 100hr time limit. Going forward we have a clear plastic book onboard with all the inspections and their due dates and times. The club president is now aware that the 100hr is hard time and will schedule early going forward. We are prepared to ground the aircraft if we are unable to schedule with the Inspection Authority and I'm working on gaining access to the locked closet area where the logbooks are kept. At this time the seat rail is in compliance with the AD and will not overfly ever again. Thank you.
ASRS:1773419.s: The owner of a Cessna 172N leased to a flying club admitted to two overfly events of a seat rail Airworthiness Directive by 53 and 11.6 hours due to misinterpreting 100-hour inspection requirements. The club has since corrected the AD, implemented better logbook tracking, and committed to grounding the aircraft if maintenance cannot be scheduled.

ASRS:1773426.n: I was CPC [Career Professional Controller] training an FLM-IT [Front Line Manager-In Training]. We had a Small Aircraft (Aircraft X) overflight at 090. Air Carrier X (Aircraft Y) departed. Trainee climbed Aircraft Y up to 100. There was plenty of room to turn Aircraft Y, so I did not have trainee amend altitude. But then FLM-IT got distracted with traffic on the east side of the airport. I prompted trainee to turn Aircraft Y. FLM-IT keyed up, so I thought that is what FLM-IT was doing, then FLM-IT talked to other aircraft. I still felt FLM-IT had time to fix it, so I prompted again a second time. FLM-IT keyed up and talked to another same Air Carrier X (Aircraft Z) on the east side of the airport and not Aircraft Y that I was referring to. Finally the third prompt FLM-IT talked to Aircraft Y. I knew it was close to a loss of 3 miles, but thought FLM-IT turned Aircraft Y early enough, but it was not. When discussed after the session, FLM-IT did not hear me say to turn Aircraft Y.
