Which could have been because I was talking thru a mask and communication is muffled.When training I need to use full call sign with the numbers when telling the trainee to do something. I kept saying turn Air Carrier X. We had more than one Air Carrier X that we were working. So I need to be more specific. I can also just key up and turn the aircraft myself which I normally do if I feel like it is warranted. I honestly thought she caught it early enough.
ASRS:1773426.s: A Career Professional Controller training a Front Line Manager-In-Training failed to prevent a near loss of separation between two Air Carrier X aircraft due to ambiguous instructions and communication issues. The trainee did not hear the initial turn prompts for the specific aircraft, resulting in a separation breach that was corrected only after the third prompt.

ASRS:1773454.n: During my briefing with FAs I communicated that masks were not going to be worn while in the cockpit, at any phase of the operation by me or my First Officer and that we were going to keep cockpit door closed while on the ground and no visitors.At that time FA A proceeded to instruct me about her own requirements to visit the cockpit, if pilots didn't have a mask...pilots will not speak while she's in the cockpit and if they needed to, it would be only facing forward and not facing her at all.I immediately told her that her demands were not part of any policy or procedure stated in any company publishing and that it was not going to be granted.FA A's attitude was very receptive and she conducted herself in a very nice and respectful manner.As I was deplaning the plane in ZZZ, FA A and Chief Purser called my attention to the screen of the Purser's cell phone, stating that it was a note from my Flight Duty Manager showing that masks must be worn during flight attendant's visits to the cockpit regardless.I suggested them to file a report because I had no time to go over their claim as I had just few minutes to go to our next flight.
ASRS:1773454.s: The Captain and Flight Attendant A disputed cockpit entry requirements regarding mask usage and communication restrictions during ground operations at ZZZ. The crew disagreed on policy compliance after the Flight Attendant presented a conflicting message from the Flight Duty Manager on a mobile device.

ASRS:1773468.n: I am a Ramp Agent in ZZZ. There is no one to take employees temps as they report to work at the airport. There is currently a sign that reads, take your own temperature and sign your name off. That thermometer has given me reading of 90, 91, 96, etc... Recently, I cannot absolutely confirm, but one of my fellow employees is quarantining with no taste etc...no one that I know of that was working with that employee last week has been notified that they may have been exposed. Why isn't airline following the rules that are so important. We have had fellow employees close family members die of COVID and I along with many others are high risk. It feels like they are not taking this seriously and many of us are concerned and don't want to die.
ASRS:1773468.s: A Ramp Agent at ZZZ reported that no staff were available to take employee temperatures, forcing reliance on an inaccurate thermometer and self-reporting. The agent expressed concern that a potentially infected coworker was not quarantined and that exposed employees were not notified, citing a failure to follow safety rules.

ASRS:1773484.n: Takeoff and initial climb from DCA, Runway 01. Captain Pilot Monitoring, First Officer Pilot Flying. Pre-flight duties completed and route review completed at gate. Engine start and taxi was normal to Runway 01, before takeoff checklist completed to the line before crossing Runway 04, below the line after crossing Runway 04. As we taxied to runway, Aircraft Y was cleared to cross Runway 04 before us on another taxiway then into the box. As we were approaching Runway 01, Tower Controller asked Aircraft Y if they were ready for departure, Aircraft Y responded they needed 2 minutes. Tower asked if we were ready for departure and we responded we were ready, completed final checklist items. We lined up on Runway 01 and were cleared for takeoff. I do not recall checking FMA for NAV annunciation as we taxied on to the runway and checked final for traffic. Light passenger load/light takeoff weight. After takeoff, aircraft climb was rapid with a quick change to Departure frequency. We were at clean-up altitude quickly after takeoff. After thrust set to climb power and frequency change to departure (prior to check-in on frequency with departure) I noticed FMA annunciation was RWY TRK and we had not yet initiated a left turn for the departure. I told the First Officer to turn left, which he accomplished, initially coming left to approximately a 290-300 degree heading. I cross checked Nav Display for 1 NM circle around point PLVIA and outside references. I do not believe we entered Prohibited Area 56A or Prohibited Area 56B. After initial left turn, we then turned back to the right to rejoin the departure. A turn to point ADAXE would have required an aggressive right turn, so we turned to rejoin the departure between ADAXE and BEBLE After turning to rejoin departure I checked-in with departure control when they asked if we were on frequency. Remainder of the flight was uneventful.This was my (Captain) first flight back on the line after several months away due to combination of leave of absence and quarantine for close contact with [someone] with COVID-19. I had just completed recurrent training the week before this flight. In the pre-flight briefing the First Officer had noted that with light passenger loads the aircraft takeoff and climb would happen quickly. Given my lack of recent flying, I should not have accepted departure prior to the aircraft in front of us on the ground, even though I felt I was in the green. I was slow to notice we had not initiated left turn on the departure where I would normally expect to begin a turn, possibly due to lack of recent line flying experience, the combination of quick climb after takeoff to acceleration altitude and frequency change slowing my monitoring and recognition of aircraft not being in NAV mode. Though I did direct the pilot flying to make a left turn, if I had done so earlier we would have been able to maintain the departure track without tracking close to Prohibited Area 56.The time from takeoff to overshooting the departure turn on takeoff from Runway 01 at DCA happens fast! I would like to see a similar event during simulator training to illustrate just how quickly you can get close to Prohibited Area 56 after takeoff from DCA when combining a timely distraction with lack of aircraft going in to NAV mode. PLVIA with 1 NM ring on NAV display did assist me as a barrier for this event. Takeoff and initial climb from DCA, Runway 01. Captain Pilot Monitoring, First Officer Pilot Flying. Pre-flight duties completed and route review completed at gate. Engine start and taxi was normal to Runway 01, before takeoff checklist completed to the line before crossing Runway 04, below the line after crossing Runway 04. As we taxied to runway, Aircraft Y was cleared to cross Runway 04 before us on another taxiway then into the box. As we were approaching Runway 01, Tower Controller asked Aircraft Y if they were ready for departure, Aircraft Y responded they needed 2 minutes. Tower asked if we were ready for departure and we responded we were ready, completed final checklist items. We lined up on Runway 01 and were cleared for takeoff. I do not recall checking FMA for NAV annunciation as we taxied on to the runway. Light passenger load/light takeoff weight. After takeoff, aircraft climb was rapid with a quick change to departure frequency. We were at clean-up altitude quickly after takeoff. After thrust set to climb power and frequency change to departure (prior to check-in on frequency with departure) PM noticed FMA annunciation was RWY TRK and we had not yet initiated a left turn for the departure. PF was focused on aircraft control since it was a light aircraft and I did notice the PLVIA circle rapidly approaching with no direction to turn by the Flight Directors. I also noticed the route was dashed and started a shallow turn to the left primarily due to the PLVIA circle. The PM/Captain having SA told me to turn left, which I accomplished, initially coming left to approximately a 290-300 degree heading. I cross checked Nav Display for 1 NM circle around point PLVIA and outside references. I do not believe we entered Prohibited Area 56A or Prohibited Area 56B. After initial left turn, we then turned back to the right to rejoin the departure. A turn to point ADAXE would have required an aggressive right turn, so we turned to rejoin the departure between ADAXE and BEBLE. After turning to rejoin departure PM checked-in with departure control when they asked if we were on frequency. Remainder of the flight was uneventful.I used a technique taught in the school-house of Red over Blue, Climb/NAV, Flight Dir 1 and 2 while at the gate. I do this on every flight. We are supposed to check NAV again prior to departure and due to the rushed situation and proficiency I don't recall either PM or PF saying anything about NAV. We had briefed the departure in full to include Prohibited Area 56 and the EO SID. I still don't know why it was not in NAV after takeoff roll. I had seen a technique of starting the turn regardless of the flight directors in DCA but up until now I have always used the flight directors. In this case the PLVIA circle was a timely final barrier that prevented me from going into Prohibited Area 56 along with the PM's callout.The time from takeoff to overshooting the departure turn on takeoff from RWY 01 at DCA happens fast! I would like to see a similar event during simulator training to illustrate just how quickly you can get close to Prohibited Area 56 after takeoff from DCA when combining a timely distraction with lack of aircraft going in to NAV mode. Keep the PLVIA circle in the 10-7 and emphasize in training, it is a critical last barrier.
ASRS:1773484.s: During takeoff from DCA Runway 01, the Captain and First Officer failed to verify NAV mode, causing the aircraft to track RWY TRK and overshoot the departure turn toward Prohibited Area 56. The Captain corrected the heading using the PLVIA waypoint as a visual barrier, allowing the crew to rejoin the departure without entering the prohibited airspace.

ASRS:1773491.n: My first trip 'solo' as CO [Commanding Officer] was going well. I had a good crew and we performed well as a crew. On arrival after receiving vectors for approach to Runway XXL and established, the PF was looking around - sighting...flaps were at 15...I was focused on the required speed and frequency change at ZZZZZ, and the Relief Pilot was daydreaming as well. At 1,000 feet the PF called 'stable'...and I saw his speed and ILS tracking were spot-on...and then we both realized at the same time that the gear was still UP and the flaps were at 15!! He called gear down and flaps 25, which I did out of habit as response to the fallout. I realized then, at the same time he did, that the approach was NOT going to work, at which point we both called 'go-around'. The go-around was at 800 feet AFL and was UGLY!! Go-arounds from this altitude are often UGLY!! The subsequent vectors and second approach went as it should and we landed safely...the desired outcome. The debrief at the gate was thorough and each of us contributed, as well as took appropriate blame for our individual contribution to such an embarrassing and actually humiliating event.We each had recently been through a simulator check. The Relief Pilot and I (CO) each having less than 40 hours in type, and the FO having just returned from a 7 month period of not flying. Combined total flight time of this 3-man crew exceeded X0,000 hours. However on this day we were each victims of a few different causal factors: fatigue...we had just flown XA+45 hours from ZZZZ, neither of us slept well the previous night, and we were each the victims of relative inactivity due to COVID-related restrictions, each of these led us to be distracted, lackadaisical, and only partially effective as a crew.Causal factors contributing to this outrageously ridiculous display of airman-ship are deemed to be at least the following: longer layovers, [lack of] more well established activity schedules during our layovers-even during times of social restrictions, [lack of] better food onboard flights for crews, [lack of] better procedural discipline is possibly another even considering each of us had been through simulator training very recently.
ASRS:1773491.s: A fatigued three-person crew on a solo Commanding Officer's first flight missed the landing gear and flap configuration during a stable approach at 1,000 feet, forcing an ugly go-around at 800 feet. The incident resulted from fatigue, inactivity, and distraction, though the crew executed a safe second approach and landing.

ASRS:1773498.n: Air Carrier dispatch reported ZZZZ ramp failed to document dry ice on the W/B paperwork. 'OK--ZZZZ ramp just relayed to me that possible cargo 8r has 229KG Ice.' They [ramp] inadvertently did not include that in the paperworkReporter included ramps notification: Dispatch can you pass on to Aircraft X flight crew that position 8R has 229 KG ice... The station did it wrong and they had it going to ZZZZ1 to ZZZZ2.
ASRS:1773498.s: Air Carrier dispatch and ZZZZ ramp personnel failed to document 229 kg of dry ice in cargo position 8R on the weight and balance paperwork for Aircraft X. The ramp agent inadvertently omitted the hazardous material, causing a documentation error for the flight to ZZZZ1 and ZZZZ2.

ASRS:1773509.n: On Aircraft X to ZZZ, we were given a turn to base for a visual approach to XR inside the final approach fix 600 feet above the FAF. We realized we weren't going to be able to complete the approach under the stable approach criteria so I called the go-around at 1,000 feet AGL. Once we got the aircraft climbing I called ATC saying that we are going around. ATC said climb and maintain 3000 feet, we were already climbing and had a high rate of climb because we only had about XX people on board. While we were cleaning up the aircraft and setting up the FCP, I realized our Climb rate was high and we were approaching 3,000 feet quickly. I said 'watch your altitude' and asked ATC if we could get 3,500 feet. ATC denied it and said to maintain 3,000 feet and contact departure. Unfortunately, the correction of bringing the nose down and power back happened too late and we climbed through our altitude by about 200 feet. The correction came and we corrected our altitude back to 3,000 feet. On the second attempt approach tried to do the same thing to us again however we denied it and asked to be vectored for the ILS. ATC turned us to intercept the final approach course too close and I told them we won't be able to do it due to us having a tailwind, and that we are going to need to intercept it from the other side. I told ATC the intercept we would need. On that attempt we completed the approach successfully and landed with no further complications.Due to having a poor vector for the approach, and no warning of a close approach, we ended up high on a visual approach to Runway XR. For that reason we decided to go-around. The altitude assigned to us was only about 1,200 feet above the altitude we decided to go-around at. By the time we got the aircraft configured for the go around and contacted ATC we were even closer to that altitude. Due to having a high workload in that environment, a light weight, and being already close to the altitude assigned to us the climb rate was too high when I made the call out to the Captain. I also tried to rectify the situation before it happened by asking ATC for a higher altitude but was denied.Deny the visual approach and ask ATC to just fly the ILS to give us more time. Say unable instead of asking for a higher altitude. Today on Aircraft X to ZZZ we were given a turn inside of the FAF for Runway XR into ZZZ. ZZZ Approach had us at 3,000 feet. The FAF is 2,400 feet. We were unable to widen the approach due to a snowstorm to the west and had been cleared for the visual. We were too high, so we completed a missed approach. On the missed we went above our assigned altitude of 3,000 feet by 200 feet. We requested higher but were rejected, so we descended the 150-200 feet. On the second attempt, approach tried to give us the same turn at the same altitude. We asked for the ILS. We were again given a bad vector, however, farther out. We were given a 060 heading to intercept. Due to a 40 knot tailwind we flew through and requested a 120 heading to join. It was accepted. We landed successfully.We got a bad vector inside the final approach fix while 600 feet above the FAF altitude. We were given no indication or expectation of a short approach. We were too high and too fast for our approach. We conducted a go-around and subsequently climbed 150-200 feet high.
ASRS:1773509.s: Pilots on Aircraft X to ZZZ executed a go-around during a visual approach to Runway XR after receiving a poor vector inside the final approach fix that left them too high and fast. The aircraft subsequently overshot the assigned 3,000 feet by 200 feet due to a high climb rate from light weight and high workload, though the crew landed successfully on a subsequent ILS approach.

ASRS:1773515.n: Shortly after departure from ZZZ I went to switch to the app to check on turbulence. At this point I noticed that my iPad screen was completely frozen. I could not change anything and had to reboot my iPad to get it back functioning. I would not have been able to switch to the complex engine out procedure had we had an engine failure!I always only have flight related apps running in the background while flying to help prevent this from happening. Didn't work this time. We need new iPads. Now, I understand this is expensive but our old iPads are starting to become a safety hazard with apps locking up all the time. It's not uncommon for the Jepp app to lag and require closing and reopening. That's a quick fix, rebooting an ipad in the middle of an engine failure is not
ASRS:1773515.s: A pilot reported that shortly after departure from ZZZ, their iPad froze while attempting to check turbulence, requiring a reboot. The pilot stated that aging iPads frequently lock up, creating a safety hazard by preventing access to critical engine-out procedures during emergencies.

ASRS:1773533.n: During initial climb out of ZZZ I noted a distinct burning or melting smell. I noted it and continued climbing monitoring the engine gauges for abnormalities. When climbing through approximately 7,000-8,000 feet the left hand fire T-Handle illuminated. After acknowledging it, I performed the memory items and started my timer per the SOP. I then observed the #1 engine gauges and visually inspected the nacelle for any actual fire indications. Knowing the T-handle is prone to erroneous indications during heavy precipitation or sunlight in the cowling, I took those factors into account. I did not note a fire but the burning smell persisted along with the fact I was not in precipitation and the sun was down. These three factors did not satisfy my thought that this was a false indication. I continued with the memory items and secured the #1 engine. I advised ATC and [told them] to standby while I focused on completing my checklists. I completed all the items on the checklist including deploying the halon bottle due to the T-handle still being illuminated. The T-Handle extinguished approximately a minute or so after I deployed the extinguisher. I then [advised ATC] and asked [them] if the weather was better at any other nearby airports, to which we determined was not the case. I determined the best course of action was to return to ZZZ due to my familiarity with the approach and the fact that my radios were already set up for the ILS XX from the departure. ATC also advised me that they were going to roll the emergency vehicles. I received vectors, executed the approach, and landed without incident. I exited the runway and shut the plane down. I then called the Operations, Dispatch, and Maintenance Control in that order. I was eventually towed to the hangar and the cargo was offloaded by the customer.
ASRS:1773533.s: During initial climb from ZZZ, the pilot secured the #1 engine after a fire T-handle illuminated and a burning smell persisted. The crew deployed the halon bottle, returned to ZZZ, and landed safely before towing the aircraft to the hangar for maintenance.

ASRS:1773581.n: Radio communication with ZZZ Center was not established over State X enroute on a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was able to re-establish radio communication with ZZZ1 Center North of City X on frequency XYZ.AB using the number 2 communications radio. I regularly fly this route and I know most of the high altitude center frequencies by memory. While speaking with ZZZ1 Center I was advised to call ZZZ Center after landing. My normal procedure is to monitor 'On-Guard XYX.BC with the number 2 radio, however, there was an ELT transmitting. The XYX.BC frequency was congested and was only occasionally monitored to wait for the ELT transmission to dissipate. The number 2 radio was operating with much less static than the number 1 radio. After landing I spoke to the pilot that previously flew the aircraft and they confirmed that the number 1 radio has been having reception issues. The number 1 radio was troubleshot and found to have a bonding issue between the fuselage and number 1 communications antenna due to corrosion. The antenna is in the process of being replaced. In conclusion, improved aircraft maintenance would have prevented this event.As a side note: I have noticed more 'NORDO' events since the COVID-19 pandemic began. Now, a day does not go by that an aircraft is not being summoned to remedy a 'NORDO' situation. Previously, these events were less. I speculate that a change in ATC staffing and increased size of control boundaries for one Controller to be responsible is a possible contributing factor. I notice now that the high sector controllers (usually working FL260 and above) are working considerably larger areas including the low sector. It is now not uncommon to hear a high sector Controller clearing low altitude aircraft for approaches and handing them off to Local Approach ATC. Juxtaposed to this increased workload for the Controller is less flying for air crew. The reduced flying during this pandemic may contribute to these 'NORDO' events due to crews having reduced flying schedules and reduced recent experience."
ASRS:1773581.s: The pilot experienced a radio communication failure enroute due to a bonding issue and corrosion on the number 1 communications antenna. Maintenance confirmed the defect, which is being corrected, while the pilot attributed the event to poor maintenance and speculated that reduced crew experience and increased controller workload may contribute to rising NORDO incidents.

ASRS:1773597.n: Received numerous ATC clearances via CPDLC while enroute. First cleared us down to 38,000 ft, was accepted by Pilot Flying.. Next was a route clearance. First line of free text said 'Cleared to NIKLS'. Pilot Flying changed the Legs page with verification from me. After a few minutes ATC sent another CPDLC that said descend to 34,000 ft and then another clearance came in a couple moments later clearing us to 31,000 ft. ATC then queried via radio '(Call sign) where are you heading direct to?' I answered NIKLS and was told that is not your clearance and was given an immediate heading. We then brought up our clearance and noticed the next line of free text said 'VIA LAYED FARLN NIKLS'. ATC then read this clearance and asked what altitude we were cleared down to. We noticed that the aircraft had stopped at 34,000 ft while we figured out our navigation error. We then descended to 34,000 ft and proceeded on the correct route. While descending to 34,000 ft we received a CPDLC clearance to proceed direct to NIKLS VIA and then the rest of the clearance. We did not see the VIA part. We went direct to NIKLS. Then we received a descend to 31,000 ft. While still in the descent, ATC asked if we were going direct to NIKLS. We said yes. ATC said that we were not cleared direct. They gave us a heading, and verbally gave us the other fixes that came before NIKLS. As we were writing down the clearance, the plane leveled off at 34,000 ft. ATC asked if we were cleared to 31,000 ft. We said yes, and started to descend to 31,000 ft.
ASRS:1773597.s: The flight crew misinterpreted CPDLC route clearances while enroute, flying direct to NIKLS instead of the required VIA LAYED FARLN route. This navigation error caused ATC to issue immediate heading corrections and altitude queries until the crew identified the missing text and descended to the correct altitude.

ASRS:1773600.n: We were sent a CPDLC (Controller Pilot Datalink Communications) that cleared us to CHS. Instead of using the load function we selected direct to CHS. ATC queried if we were going direct to CHS. We responded affirmative. He then informed us the clearance in the CPDLC was to CHS via FKN. We both missed the FKN part of the route clearance. Asked if he would like us to go direct to FKN then CHS he responded no. We looked at the CPDLC and both had misread the clearance. The verbiage on the CPDLC was in my opinion a little confusing and the FKN showed up on the bottom left of the page after 'CLEARED TO CHS.' FKN was not on our file route. We didn't hear any vectoring of other aircraft do to out flight path. Upon reaching cruise altitude, we received a CPDL (Controller Pilot Datalink Communications) clearance that read in top line, 'cleared to CHS via route clearance'. Next line free text, 'Rest of route unchanged'. Next line free text 'Cleared to CHS via FKN CHS.' As Pilot Monitoring, I read first and second lines and due to expectation bias, immediately told my F/O, 'Cleared to CHS' I then went to next page and hit Send. My First Officer went to LEGS page and pulled CHS to top and executed. Both of us missed FKN inserted into new route clearance. We were later questioned by ATC. After rereading CPDL clearance, our error was clear.
ASRS:1773600.s: Two pilots misread a CPDLC clearance to CHS via FKN, selecting direct to CHS instead due to confusing text layout and expectation bias. ATC queried the deviation, and the crew acknowledged their error after rereading the message.

ASRS:1773604.n: We struggled to even get in a pushback call on Hobby Tower frequency. It was busy with high volume takeoff and landing and ground movements. We had briefed a taxi out from Gate to Runway 4. Tower and Ground were combined. The airport was using Runway 4 for takeoff and landing. Our first instructions from a very busy Tower Controller were unexpected. Tower said taxi via [Taxiway] Z, hold short [Taxiway] D. We had no way to ask for clarification. The frequency was very congested. Our role seemed to be to clear the alley to allow inbound company aircraft. The pace that the tower controller was speaking was impressive and very busy. Other Company seemed to be confused on the radio along with our crew. The pace was something you hear on LGA Ground frequency.We were issued further taxi instructions to follow Company to Runway 4. We verified our crossing clearances across [Runway] 13L and R. We discussed that the controller was in the Yellow. We used extra vigilance during this crowded taxi out to Runway 4. The pace never relented for the controller. He was doing a great job. But the situation was excessive for a routine departure out of our always bustling Hobby airport. It came as no surprise to us that we were cleared for takeoff on Runway 4, even though we were #2 in the lineup. We instantly questioned this, and our clearance was canceled. This seemed like a minor error to us, but it was confirmation that the professional controller was indeed in the Yellow. We departed minutes later without incident.Staff this busy airport with the correct amount of controllers. Loading up flight crews in this critical phase of flight over weak staffing is hazardous. I'm not sure if the guy was alone up there. He was really doing a great job. We know as crews, when the controllers are overloaded, we try to not make the situation worse with fumbled radio calls. The airport was operating in the Yellow, any small non-normal from an aircraft on the frequency could have made things go bad very quickly. We could have waited to move from our pushback into the alley until the radio calmed down
ASRS:1773604.s: Flight crew at Hobby Airport experienced severe radio congestion and unexpected taxi instructions from an overloaded controller during taxi to Runway 4. The controller issued a premature takeoff clearance that was immediately canceled, confirming the high workload, though the flight departed safely minutes later.

ASRS:1773615.n: Received an early am short call assignment. Assigned paring ZZZ. 2 gate returns were made for maintenance and FO timing out on second gate return as well. Aircraft swap was made to continue flight with new FO. After realizing how tired I was and that I was paired up with another FO who hadn't flown in nearly the same amount of time as me (9 months), and after a self-perceived degradation in my performance from the extended maintenance delays, I removed myself from the operation due to safety concerns. I feel as though if I had been flying more I could have powered through this event by relying on recent 'habit patterns or 'muscle Memory' from currency of a normal schedule. That, with the self-awareness of fatigue setting in led me to believe that the safe thing to do was to remove myself from the flight. I have flown aircraft for decades. I know when to remove myself from flight duty. I believe that this extended duty period with disrupted sleep and a degraded sense of performance would have been in poor judgement for me to continue."
ASRS:1773615.s: A pilot removed themselves from an early morning flight after extended maintenance delays and a crew swap caused fatigue and perceived performance degradation. The pilot cited disrupted sleep and lack of recent flight currency as the reasons for voluntarily ending the duty to ensure safety.

ASRS:1773620.n: Passenger in seat XX3 was removed due to repeated requests and non-compliance with requests to use his mask, and then he cussed [at] the FA. Other passengers confirmed his behavior, had customer service remove passenger.
ASRS:1773620.s: A passenger in seat XX3 was removed for refusing to wear a mask and cursing at a flight attendant. Customer service removed the passenger after other passengers confirmed his non-compliant behavior.

ASRS:1773622.n: This is a pilot pushing issue. Due to fog and visibility below minimums we could not get into [planned destination] last night. It was unforecasted and we did not have an alternate and/or fuel to try again so we diverted to [an alternate]. Shortly after arriving, as I was on the phone with Dispatch, someone walked in the cockpit and starts talking even though I was on the phone. I told him to hold on. I finish my call and he said, '[another air carrier] just landed in ZZZ1, so I was wondering when you were going to head back there. I was honestly taken aback. I told him, 'I don't know, the F/O and I have to look at the weather again', and I would let him know. I conferred with the F/O (First Officer) who was comfortable trying again as was I, as well as the flight attendants (although one was going to run into a legality issue if the delay was any longer). However, I wanted to speak to the OPS guy. I called OPS and asked him to come back. At first he wanted to just talk on the radio, but I asked him to come to the cockpit. When he arrived, I let him have it. I told him that the weather was below legal landing minimums, and that flight landing after us was probably done illegally. The RVR when we went missed had dropped to 800 after we passed the FAF (Minimum RVR for landing on Runway X is 1800). I can assure you when we got to minimums we saw nothing. So the fact that Name1 comes up and tells me to essentially continue an illegal operation because another airline did it is pure and simple pilot pushing and unprofessional on so many levels.
ASRS:1773622.s: A pilot reported that an operations representative pressured the crew to attempt an illegal landing at the original destination after another carrier landed, despite visibility being below minimums. The crew refused the request, citing safety regulations and the fact that the other flight likely operated illegally.

ASRS:1773635.n: Our release for this flight included the following under the MEL Item Info 'Treated Fuel'. A search of the MEL manual and the FOM revealed no information to further describe what this means. The Captain called Dispatch who had to conference in maintenance to inform us of the meaning. Maintenance said the plane had been in storage and was only on its second leg after coming out of storage. A review of all the maintenance paperwork provided to the pilots did not communicate this information.
ASRS:1773635.s: The flight crew encountered an undefined MEL item "Treated Fuel" with no explanation in the manual or maintenance paperwork. Dispatch and maintenance clarified the aircraft was on its second leg after storage, revealing a failure to communicate this status to the pilots.

ASRS:1773638.n: I came from ZZZ airport and boarded the employee bus to the employee parking lot. The bus sat for about 20 minutes before leaving and waited to overfill the bus with employees. There were more employees than seats available on the bus. The driver still continued to wait for more people to board after people were already standing without seats. This not only puts everyone on the bus at increased risk for the spread of COVID, but also increases risk for injury for those standing on the bus. We were just asked to not board a crowded bus and instead wait for the next one, however, if all the buses are being filled in this way than this leaves no choice for everyone, but to either put themselves in an unsafe situation or find other means to get to the employee parking lot.
ASRS:1773638.s: Employees reported that a shuttle bus driver waited to overfill the vehicle, forcing passengers to stand without seats. The reporter stated this practice increases risks for COVID-19 spread and injury, leaving staff with no safe alternative but to board crowded buses or find other transport.

ASRS:1773641.n: Almost three months ago the building and maintenance failed to complete to provide a barrier of the partition to separate an employee sitting across from another employee. They provided the partition on the customer service side and failed to do the one on the employee's side which as a result expose the sitting employee to more virus.
ASRS:1773641.s: Building and maintenance staff failed to install a partition on the employee side of a workspace, leaving an employee exposed to increased virus risk. The missing barrier was not provided despite the installation of a partition on the customer service side.

ASRS:1773693.n: During cruise flight at 40,000 ft. in the vicinity of ZZZ we began to smell an electrical type smoke. Moments later the A Flight Attendant called the flight deck to report smoke in the cabin. Simultaneously the master caution came on for ELEC and the TRU (transformer rectifier unit) light illuminated on the overhead panel. I as Captain was Pilot Flying and initially transferred control to the First Officer for me to chase down the TRU checklist. I accomplished the checklist, noting that approach mode with the flight directors would be unavailable... At this point the smoke was getting thicker, and we decided to accomplish the smoke/fire/fumes memory items. After communications were established we notified ATC and asked for a left turn direct to ZZZ1. We considered ZZZ2 but figured in terms of time we were about the same distance away due to our altitude, and that with a straight line to ZZZ1 we would be able to keep both our heads in the game running through checklists and monitoring the aircraft vs a circling descent into mountainous terrain. It was at this point that the First Officer made me aware that all his flight and NAV displays had failed. He thus transferred control back to me as the Pilot Flying and he took over the smoke/fire/fumes checklist in the QRH.ATC told us to expect one of the north runways into ZZZ1, but we told them we wanted [Runway] XXL as we were just on the north side of the airport so that was closest. We requested direct ZZZZZ on the ILS to backup our visual approach, and used our emergency authority to proceed at about 320 knots in order to expedite landing. At this point the First Officer discontinued the smoke/fire/fumes checklist at step 20, having noted at step 16 that we should not delay landing in order to complete the checklist. We then briefed and ran a descent and approach checklist. I asked the First Officer to call ZZZ1 OPS to let them know we were coming and for them to relay the info to Dispatch but at that point the #2 radio and comm panel had failed and the ACARS was no comm. It was with the master caution recall on the descent checklist that we realized how many issues were piling up beyond the TRU and smoke. Looking up after being prompted by the recall we saw a solid portion of the overhead panel was lit.With the glare from the smoke and setting sun we were only able to pickup the airport just outside of ZZZZZ. I disconnected the autopilot and proceeded to fly a visual approach backed up by the LNAV track for the ILS XXL. I quickly realized that electric trim was inoperative and proceeded to trim manually. With the landing checklist we also discovered that the auto speed brake would not arm, so I asked the First Officer to back me up for the manual deployment. We landed in the touchdown zone and exited at gate without incident where CFR was waiting. We stopped in order for CFR (crash fire rescue) to do a quick external inspection. As it was pretty quickly obvious the smoke was inside the aircraft and they weren't seeing anything outside, we asked them to get out of the way so we could get to a gate and let our passengers stop breathing fumes.After shutting down the engines the APU appeared to be supplying only partial power and the ground call horn sounded constantly. Due to this issue the cabin was already dark, and knowing we were dealing with an electrical issue we opted to remove all power from the aircraft and performed the secure checklist. Then we took a breath and asked each other (at the same time) 'well, how'd that go'. Of course sitting on the ground I feel like I can armchair quarterback the situation and nitpick some of the decisions, but overall I feel like we handled the situation well. We had good crew coordination given the circumstances (on O2) and the First Officer did a great job of running the checklists as well as keeping an eye on my flying once we had to transfer controls back to me. It did feel weird turning away from ZZZ2 since it was practically right below us, but I still feel like it was the correct decision given the circumstances and the amount of time it would take to descend, and how much of a distraction an orbiting descent into mountainous terrain would be while trying to deal with smoke.One thing I would do differently has to do with after the situation was over on the ground. I ended up talking with the Chief Pilot, then the firefighters, then the mechanic outside the aircraft on the ramp. By the time I got back inside I couldn't find the flight attendants to debrief and see how they were doing. Upon opening the flight deck door the A had told me that they were all fine, but I would have liked to make sure and check in with them individually. I called scheduling to try and get them to transfer me in order to at least talk with them on the phone, who then transferred me to the scheduling desk where I waited on hold until it disconnected. I still hope to talk with them at some point to learn how things went in the back and find out what we could have done better for them. During cruise flight at 40,000 ft. in the vicinity of ZZZ we began to smell an electrical type smoke. Moments later the A Flight Attendant called the flight deck to report smoke in the cabin. Simultaneously, the Master Caution came on for ELEC and the TR (transformer rectifier unit) light illuminated on the overhead panel. The Captain was Pilot Flying, and initially transferred control to me, in order to run the TR checklist. He accomplished the checklist, and it was around this same point the smoke was getting thicker, and we decided to accomplish the smoke/fire/fumes memory items. After communications were established the Captain told me to notify ATC and asked for a left turn direct to ZZZ1. We considered ZZZ2 but figured in terms of time we were about the same distance away due to our altitude, and that with a straight line to ZZZ1 we would be able to keep both our heads in the game running through checklists and monitoring the aircraft vs a circling descent into mountainous terrain. It was at this point that I noticed all my flight/nav displays and radios had failed as well as ACARS No Comm" being displayed on the FMS. I immediately notified the Captain and said that it might be better if he flew. He agreed and took control back as the Pilot Flying and I took over the smoke/fire/ fumes checklist in the QRH. ATC told us to expect one of the north runways into ZZZ1, but we told them we wanted [Runway] XXL as we were just on the north side of the airport. We requested direct ZZZZZ on the ILS to backup our visual approach, and the Captain used his emergency authority to proceed at about 320 knots in the descent order to expedite landing. A short time later I advised the Captain that I'd like to discontinue the smoke/fire/fumes checklist at step 20 since I had reached a decision point in the QRH, and it appeared I would most likely be heads down for almost all of the rest of the flight into ZZZ1 with this exhaustive checklist, and not be able to properly, and safely perform my duties as a PM. I came to this decision based on the fact that step 16 states we should not delay landing in order to complete the checklist. He agreed. We then briefed and ran a descent and approach checklist. The Captain asked me to call ZZZ1 OPS to let them know we were coming and for them to relay the info to Dispatch, but I reminded him that the #2 radio and comm panel had failed and the ACARS was no comm. It was with the Master Caution recall on the descent checklist that we realized how many issues were piling up beyond the TR and smoke. Looking up after being prompted by the recall we saw a solid portion of the overhead panel was lit. With the glare from the smoke and setting sun we were only able to pickup the airport just outside of ZZZZZ. The Captain disconnected the autopilot and proceeded to fly a visual approach backed up by the LNAV track for the ILS 17L. I noticed during the approach that the Captain had to trim manually, which led me to believe that we had obviously lost electrical control. With the landing checklist we also discovered that the auto speed brake would not arm, so the Captain asked me to back him up for the manual deployment. We landed in the touchdown zone and exited at gate without incident, where CFR (crash fire rescue) was waiting. We stopped in order for CFR to do a quick external inspection. As it was pretty quickly obvious the smoke was inside the aircraft and they weren't seeing anything outside, we asked them to get out of the way so we could get to a gate and let our pax stop breathing fumes. After shutting down the engines the APU appeared to be supplying only partial power and the ground call horn sounded constantly. Due to this issue the cabin was already dark, and knowing we were dealing with an electrical issue we opted to remove all power from the aircraft and performed the secure checklist. A short time later, CFR and a maintenance person were able to find the cause of the TR failure and pulled one of the TR boxes out of the E&E bay (electronics & engineering), which showed significant electrical fire damage. Lesson learned: maintain awareness of the type of emergency and aircraft state, compared to how long QRH steps could take you out of the critical Pilot Monitoring role. This checklist taught me to bring my head back up and get a grasp on the fact that we were in a rapid descent, over mountains, with half of our displays and comms out and I was only half aware of some of the radio calls and aircraft state. This was more concerning to me."
ASRS:1773693.s: During cruise at 40,000 ft, the crew encountered electrical smoke and a TRU failure, leading to multiple system losses including flight displays and radios. They diverted to ZZZ1, flew a visual approach with manual trim and speed brakes, and landed safely with no injuries.

ASRS:1773707.n: Crew briefed the Visual Approach backed up by the ILS RWY 23. The Jeppesen 11-1 chart, dated 13 NOV 20, depicts a PAPI on the left side of the runway. Crew did not see a PAPI during the approach, and Air Traffic Control confirmed there has never been a PAPI installed on either RWY 23 or RWY 05. [Cause was] incorrect charting. Although this event was Day-VMC, the charting error could seriously mislead a crew at night, particularly if the ILS or GS is inoperative on RWY 23 and the crew is expecting a visual glide path.
ASRS:1773707.s: The flight crew expected a PAPI on the left during a visual approach to RWY 23 based on an incorrect Jeppesen chart. Air Traffic Control confirmed no PAPI exists, identifying the cause as charting errors that could mislead crews at night.

ASRS:1773708.n: I entered the ramp from Taxiway E5, established on the center line. Traveling parallel, same direction, in the designated vehicle lane to my left was a large fuel truck. Rate of travel was approximately 10 - 15 mph with my aircraft overtaking. As I approached where the vehicle lane has a T intersection and runs across the taxi line to the parking ramp, the fuel truck took the turn without stopping. As soon as I noticed the vehicle taking the turn, I immediately initiated a stop with foot brake and full engine reverse. The driver noticed my aircraft as soon as he made the turn and also stopped. The fuel truck then reversed to provide wing tip clearance so I could proceed. If I had taken evasive action that involved any turn away from the fuel truck, it is likely that the left wing tip would have been close to, if not impacting the front area of the fuel truck. There was little to no margin. After parking and securing the aircraft, I did talk to the fuel truck driver. He admitted that he did not see my aircraft and that the large fuel trucks have a blind spot on the right hand side, which is where I was in relationship to him. However, he acknowledged that he did not stop to clear the turn. This vehicle roadway and subsequent T intersection does not have any mandatory vehicle stop markings before traveling across the ramp center line. It may be suggested to add markings to reinforce the practice of stopping to clear the turn. I would also suggest that [the truck operator] add larger mirrors or combination of mirrors to address the blind spot issue if they haven't already. Finally, this underscores the necessity of reasonably slow travel speeds for both aircraft and service vehicles for ALL operators. Had either fuel truck or my aircraft been traveling faster, which has been observed in the past, it is very likely a collision would have occurred despite the evasive action taken.
ASRS:1773708.s: A pilot taxiing an aircraft on the ramp nearly collided with a fuel truck that failed to stop at a T-intersection crossing the taxi line. The incident was caused by the truck driver's blind spot and lack of stop markings, resulting in a close call where the pilot used reverse thrust to avoid impact.

ASRS:1773715.n: Lost SA partially on arrival. Approach gave us a 240 heading and asked us to call the field. I had selected managed speed out of 10,000 and was configuring. Extended gear descending through 9,200, so we could continue to slow. Aircraft wasn't slowing. Captured LOC, but overshot a bit. Glide slope didn't capture. Once I saw the PAPI I saw I was low I leveled, continued to configure and slow. Leveled at 1,000 feet AFL momentarily to rejoin glideslope and ensure configured for stabilized approach. Had runway in sight the whole time after turning final, met gates at 1,000 feet AFL and 500 feet AFL, but felt behind and should have gone around. Maintenance delay, unfamiliar airport, late runway change, long day (nearly 9 hours of flying), no approach control (ZZZ Center handling approach due to COVID outage).I should have asked for vectors onto the approach rather than accepting visual. ZZZ is surrounded by high terrain, I was unfamiliar even though I felt I had prepared carefully, vectors would have provided a less dynamic environment. Also, if I were in a similar situation, I would go-around and ensure I don't press when I feel at all like I have lost SA. Also, the high altitude made slowing the aircraft down more difficult. I didn't include that in my briefing. I know better, but after the long day I failed to consider that as a factor. ATC gave us a 90 degree plus vector for Runway XXR and asked us to call the field. We had it in sight and were cleared for the visual. We were above the glideslope, with flaps 1, put the gear down to slow down, and used managed speed. The approach was armed, caught, but overshot the localizer because the aircraft wasn't slowing down. The glideslope didn't capture and we were then low on the glide slope as we passed through it from above. We leveled off, slowed down and finished configuring. We were within stable criteria at 1,000 and 500 feet, but it was a messy approach.Cause - Long duty day, extended due to maintenance. Bad vector from ATC and pressure to go visual. Approach was closed and Denver center was handling approach.Don't be pressured into accepting a visual at night with mountainous terrain. Go-around if an approach is feeling uncomfortable. Slow down earlier when at a higher elevation airport.
ASRS:1773715.s: The crew experienced a loss of situational awareness during a visual approach at a high-altitude airport due to a long duty day, maintenance delays, and an aggressive ATC vector. They stabilized late after overshooting the localizer and passing below the glideslope, attributing the event to fatigue and pressure to accept a visual clearance in mountainous terrain.

ASRS:1773721.n: While setting standard takeoff power, EICAS annunciated 'overspeed' with the associated aural warning momentarily (approximately 1 sec). 80 KTS airspeed check was missed during the distraction, and airspeed was compared at 110 KIAS. Immediately at 110 KIAS, Captain's airspeed decreased to 30 KIAS, the lowest value on the indicator. I elected to discontinue the takeoff at that time due to the lack of airspeed and the convective weather along the initial climb out and departure routing in the terminal area. After the accomplishment of the rejected takeoff maneuver, the First Officer stated that the speed was 120 KIAS at the initiation of the reject maneuver. V1 was 135 KIAS. All associated checklists were accomplished after clearing the runway. Brake energy was calculated to be under the caution zone. After conferencing with [Operations and Maintenance], and a 757 Check Airman who was jumpseating with us, the decision was made to reattempt the takeoff. Prior to the second takeoff attempt, Tower issued a halt to all departures due to windshear alerts. At about the same time, the Captain's PFD showed a flashing and sometimes steady yellow boxed ALT. The decision was then made to terminate and return the aircraft to Maintenance. Captain's airspeed indication loss for unknown reasons at the time. Contributing factors were the momentary 'overspeed' warning, and the convective activity on the climb out and departure.
ASRS:1773721.s: During takeoff of a Boeing 757, a momentary overspeed warning distracted the crew, causing a missed 80 KTS check and a Captain's airspeed indication drop to 30 KIAS at 110 KIAS. The crew rejected the takeoff, but subsequent windshear alerts and a flashing altitude indication led to terminating the flight and returning to maintenance.

ASRS:1773722.n: The airplane was released with Auxiliary Power Unit (APU) deferred, thus required air-cart start procedures in the gate. Preflight, airplane setup, briefings, checklists, crew duties, paperwork, ground interactions were all normal, and (Minimum Equipment Lists) MELs were complied with. Normal air-cart start and subsequent pushback were all normal. After clearing the ground crew off the headset, the Right, Number 1 Inner Tank Fuel Pump faulted. We complied with the instruction to turn off the pump, and contacted Ramp Control and Maintenance on separate radios.The Captain worked with Maintenance while the First Officer worked with Ramp Control. The Captain discussed the need to do a deferral and the First Officer received instructions for us to taxi to spot for off the gate maintenance, or something to that effect. Neither of us had ever heard of such a thing, and I told the First Officer to say, 'No, we're not doing that.'I called on my cell phone and told them about the situation, and we began discussing the need for a maintenance deferral, and whether or not we had enough fuel under the circumstances. I suggested we look at deleting the alternate from the flight plan if it would be legal to do so. The Dispatcher said he'd begin working on it. It was about this time that Maintenance suggested we go to a designated spot for hot refueling. I again said we wouldn't do that and that the best plan should we need fuel would be to just taxi into the gate we just left, shut down, get fuel, and have Maintenance sign off the fuel pump. Maintenance told me that that wasn't the best idea because if we did that we'd have a long delay and have to do the paperwork over again. I called Dispatch back and he said there was no way we could just do the deferral and that we'd need to go back for fuel, and I said fine we will do that. As a note, Dispatch told me that he had also never heard of hot refueling. At that point I told Maintenance what we were going to go back into the gate. Maintenance proceeded to explain that the hot refuel was done all the time and that the FAA and that Company Safety had approved of the procedure. He was adamant that the hot fuel was the best way to proceed. Ramp also confirmed the procedure, so after discussing it as a crew, we agreed it sounded like a legitimate request, and we agreed to go to the spot and proceed with the fueling there. When we arrived, we were stopped by a pickup truck pulling close to the airplane that made me stop. There was no further guidance from Ramp, other than to ask us to pull the tail clear of a taxi lane. A second vehicle with built-in airstairs arrived at the airplane. He began giving us hand signals that made little sense, and eventually hooked up to the intercom system, and asked us to shut down the engines. I suggested that was not a very good idea and that we could have done that in the gate and that we were there for hot fueling. He then said to just shut down engine number two and to open the door so he could give us a fuel slip. I asked the First Officer to do an after landing flow to make sure we were caught up, and then to open the door after disarming the slides.We received fuel, a fuel slip, coordinated hand signals, ran appropriate checklists, did a cross-bleed start to get engine number two back on line, accomplished the after-start checklist, and taxied via Ramp's instructions. The First Officer made adjustments to the aircraft performance data and we ran a new performance briefing, noting a two knot increase in the new V speeds, and feeling comfortable that we had returned to safely normal operations. We proceeded to taxi and takeoff with normal operations.At cruise we received a message from Dispatch that we didn't do a new weight and balance. He asked for our fuel onboard, we sent them. Either an ill conceived procedure or a lack of adequate resources for flight crews to safely conduct this procedure.The Pilot in Command shouldhave stuck to his first decision. And from a more proactive approach, a checklist should be developed and added to the QRH. The maintenance deferral flowchart should mention the need to revisit weight and balance. requirements and anything else we might have missed. Additionally, I would highly encourage a module during simulator training that runs crews through this exercise and the use of new flow charts and a checklist. The flight blocked out and then had a maintenance problem. Right Inner Tank Inoperative. This not a flagged item, so the decision was made to put the aircraft in a maintenance area on the ramp. The Minimum Equipment List (MEL) requires 8800 lb penalty fuel and adjust fuel for FL200. Fueling is allowed in the maintenance area. Since it was not a block turnback, a new release was not required. We did the prescribed procedure with Maintenance and I then sent a mini flight plan showing the new numbers with fuel penalties. After fueling was finished, I sent an ACARS asking for the new fuel breakdown so the hub could send a new Weight and Balance. However, the plane had already blocked and departed without an up to date to the weight and balance. I informed the Duty Officer and then tried to send the new weight and balance. The new weight and balance never showed up in the crew's ACARS messages although it showed up in the playback screen in ACARS. So I copied and pasted and sent the information, but did not notice that the information in the weight and balance that the hub sent was the information from the original block out. Even though we had received the correct fuel breakdown from the crew enroute. The flight landed at its destination and I talked with the crew and passed them on to the Duty Officer. The initial problem was caused by crew departing without an updated weight and balance. I suggest following procedures when an aircraft blocks back to a maintenance area
ASRS:1773722.s: The flight crew and maintenance personnel addressed a Right Inner Tank Fuel Pump fault by performing a hot refuel on the ramp, but the aircraft departed without an updated weight and balance. The reporter attributes this error to an ill-conceived procedure and a lack of adequate resources, noting that the crew should have stuck to their initial decision to return to the gate.

ASRS:1773734.n: While crew was preparing for departure in the aircraft, an ACARS was sent from Captain to Dispatch notifying that there was dry ice in the lower forward compartment and this was not reflected on the release. I was not notified by the ramp agent that there was any dry ice on the aircraft. I calculated the required overburn and forwarded the information to the crew via ACARS. I phoned Ramp Agent to inform that I was not notified of any dry ice in the lower compartment of this 777 aircraft. The response was [the] agent not aware that Dispatch should be notified of dry ice in the lower compartments. Agent assumed a very defensive tone and I terminated the call. I explained the situation briefly to Flight Coordination. The response was that agent was never aware of any requirement to inform Dispatch in this situation also. My concern is that these two ramp agents are relatively senior company ramp agents and neither one claims to be aware of this essential procedure. The cause was two senior ZZZ ramp agents claim to be completely unaware of an essential procedure to notify Dispatch in the event there is dry ice in the lower compartments of a 777 aircraft. I suggest remedial training for any or all ZZZ ramp agents to familiarize them with their required function in this instance.
ASRS:1773734.s: Dispatch notified the 777 crew of unlisted dry ice in the lower forward compartment during departure preparation. Two senior ZZZ ramp agents claimed unawareness of the essential procedure to inform Dispatch, prompting a recommendation for remedial training.

ASRS:1773737.n: It was night. We were on the ground taxiing to the runway. We had a jumpseater in the cockpit as well. We were cleared across one runway and to taxi to our assigned runway. After crossing I called for the Before Takeoff checklist. The First Officer proceeded to accomplish those duties which included contacting the cabin crew. While the First Officer was communicating with the cabin we were cleared for take off. When the First Officer was done with the cabin notification I informed him that we were cleared for takeoff. The First Officer ran the checklist. As I was taxiing to the runway there were a lot of lights due to the proximity [of] two runways beginning in about the same location. It was a little confusing and I verbalized my confusion by saying 'Is this the right runway' meaning the one I was about to taxi onto. The jumpseater piped in and said it was a different runway. I was referring to the one in front of me he was referring to the one to my left. So, I proceeded forward crossing the runway we were cleared to takeoff on looking for the entrance to my runway and stopped on the other side realizing I had been on the correct runway. Tower saw what happened and canceled our takeoff clearance. We were in fact on the correct runway, I just wasn't sure that we were. We never lined up for takeoff on any runway. We just proceeded across the one [we] were cleared to take off on. The cause was partly due to my limited use of that runway in the past and especially at night. There was a degree of unfamiliarity with that runway. Another factor was my accepting a takeoff clearance before the First Officer was back fully engaged with me and feeling a little rushed. On my part, I could have declined takeoff clearance until we were finished with the 'before takeoff checklist' and both of us of us could have been fully engaged in only taxiing. Pilots were not familiar with the runway configuration at night. Confused assigned runway with an intersecting runway. We taxied through approach end after being cleared for takeoff. Tower said to cancel takeoff clearance and turn around taxi back and hold short of the runway. We complied. We reviewed our taxi charts and realized our error. The Captain and First Officer were not familiar with the runway configuration at night. From our perspective it seemed the runway lights to 35 may have been turned down and due to that it could've been mistaken for 32 as we expected the lights for an active runway to be brighter. It would have also been helpful to have moving maps on taxi charts. We would have realized immediately where we were. As it stood the lights being turned down confused the unfamiliar crew into thinking they had to taxi further to Runway 35. From our perspective it seemed the runway lights may have been turned down and due to that we could've been mistaken our runway as we expected the lights for an active runway to be brighter. It would have also been helpful to have moving maps on taxi charts. We would have realized immediately where we were. As it stood the lights being turned down confused the unfamiliar crew into thinking they had to taxi further to the runway.
ASRS:1773737.s: The Captain and First Officer, unfamiliar with the night runway configuration, taxied across their assigned runway after receiving takeoff clearance due to confusion over dimmed lights. Tower canceled the clearance after the crew crossed the approach end, and they returned to hold short.

ASRS:1773740.n: After leveling at 10,000 ft MSL, IMC, we had an ICE caution message appear. We turned on the wing anti-ice system. The cowl anti-ice was already on. Shortly after an ANTI-ICE DUCT warning message posted on ED1. While we were running the QRH checklist the warning message extinguished. It did not reoccur. Then an ANTI-ICE DUCT caution message posted on ED2 for approximately 15 seconds, then cleared. It did not reoccur. Approximately 1/2 to 3/4 of an inch of rime was visible on the wiper arm at this time. We notified ATC and requested an emergency return to ZZZ and lower altitude to get out of the freezing precipitation. An intermittent R Wing A/I (anti-ice) caution message posted until landing. It did not stay up long enough to run the R WING A/I caution QRH checklist. We returned to ZZZ safely. No ice accumulation was noted on post flight inspection. Apparent equipment failure. Wing anti-ice warning and caution messages in icing conditions with ice accumulating.
ASRS:1773740.s: The crew encountered icing at 10,000 ft MSL, triggering anti-ice duct warnings and visible rime accumulation. They declared an emergency to return to ZZZ at a lower altitude, attributing the intermittent system messages to an apparent equipment failure.

ASRS:1773747.n: Approximately 3 hours into our flight from ZZZZ-ZZZ, Flight Attendant X told me that his daughter had tested positive for COVID-19 the previous day. Flight Attendant X said that he contacted Airline when he learned of his child's positive test result and was advised to continue with his pairing, despite his immediate family member receiving a positive COVID test result. It made me extremely uncomfortable to hear that Flight Attendant X was directly exposed and that he chose to continue to work, possibly endangering the health and safety of others. Flight Attendant X also mentioned that he is a [Medical Professional] and exposed to COVID positive patients regularly at his other job. While Flight Attendant X may not have received the support from the company in line with our responsibility to keep one another as safe as possible during the global pandemic, common sense and personal ethos would dictate that one would remove them self from flying until they had a negative test result and quarantine period of 14 days. I contacted ZZZ Supervisor upon landing in ZZZ and expressed my concerns.
ASRS:1773747.s: During a flight from ZZZZ-ZZZ, a pilot reported that a flight attendant continued working after his daughter tested positive for COVID-19, despite airline approval. The pilot expressed concern over potential health risks and contacted a ZZZ Supervisor upon landing.

ASRS:1773750.n: Passenger X boarded the aircraft and proceeded to self-upgrade himself to a better seat. When he was asked about this by another FA, he held his ground. Apparently, out in the gate area, he was quite belligerent. So, a member of the ground staff had to come on board and move him back to his assigned seat. He said that he was fine. After takeoff and constantly throughout the flight, I had to ask him to put his mask on. It happened several times. He was not happy that I kept asking him. I guess he felt that he was exempt from the wearing of masks.
ASRS:1773750.s: A passenger boarded, self-upgraded his seat, and acted belligerently, requiring ground staff to move him back to his assigned seat. During the flight, the flight attendant repeatedly asked him to wear a mask, which he refused, apparently believing he was exempt.

ASRS:1773754.n: The last few month wearing a mask has affected my health. I have had constant headaches, brain fog, difficult concentrating and exhaustion. My eyesight is also affected when wearing a mask. The depletion of oxygen, increased exposure to carbon dioxide may be to blame. I fear risk of infection only because we are all touching our faces more than EVER with masks on. I used an oximeter to check my levels on a deadhead segment from ZZZ to ZZZ1. In hotel room [it was] 99, when on flight [it was] 89-94 for just a 2 hour flight. We are masked for 10-15 [hours] lately, sometimes 5 days a week. I have noticed I'm also sneezing a lot more, which, now finding out may be the poisonous spray being sprayed on the planes. Every flight attendants health is being affected.
ASRS:1773754.s: A flight attendant reported health issues including headaches and low oxygen saturation (89-94%) while wearing a mask during a two-hour deadhead flight. The crew member attributed these symptoms to oxygen depletion, increased carbon dioxide, and potential exposure to poisonous sprays on the aircraft.

ASRS:1773755.n: A party of 3 came on just as we were to close the flight, the agents stated he was exempt from wearing a mask, to which we questioned what he was told he was going to be able to do for the flight, which was not to wear his mask. The crew on the whole questioned what the Agent was saying, the Purser approached the Captain who said he would ask ZZZ operations, in the meantime the Lead came down and agreed with the crew that there were no exceptions to our mask policy, with debate and talking to the passenger we all looked to find it in black and white, while waiting for ZZZ to call back, the gate agents closed the door and pulled the jet bridge. The Purser explained to the passenger from [seat number] that he and one of his guests could move to seat area X to keep them separated from the majority of our guests, during the flight I have to say I had to tell his friend to keep his mask on more, I chatted to them prior to landing and informed them they would have to wear their mask for their trip itinerary as there were no exceptions...that they had been miss informed prior to our flight. They actually seemed nice.
ASRS:1773755.s: Cabin crew encountered a passenger claiming a mask exemption during boarding, leading to a dispute with gate agents who closed the door before operations confirmed no exceptions existed. The Purser relocated the passenger and a guest to a separate seat area, and the crew enforced mask compliance throughout the flight after clarifying the policy.

ASRS:1773757.n: I was [the] Purser on Aircraft X. When we boarded I noticed the entire phone was missing from XLR Jumpseat. The cockpit also informed me it was missing and that it was okay to go. I said that used to be a 'no go' item. I have no way of notifying the cockpit if there was any emergency- be it evacuation, a threat level, a medical emergency, etc. I asked if there was another plane that we could take. I notified the system that we were checking within maintenance on an issue before we board. We still had 15 minutes left to board. I was told that I was to refer to the Flight Attendant Manual regarding other means of communicating. I'm not sure if you've worn a mask and spoken through a megaphone, but that's not really a reliable means of communication with a mask on. And it still does not allow me to communicate with the cockpit. We were on a type X aircraft where the other FAs are backwards facing and would not know if a situation were to arise up front. We were also advised that it was to be a bumpy flight and we might need to remain seated for the duration of the flight. An in-flight Supervisor met the aircraft. Captain said he would refuse the aircraft if I was uncomfortable. I said that decision should not solely rely on me. However, this was the second flight in a row where the forward intercom was broken. This one happened to be completely missing a phone. The one prior was hanging off a screw. A Mechanic also came up during boarding to see what the problem was. I said this should be a 'no go' item referring to the missing phone. He said he deferred it that morning and that the part was awaiting the aircraft in ZZZ. So the aircraft had flown two previous legs before mine in this condition. I believe that a PA INOP is 'not' a no-go. A missing intercom should be a no-go item.
ASRS:1773757.s: The Purser on Aircraft X reported the forward intercom phone was missing during boarding, a defect deferred by a mechanic despite the aircraft flying two prior legs. Although the Captain offered to refuse the flight, the crew proceeded after being advised to use unreliable alternative communication methods.

ASRS:1773770.n: Two passengers, traveling together, in seats, X1 and X2, were wearing non-compliant masks. FA C noticed the non-complaint masks in main cabin when I was beginning the safety announcement. From the front of plane, I could see the couple arguing with FA C and refusing to put the company provided masks that Flight Attendant was offering. I approached passengers, with FA C still present, and asked them to wear the compliant masks, and they initially refused me as well. I then asked them to make a decision to wear the compliant masks, or we would be required to return the plane to the gate. They complied. We took off. Once at cruise phase, the gentleman in X1 stopped me and started to engage me as to how he has been allowed to wear those masks on previous flights and that they were safer masks. I responded that he could reach out to customer care and write to the FAA about the masks they were wearing.
ASRS:1773770.s: Two passengers in seats X1 and X2 refused to wear compliant masks during the pre-takeoff safety announcement, prompting a threat to return to the gate which they accepted. Later at cruise, the male passenger argued about mask safety, and the flight attendant directed him to contact customer care or the FAA.

ASRS:1773776.n: In ZZZ airport, we have employees testing positive for COVID-19, but yet the process of notification (notifying the crew) is very subjective. There are technicians, which have tested positive. The company has only notified a selective few to quarantine.There are technicians who have tested positive and have contaminated the rest of the crew. Some have been forced to take their own sick time because the company refuses to acknowledge they have been exposed at work. The exposure happened at work because they were all in the same room and worked together. The company says they have followed CDC guidelines, but how can that be when more technicians are testing positive at work. Let's have guys who were at work quarantine and have the company notify the work areas that maybe have been exposed.
ASRS:1773776.s: Technicians at ZZZ airport tested positive for COVID-19 and exposed other crew members while working in the same room. The reporter states the company's selective notification process failed to quarantine exposed staff, forcing some to use personal sick time despite workplace exposure.

ASRS:1773777.n: Bus overcrowding every day. The lack of buses and social distance is not followed. We have told the company numerous of times regarding to inability to social distance. Their response is 'do not take the bus, wait for the other bus.'
ASRS:1773777.s: Crew members reported daily bus overcrowding and a failure to maintain social distance. The company advised staff to skip buses and wait for the next one instead of addressing the lack of available transport.

ASRS:1773796.n: What happened: Aircraft Y was given a take off clearance for a runway that was occupied by a helicopter that had landed on the opposite end and was awaiting taxi instructions.What led to this: The helicopter was coming in from the east and requested to land on the western side of the airport. The active runways at the time were south to north (XXL and XXR). The Tower cleared the helicopter to land on the numbers of an inactive runway XY, which would keep the helicopter on the eastern side of the airport, away from the flow of fixed wing traffic. About 5 minutes elapsed between the time the helicopter landed and Aircraft Y flew over the helicopter.During that time I believe the Controller may have been distracted by pattern traffic, Aircraft Z arrival (this was a factor prior to the helicopter landing which resulted in the controller deciding to keep the helicopter on the eastern side of the airport), a change in Aircraft Y IFR clearance, and by a pilot of an airplane who mistakenly made a final approach to the wrong parallel runway.Starting from the point at which the helicopter lands, the following exchanges were heard.Aircraft A was cleared for touch and go #2 behind Aircraft Z for runway XXL.Aircraft B was cleared to Land runway XXR.A few seconds after Aircraft B acknowledged the landing clearance the tower issue a taxi instruction to the airborne Aircraft B 'hold short of runway XXR I am going to have a departure off runway XZ.'Aircraft B responded 'I am in the air.'The tower replied 'Disregard, Land and hold short of runway XZ, land and hold short of runway XZ.'Aircraft B responded that this was their intention and would be parking in an area that would not put them at risk of crossing into runway XZ.The tower approved a request to taxi back to parking after Aircraft B completed a 180 degree turn on the runway after landing.30 seconds later the tower controller said to Aircraft B, 'Disregard the land and hold short clearance. I won't have that departure. He will be holding in place, though.'The tower instructed Aircraft Y to line up and wait on runway XZ.The 737 had already landed on XXL and the tower cleared a Cessna for takeoff runway XXL.20 seconds later Aircraft B realized he was about to land on top of Aircraft A who had just been cleared for takeoff and asked the tower if he should go around. There was no response. Aircraft B hailed the tower again. I observed Aircraft B descend below 100 ft AGL before deciding to go around. 40 seconds elapsed between the 1st and 3rd time Aircraft B called the tower.The tower gave the departing Aircraft A, a mixed up call starting with 'line up and- cancel take off- cleared for takeoff runway XXL'The tower then gave Aircraft B instructions to remain in the upwind, he would give him a crosswind instruction to follow.Aircraft B apologized for lining up to land on the wrong runway.As soon as the frequency congestion allowed, knowing there was a jet on the opposite side of my runway, I made a call 'Tower, Helicopter (call-sign) holding position on the numbers of [Runway] XY ready to taxi to (name of ramp)'. The call was not acknowledged and 55 seconds later an amended departure clearance, combined with a takeoff clearance, was given to the waiting Aircraft Y. I did not hear the departure clearance and Aircraft Y began racing towards us. Ironically, I may have turned to my student and said to keep an eye on Aircraft Y. As it rushed overhead I made an aggressive maneuver off of the numbers and onto the closest available vacant spot beyond the runway safety area.Previous experiences at this airport have made it clear when a helicopter accepts a landing clearance to a spot, taxiway, intersection, or helipad, they are expected to remain there until given a clearance to taxi. Quite often the controllers will vector an arriving helicopter far around the approach or departure center lines of the active runways and restrict them to altitudes below 600 MSL instead of accommodating a flight path crossing the active runways at a higher safe altitude. Less often are we allowed to land as in the case above in a place safely away from the departing/arriving aircraft, and in a position where we can easily air taxi at a moment's notice. A helicopter is highly maneuverable and this aspect should be used to the utmost advantage when minimizing delays to arriving or departing airplanes. As mentioned earlier the helicopter's arrival was prior to Aircraft Z checking in with the tower. There was Aircraft A on a half-mile final to runway XXL ahead of Aircraft Z.
