With several miles of spacing between Aircraft Z and Aircraft A, the tower began to ask the helicopter to pass behind the landing Aircraft A. We accepted. The tower immediately reversed their decision due to Aircraft Z scheduled arrival and cleared us to land on the numbers of [Runway] XY with the restriction 'remain north of XX'. We accepted the clearance to land. It is very likely that a helicopter crossing the approach end of XXL shortly after the landing Aircraft A would have had little to no effect on any of the other present arriving or departing aircraft.
ASRS:1773796.s: A helicopter landed on inactive Runway XY while awaiting taxi instructions, but the controller issued a takeoff clearance to Aircraft Y on the same runway due to distraction from multiple traffic conflicts. The helicopter pilot executed an aggressive maneuver off the runway to avoid a collision as Aircraft Y raced overhead.

ASRS:1773797.n: On date I was conducting training in an R22 Helicopter departing out of ZZZ at XA:45 local time to ZZZ1. Winds were predominantly out of the west at around 10 kts and we joined left closed traffic for RWY 26 at ZZZ1. There was high training volume and I estimate 7 aircraft were on the ground waiting to depart or actively in the Right Closed Traffic for RWY XX plus our Helicopter. At around XB:10 local time a Jet taxied to the active with no Radio (or no radio communication was made) as we were on a left downwind for [Runway] XX. Local pilots made calls on the radio so all would be aware of his departure and be vigilant/use caution. The jet took off without incident and departed to the North. As pilots worked together to sequence traffic we made our base and final leg before again departing XX to rejoin left closed traffic. At approximately XB:15 local time on the upwind of XX roughly 300ft AGL without warning the jet made a low pass on runway XY at very high speed. I would estimate the pilot was 300ft off our starboard side and about 100ft below our current altitude. I was able to track his flight after the incident to find his Ground Speed was in excess of 330mph. The Jet than proceeded back out to the North again and ended up circling to land on RWY XY this time to a full stop. (The following is my personal opinion) I believe this pilot does not have any remorse for his action. He has an attitude that the FAA can't/won't get him in trouble for this reckless behavior. He wasn't breaking any REG by operating without a radio in an ECHO airspace but his speed certainly was in violation of FAR 91.117(a) and given the high training volume being conducted on this day the pilot showed a clear disregard for other pilots or even his/her own safety.
ASRS:1773797.s: A pilot conducting R22 helicopter training at ZZZ1 reported a jet made an unannounced low pass at 300ft AGL and 330mph, passing 100ft below and 300ft to the right of the helicopter. The reporter attributed the incident to the jet pilot's reckless disregard for safety and violation of speed limits despite operating without radio communication.

ASRS:1773806.n: Flight was from ZZZ to ZZZ2 with a stop to pick up a passenger at ZZZ1. ZZZ Approach provided flight following all the way to ZZZ1 as I was unfamiliar with the airport and had difficulty identifying it from the air. After overflying the field at 2,000 ft (Approach assigned flight following altitude) a frequency change to the CTAF was approved and made. I descended to pattern altitude and crossed midfield before entering downwind leg for runway XX. Crossing midfield, turning to downwind, base and final, position reports were made on the CTAF. No other aircraft operating at ZZZ1 were heard on frequency. Landing XX, proceeded to back taxi to the end of the runway. At the XY threshold, my passenger saw me and began approaching the aircraft. So as to not create an undue hazard to my passenger, I exited the runway onto the available taxiway and turned parallel to XY. At this point, my left wingtip was impinging on the runway.I continued to hear no other aircraft on frequency as I performed a safety briefing for my passenger and ensured he was ready to fly. Shortly thereafter, another aircraft landed on runway 19. This aircraft proceeded to back taxi on XY and then made contact on CTAF. The other aircraft pilot reported to have been making calls on CTAF and attempting to reach me prior to landing, but I did not hear him. The other aircraft pilot reported landing left of center due to the runway incursion. On resuming flight towards ZZZ2 another aerodrome on the same CTAF frequency performed a radio check with me and assured that they could receive me loud and clear.
ASRS:1773806.s: The pilot of a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ2 with a stop at ZZZ1 caused a runway incursion by exiting onto a taxiway with the left wingtip on the runway while picking up a passenger. Another aircraft subsequently landed left of center due to the obstruction, though the reporter noted no prior radio contact was heard.

ASRS:1773822.n: While on arrival into Nashville, we were being vectored by Approach. We were just assigned vectors outside of the arrival. We were notified by the controlling agency that we could expect moderate turbulence between 9,000 and 12,000 feet in the descent, which we did encounter. Upon reaching 5,000 feet, we were still encountering moderate turbulence. As we accepted our vector to heading 010, we encountered a pocket of severe turbulence which sent the airplane into an upsetting unusual attitude. My Captain immediately recognized the issue, as the autopilot kicked itself off, he initiated the proper recovery procedure. As that happened, we encountered a second pocket of severe turbulence which further upset the aircraft attitude and resulted in additional altitude loss. My Captain went full thrust and maximum nose up attitude to recover. We experienced moderate turbulence all the way to the ground that day, but were able to land safely.
ASRS:1773822.s: During arrival into Nashville, the flight crew encountered severe turbulence below 5,000 feet while being vectored by Approach, causing the autopilot to disengage and the aircraft to enter an unusual attitude. The Captain executed recovery procedures with full thrust and maximum nose-up attitude, resulting in additional altitude loss before a safe landing.

ASRS:1773824.n: In a left turn to intercept final approach course for RWY (Runway) XX at ZZZ. Altitude 1,800 ft. Received RA to descend and complied. Traffic had been previously unannounced by Approach. (If they did announce, we neither heard nor replied).We did not see traffic prior to RA. Cloud, haze, and rain were factors. Our assumption is that the Cessna dropped below clouds to maintain VFR.Complied with RA. Observed traffic passing above right wing. Approximately 400-500 ft.
ASRS:1773824.s: During a left turn to intercept final for RWY XX at 1,800 ft, the crew received an unannounced RA due to a Cessna dropping below clouds in rain and haze. The crew complied with the RA, observing the traffic pass 400–500 ft above the right wing.

ASRS:1773838.n: On [Date], I was acting as Pilot in Command (PIC) of a UH-60 L Army National Guard Helicopter conducting a round-trip air movement of crew and passengers from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. I was sitting left seat, my Co-pilot (PI) sat right seat. I had two crewmembers in the gunner's seats (Row 2), and one passenger in Row 3. Total: 5 souls on board.Earlier in the day, we had flown IFR from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 for a fuel stop before heading to ZZZ. We had received a military weather briefing and were aware of an AIRMET Zulu for moderate icing along the route. We monitored PIREPS and determined as a crew that the risk of anything beyond moderate icing was minimal, as the few PIREPS observed were for light rime ice at flight levels above our planned flight altitude.The conditions observed on the flight from ZZZ2 to ZZZ were very stable. There was a stratiform cloud layer, approximately 1,000 to 2,000 ft. thick, that we either flew below or above the cloud layer the entire way to ZZZ. We observed no icing.We were on the ground for approximately two hours after landing at ZZZ. I continued to monitor weather conditions, and it appeared they had not changed from the time we landed. I observed the same AIRMET Zulu and a couple of PIREPS reporting light rime above our planned flight level.Prior to departure, my crew and I conducted de-ice checks in accordance with our aircraft's technical manual, which all passed.After an uneventful climb to our requested flight level of 7,000 ft. MSL, we leveled off. At this time the annunciator panel gave us a warning of 'MR ICE DETECTED'. We had discussed this as an expected possibility, acknowledged the caution, and monitored our ice rate meter, which read 'Light Icing Detected'.At this time, I asked ATC if they knew where the cloud tops were. We were informed that they were at approximately 8,000 ft. MSL. Faced with the decision to climb approximately 1,000 ft. through visible moisture, or descend approximately 4,000 ft. through visible moisture, I requested to climb to 10,000 ft. MSL. ATC gave a clearance to 9,000 ft. MSL. We began our climb.In approximately 1.5 minutes, our icing condition worsened. Our ice rate meter pegged out at its maximum indication of severe icing. The helicopter began to shake, and we lost a dangerous amount of our main rotor RPM (a true [anomaly]). I immediately pressed down on the collective to preserve our rotor RPM, took the controls from my co-pilot, [advised ATC] by announcing 'PAN PAN PAN' on ZZZ Approach frequency. I asked the controller to help me get out of the icing situation and was ultimately cleared down to 2,500 ft. MSL.My crew and I flew the helicopter well, in a level attitude at approximately 2,500 ft. per minute. We maintained 100% rotor RPM during our decent and exited the cloud layer at approximately 3,000 ft. MSL. I tested the controls as we got closer to the surface to ensure I would be able to arrest the helicopter's rate of decent. Upon exiting the clouds, the icing condition improved, and the rest of the flight home was uneventful and under VFR conditions.Chain Of Events:How the problem arose: The problem arose from the unexpected encounter into severe icing.How it was discovered: The severe icing was detected by on the on-board ice detection system, severe vibrations were felt by the crew, and the low rotor warning alarm sounded.Corrective actions: The Good: The crew responded to the [situation] well by manipulating the flight controls to preserve rotor RPM, communicating the [anomaly] to ATC, and flying the aircraft out of the icing conditions.The Bad: The crew did not respond correctly to the initial 'ICE DETECTED' caution. In accordance with the UH-60 Operators Manual, 'The ice rate meter activates the ICE DETECTED caution when the BLADE DE-ICE POWER switch is turned off, informing the pilot of the requirement to turn on the system'. Contributing Factors:Neither the UH-60 Operating Manual or checklist clearly emphasizes the immediatememory item actions required in the event of an icing [situation].An updated -1 weather brief was not obtained from the Air Force Operational Weather Squadron by the Pilot in Command.Human Performance Considerations:The perception of the Pilot in Command that the 'AUTO' function on the ice rate meter meant that the system will 'automatically operate upon detection of ice' was incorrect.The perception of the Pilot in Command that the weather conditions would be the same on the return flight as they were on the first portion was incorrect.The actions of both the Pilot in Command and Co-pilot ultimately saved the lives of the crew, however their inaction to turn the de-ice system on was detrimental to the safe operation of the aircraft.Factors affecting the quality of human performance:Neither the Pilot or Co-pilot complained of fatigue or other exogenous factors prior the flight. Both had a good night's rest and were well within the confines of their duty day at the time of the incident.Recommendations:Ensure aircrew are intimately familiar with the de-ice equipment and capabilities on their aircraft. Recommend that changes be made to the UH-60 Operator's Manual and checklist to emphasize the seriousness of an icing [situation] and the immediate response required. This should be an underlined step. Once the ICE DETECTED caution appears, the immediate action required is for the blade de-ice switch to be turned ON.
ASRS:1773838.s: The PIC and crew of a UH-60 encountered severe icing at 7,000 ft after failing to activate the de-ice system upon the initial caution. This caused dangerous rotor RPM loss, requiring a PAN PAN call and descent to 2,500 ft to exit the clouds safely.

ASRS:1773848.n: On a flight from ZZZ to MPR, I flew a practice approach into MPR (RNAV 18) visually in VFR conditions with no view limiting device. As I was touching down on Runway 18 at MPR, I observed another aircraft taking off from the grass Runway 8. The other aircraft crossed in front of me about 400 feet ahead of me and was about 100 feet above me and climbing. I had made a number of radio calls including a 10 mile straight-in final, 5 mile final, 2 mile final and short final. I never heard the other aircraft make any calls. Upon landing, I realized that although I had plugged the MPR CTAF frequency into my radio, I never flipped that frequency to active. Therefore, I had been transmitting on and listening to the incorrect frequency (departure Tower frequency). I take full responsibility for not having the correct frequency active in my radio and will use this as a learning opportunity and a reminder to be more vigilant about confirming proper frequencies. I am surprised that the ZZZ Tower did not hear my 10 mile, 5 mile, 2 mile and short final calls and inform me that I was on the incorrect frequency.
ASRS:1773848.s: The pilot landed an aircraft on Runway 18 at MPR while another aircraft took off from Runway 8, crossing 400 feet ahead and 100 feet above. The near-miss occurred because the pilot transmitted on the incorrect departure Tower frequency instead of the active CTAF, failing to hear or be heard by other traffic.

ASRS:1773859.n: Early morning at roughly XA:30, Aircraft X flew from the west into ZZZ for pattern work. At the time Aircraft X was the only aircraft that was currently in ZZZ's airspace at the time of the event. Initially Aircraft X made a call to ZZZ Tower asking for pattern work. Since the aircraft was positioned over the mountains the response for ZZZ Tower came in weak. Clarification was requested by pilot flying and stated that the Air Traffic Control Tower was closed. The pilot flying treated the airport as a non-towered airport and switched frequency to XYY.Z. From that point the pilot flying used non-towered airport call outs to announce position. After completing three laps in the pattern an airport operations vehicle flagged down the pilot in command. The pilot in command then preceded to reject the takeoff and continue to the run up area. Airport operations advised the pilot to contact Tower at XXZ.A where the pilot was advised that he could continue pattern work yet had to take a phone number down. Pilot took down phone number and contacted Tower staff after the flight.Due to COVID-19 many ATC facilities are having to temporary close down due to cleaning. ZZZ has also been changing hours of ATC operation in the last ninety days. Pilots from ZZZ1 have also run into the problem of not properly reaching Air Traffic Control due to altered non-posted hours.The pilot in command flying was a student pilot that had recently soloed. When contacted by an airport operations vehicle, [they] only asked for intentions which the pilot responded that he was doing pattern work. At the time it could not be depicted if the airport operations vehicle told on XYY.Z to contact Tower on XXZ.A. In the future [if] airport operations could do this it would help. At the time the pilot thought the airport operations vehicle was attempting to do a FOD patrol of the runway since it was the early morning. The aircraft has been in the past known to have radio issues at random times.The student pilot will go over procedures with Class Delta airports with a flight instructor to mitigate problems in the future.
ASRS:1773859.s: A student pilot flying Aircraft X attempted pattern work at ZZZ, mistakenly treating it as non-towered due to weak radio reception and unposted tower closure hours. An airport operations vehicle flagged the pilot to reject takeoff, leading to a clarification that the tower was open on a different frequency.

ASRS:1773865.n: The incident with Aircraft X can best be described as the perfect storm where in this case the R-side Controller working [two sectors] was very busy and on top of that had numerous aircraft that departed ZZZ Approach level at 160 in his airspace without communication. Prior to me sitting on his position he reached out to the Supervisor to request a D-side along with advising that ZZZ Approach was not shipping aircraft in a timely manner. One aircraft he had was Aircraft Y who was 53 miles into his airspace level at 160 still not on frequency and Aircraft Z, 23 miles into his airspace with the same issue. I mention this because I believe this was the biggest contributing factor to the event with Aircraft X. Aircraft A was at 160 and he descended the aircraft to 10,000 thinking he was a ZZZ1/ZZZ2 arrival and to alleviate all potential traffic conflicts. The main problem was as soon as I sat down and signed in, the R-side was too busy to give me a brief but I was eager to help and to catch up on anything. As I was beginning my scan I noticed Aircraft X getting close to the ZZZ1 Approach airspace at 10,000 without a hand-off and I immediately jumped on the line to coordinate with the ZZZ1 Approach Controller. I began to try to APREQ the aircraft at 10,000 but the ZZZ1 Controller realizing he had an arrival to ZZZZZ [Intersection] already at 10,000 he instructed me to descend Aircraft X to 080, the R-side complied. There was no loss of separation between any aircraft, however, I have decided to report this event because I was talked to by management because of it. I advised my Supervisor in the X area that I did the best I could given I had just sat down and had just noticed the aircraft not handed off to ZZZ1 Approach. Given the coordination could have been done in a more efficient and timely manner I had to work with what I had.According to the safety board's review of the event there was an airspace violation as a result of this coordination. In my opinion this happened because the ZZZ1 Controller and his uncertainty of what needed to be done. I offered to descend Aircraft X to 080, but he advised me to just leave him at 10,000 and then instructed another aircraft to descend below the Aircraft X flight. This back and forth coordination and being reluctant to take the hand off is what resulted in Aircraft X entering his airspace without a hand off. I would like to add that overflights are not allowed over ZZZ NAVAID per our LOA, however the situation dictated a different solution. I would also like to emphasize that as the D-side Controller in this situation had I not immediately gotten on the line with the ZZZ1 Controller this would have been a much different and ultimately worse issue. I am almost certain a loss of separation would have occurred. My Supervisor agreed and the R-side backed me up on it. I have chosen to report this event because even though management advised me this was not disciplinary in any way shape or form, I would still like to bring this up to the safety council's attention.Because of COVID, staffing has been an issue and the traffic volume was high. We had staffing later in the day that helped tremendously but this particular situation we were at minimum. I would also like to receive guidance as to what I could have done better given I was forced into a bad situation and I did my best to separate aircraft and coordinate what I could before an incident may have occurred.
ASRS:1773865.s: A D-side controller reported an airspace violation involving Aircraft X during descent to 10,000 feet, caused by the busy R-side controller failing to hand off the aircraft to ZZZ1 Approach. The reporter attributes the event to delayed coordination and staffing shortages, noting that immediate intervention prevented a loss of separation.

ASRS:1773871.n: Aircraft X was advised of airport conditions as well as the work in progress on the runway and was cleared for the VOR 26 approach and told to change to advisory frequency and report cancellation on the frequency. About 15-20 minutes later the pilot called and informed me he was in the hold over ADQ VOR at 2,000 ft but had not completed the approach or the missed approach. I double checked the approach plate and immediately issued a climb to 3,700 ft. Once the aircraft reported reaching 3,700 ft I issued a holding clearance as depicted on the approach plate for the missed approach holding pattern with an EFC and probed for more information which he provided. The aircraft eventually ended up diverting back to ZZZ due to the poor runway conditions. The pilot needed to inform us of his intentions prior to entering the hold he was not authorized.
ASRS:1773871.s: An air traffic controller issued a climb to 3,700 ft after Aircraft X held unauthorized at 2,000 ft over ADQ VOR during a VOR 26 approach. The pilot failed to report intentions before entering the hold, leading to a diversion to ZZZ due to poor runway conditions.

ASRS:1773874.n: Aircraft X was handed off at 4,000 feet direct to the initial approach fix. The weather was good for a visual approach so I queried the pilot if he would prefer a visual approach and offered a 6 mile straight in. The pilot concurred and I initiated a descent to 2,100 feet. I did not check the (minimum vectoring area (MVA) map and believed with the descent the pilot would enter the 2,100 foot MVA west of the airport. As the aircraft left 2,600 feet the adjacent facility Controller advised me of a low altitude alert. I was not receiving an alert and mistakenly believed they were getting a false alert due to rate of descent. Shortly after I checked the MVA map and noticed the aircraft was just leaving a 3,000 foot MVA area level at 2,100 feet. Three things contributed to this, two directly under my control: I believed the edge of the 3,000 foot MVA shelf was further north than it was. I should have rechecked the MVA map before issuing a descent. Having had false low altitude alerts before, I believed the other Controller was getting a false alarm. I should have immediately went to the MVA map. And we never received a low altitude alert.
ASRS:1773874.s: An air traffic controller cleared Aircraft X for a visual approach descent to 2,100 feet without checking the Minimum Vectoring Area (MVA) map, placing the aircraft below the 3,000-foot MVA. The controller ignored an adjacent facility's low altitude alert, mistakenly believing it was false, until later verifying the aircraft was in a prohibited area.

ASRS:1773877.n: Working in a north flow, with arrivals coming in on the downwind, spacing not really an issue, and I had just been in a rhythm bringing the arrivals in for visual approaches. My general method is to give a descent to 9,000 feet which is the downwind Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA) when clear of traffic, then slow to 180 knots 2 miles from the base turn, then turn to a 070 heading, then when the first turn is observed and they are now crossing the 9,000 foot MVA line into the 8,000 foot MVA, give a descent to 7,000 feet, then call the airport, then clear them for an approach with a turn to final. This sequence requires 5 or 6 transmissions per plane, but I feel like it is an expeditious way to safely get aircraft in with such a high MVA on the downwind. After having worked many aircraft in without issue and rather monotonously, Aircraft X checked on and was one of the last aircraft in the bank. I descended them to 9,000 feet, slowed to 180 knots at the normal place, then got distracted by something going on with another sector, I can't remember what, but I returned my focus to Aircraft X, incorrectly thinking that I had already given the base turn, and I was watching for the target to start a turn to the east. I saw the target move and started the transmission to descend. The pilot read it back, but I soon could tell that they were not in the turn and were not leaving the higher MVA for lower terrain. I asked the pilot if they were in the right turn heading 070 yet, and they responded that they were turning to 070 degrees, but in reality I had not yet issued it and didn't realize that until reviewing it afterward. The aircraft was soon in the base turn leaving the higher MVA, I called the airport and the pilot responded in sight, and I issued a visual approach clearance. It was my mistake that I did not catch it earlier. I will practice more vigilance in ensuring a complete turn out of the MVA before issuing the descent.
ASRS:1773877.s: An air traffic controller working north flow arrivals mistakenly issued a descent to 7,000 feet to Aircraft X before clearing the base turn, causing the aircraft to remain in the higher 9,000-foot MVA. The controller realized the error after the pilot read back the descent, corrected the situation by confirming the turn, and subsequently cleared the aircraft for a visual approach.

ASRS:1773879.n: Aircraft requested IFR clearance airborne. I proceeded to find the flight plan and issue a clearance when pilot was out of 2,900 feet when the MIA was 3,000. This was my first day back in the facility in 4 months due to COVID. Prior to that I worked straight mid shifts for the preceding months. I haven't seen any day/evening traffic since month (8 months). This session appeared complex for me due to my absence. I was told I would have this 1 single day to OJT and then I must get an Over The Shoulder. Jumping immediately into the job made me overthink a lot and I rushed the clearance without thinking of the MIA.Provide more than 8 hours of OJT prior to forcing people to re-certify. This would make the transition back a little smoother.
ASRS:1773879.s: An air traffic controller issued an IFR clearance to a pilot who was below the 3,000-foot Minimum IFR Altitude. The controller attributed the error to rushing due to inexperience after a four-month absence and insufficient on-the-job training.

ASRS:1773882.n: High speed abort.Captain at controls.Cleared for takeoff and Tower advised aircraft on 5 mile final as we approached the RWY (Runway). Approximately 1/4 way down runway into our takeoff roll, Challenger announced going around left side. At approximately 1/2 way down runway into our takeoff roll, Tower directed us to abort our takeoff. We were in the high-speed regime at approximately 115 kts. I could see the jet going around on our left abeam, in my peripheral vision as we were aborting.Maximum reverse application w/ maximum brakes. Uneventful abort, cleared runway onto Taxiway F and brought jet to a stop. Manually held brakes while running all applicable checklists. 2 MLG (Main Landing Gear) trucks reached 610 C, others approximately 590 C. Brake temp cooling chart referenced 35 mins used, brakes took approximately 50 min to cool to 270 C. In the meantime, ZZZ Fire-Rescue examined MLG. No evidence of overheat. Conferred with [Maintenance Control] for any further guidance. Later, Maintenance came to the jet, examined MLG per [Maintenance Control] guidance and gave us a thumbs up.In the meantime, we had a conference call with Flight Ops Management and ZZZ Station Ops. Both gave us the ok to continue'.Maintenance Control sent us a new maintenance release, Dispatch sent Release 3. Brake temp left main was the highest temp, at approximately 240 C when we began taxi. No noticeable increases.We departed ZZZ, kept gear down for approximately 5 minutes til all MLG brakes were below 200 C and decreasing. Retracted gear and continued to ZZZ1 via the flight plan.As a side-note, we received an ACARS message at approximately 7,000 ft., on climbout, directing us to return to gate for another check. We leveled at 9,000 ft., called Dispatch for clarification. He talked to Maintenance Control and surmised the return to gate message was an old message and may have been caught up in the ACARS system somehow and decided to transmit to us after takeoff roll. Anyhow, message was deemed as received in error and we got a thumbs up to continue OPS (Operations) normal to ZZZ1. I'm not sure if this is something systemic to Company 2 ACARS interface or not, but this issue might need to be examined." Cleared takeoff at ZZZ with aircraft on 5 nm final. As we began our roll I heard the aircraft on final say they were initiating a go-around. Around 115 KIAS the Tower directed us to reject which we accomplished. We told the passengers to remain seated and we taxied clear to find a place to cool our brakes, get Maintenance to inspect our brakes/tires, and coordinate for a new maintenance release and Dispatch release while re-initializing our FMC. We accomplished all pre-flight, before push and before takeoff checklists again and accomplished an uneventful takeoff over an hour later and landing uneventfully in ZZZ1.
ASRS:1773882.s: The Captain aborted a high-speed takeoff at 115 kts after Tower directed a reject due to an aircraft on final initiating a go-around. Following a brake overheat inspection and a delayed departure caused by an erroneous ACARS return message, the crew completed an uneventful flight to ZZZ1.

ASRS:1773888.n: The foreign City X flights are a big problem with the issue of a large number of the passengers refusing to wear their mask from after boarding and throughout the entire duration of the flight. The flight attendants are nonstop in the processes of enforcing the mask requirement and a constant barrage of calls to the cockpit, in addition they are being verbally abused and disrespected by the non-compliant passengers . Company needs to find a way to strongly inform the passengers of the requirement and the seriousness of the lack of respect to the crew and fellow passengers. This is becoming such a problem that I as Captain of the aircraft am going to be forced to land the aircraft at the nearest suitable airport along our route and deplane the instigators.
ASRS:1773888.s: The Captain reported that on a City X flight, numerous passengers refused to wear masks, verbally abusing flight attendants who enforced the rule. The Captain stated they may be forced to land at the nearest suitable airport to deplane the instigators due to this ongoing non-compliance.

ASRS:1773891.n: I unknowingly rode in a van with, and flew with a Flight Attendant who had exhibited COVID symptoms the day prior to our flight. On [date 1], the Flight Attendant reported from ZZZ that she had been vomiting and had a temperature above 100. She reportedly called in sick at that time, but still flew the next day with us ZZZ-ZZZ1. That day she also rode with us in the van, a 15 minute ride from the hotel. Only once airborne, from ZZZ-ZZZ1, was I made aware of the Flight Attendant's situation, and reported it immediately. I must not have all the information, because it appears that she called in sick on [date 1] with COVID symptoms, but was allowed to fly the [to] ZZZ1, then was on sick list again when she got to ZZZ1. Because I was in close proximity to the Flight Attendant with COVID symptoms for more than 15 minutes, I called in sick for the remainder of my trip.
ASRS:1773891.s: A pilot flew with a Flight Attendant who had reported COVID symptoms the day prior but was still cleared to fly the ZZZ-ZZZ1 sector. After learning of the situation in the air, the pilot reported it and subsequently called in sick due to close proximity exposure.

ASRS:1773899.n: Hand flying on climbout when ATC asks us about icing and temperature. We respond with light rime and the SAT. This happened just before reaching FL210. I looked down at EICAS for temperature and in the process climbed through FL210 by 400 feet, but immediately corrected. ATC did call us on it but we were back at FL210. At no time was there any traffic conflict or separation issue. Being new to the airplane, I was hand flying to get a better feel for the airplane. Might be worth mentioning that plane was light and was climbing like a rocket ship but previous to this event, we had complied with correctly with all other altitude assignments.
ASRS:1773899.s: The pilot hand-flying a light aircraft during climbout overshot FL210 by 400 feet while checking EICAS temperatures after an ATC icing query. The pilot immediately corrected the altitude, and ATC acknowledged the deviation, though no traffic conflict occurred.

ASRS:1773900.n: HKG Runway 7L/25R is closed for construction, but there is no NOTAM for this condition. It does show on the ATIS. I'm told this condition has been ongoing for a while, and I'm also told that it's been previously reported. Why is there no NOTAM for a runway closure? If the local authority will not issue a NOTAM, then our company should issue an internal NOTAM. This runway closure makes HKG a single-runway airport with diversion options that are limited and/or undesirable.
ASRS:1773900.s: The pilot reported that Hong Kong Runway 7L/25R is closed for construction without a NOTAM, though the closure appears on the ATIS. This lack of formal notice reduces the airport to single-runway operations with limited diversion options.

ASRS:1773937.n: New FO updating arrival waypoints mistakenly deleted route in legs 1 at XA:40Z. CAand FO immediately reinstated route in legs 2. CA sent position reports to ATC at XA:50Z and XB:17 Z. CA counseled FO.FO familiar with Manufacturer X aircraft type and not Manufacturer Y aircraft type. Unable to fly after training due to virus.[I suggest] more training.
ASRS:1773937.s: A new First Officer on a Manufacturer X aircraft mistakenly deleted arrival waypoints during the approach phase. The Captain reinstated the route, filed position reports, and counseled the First Officer, who lacked recent training on this specific aircraft type due to illness.

ASRS:1773963.n: While taxiing out to Runway XR at ZZZ I might have failed to hold short at the hold short line. The FO and I recognized the error at the same time. He yelled stop as I hit the brakes. Looking out at the line, it was difficult to tell if the nose of the aircraft had crossed over the line. The Tower was informed immediately. The Tower then cleared us for takeoff. No other issues. Both the FO and I had reviewed the bulletin for ZZZ about this problem and it still may have bitten us. Other issues that may have affected our situational awareness was a last minute weight and balance issue that required us to stop on the taxiway to move passengers and get our numbers. Another issue is that I and the FO are starting to fly again after three months. It is taking time to re-acclimate to line operations. Even being aware of this and taking our time to get it done right, we may have still gotten bit by the error. Approaching Runway XR hold line Captain began to apply brakes, so I thought he was coming to a stop. I looked down to bring up the legs page on my FMC and when I looked up again it was apparent he was not going to stop short of the hold line. I told him to stop and he brought the plane to an immediate stop. We had crossed the line by a few feet. Captain told the Tower we may have crossed the hold line and they asked if we could take an immediate takeoff, we said yes and proceeded to takeoff on XR without incident.
ASRS:1773963.s: The Captain and First Officer likely crossed the Runway XR hold short line while taxiing at ZZZ due to distraction from a weight and balance issue and recent return to line operations. They stopped immediately, informed Tower, and were cleared for takeoff without incident.

ASRS:1773986.n: Aircraft X. ARD had previous write-up about compressor stalls on #3 Engine. Maintenance said the morning crew rejected the takeoff for compressor stalls, we read the write-up and maintenance action in detail and discussed the issue. We identified this as a potential threat to our flight. On push back, while starting #1 Engine, we got ENG 1 FADEC ALTN alert, we referred to the QRH, it also identified 'action code' as SW. After engine start, the Captain said we could recycle the switch and asked if I was okay with that, I replied if he was okay, I was okay. We selected FADEC ALTN, then selected it again to the normal function, the alert went away. Later as we taxied out, I thought about the PDM process and not consulting maintenance, but the Captain's action corrected the alert to the proper configuration without any alerts and without an AML write-up, so I resolved my dilemma internally. Prior to taking the runway, the Captain announced he was gonna run-up all the engines a bit higher than usual while holding the brakes to ensure #3 Engine was operating correctly, I replied it was a good idea. It was my take-off (hand flown as briefed) and everything went normal up to about 700 ft. AGL.About 700 ft. AGL, with the gear up and flaps extended, we heard loud bangs associated with a compressor stall (I only heard this before in the sim) and a jolting in the plane, there were no differing indications on any of the engine instruments (all three N1, EGT, and N2 indications were identical). Around 1,000 ft. AGL, the Captain said he was gonna shut the engine down, I said okay with the bias of the previous write-up in the ARD, also thinking we'd go thru the process of 'Throttle-Idle, Fuel Shutoff Switch-Off' (I admit this wasn't the calm and rehearsed engine failure problem in the sim, and I was a bit anxious about the actual compressor stall). About that time, Tower called us and said we had intermittent flames shooting out of the left side (#1 Engine), the Captain said 'left side, I shut down [Engine] #3' (paraphrase). I looked down and noticed 0 fuel flow and the engine N2 decreasing while the banging continued. I exclaimed 'Let's start it back up' thinking #3 wasn't the problem and we definitely needed it if we had to shut down #1! The Captain quickly returned the fuel cutoff switch to on and I saw the N2 increase. I turned the autopilot on (as briefed if we had a problem) and announced I was disconnecting the auto throttles while the Captain told Tower we were returning to the field for compressor stalls and advised ATC. Tower told us to turn left downwind for [Runway] XX and I told the Captain 'I got the plane and the radios' and I replied to Tower. With the autopilot on and above 1,000 ft. AGL, the plane accelerated above Vf and I asked Tower if 2,000 ft. MSL was okay to level off, Tower replied yes. As I started the heading guided turn to the left, I adjusted the altitude to 2,000 ft. and manually retarded all the throttles for level off then selected airspeed 200 knots. With the throttles out of take-off power, the banging went away, I believe Tower said the flames stopped. While flying downwind abeam the field, I began to setup for the approach [Runway] XX, adjusted the minimums (already had it preselected), and announced I was moving the flaps to 15 degrees since they were still extended. Tower asked if we had the field insight, I replied yes and Tower cleared us the visual approach [Runway] XX and cleared to land, I repeated the clearance but said we were gonna fly out a bit to get our normal visual glidepath. After the Captain programmed the FMS and inserted the ILS frequency into the NavRad page, I called for the approach check and turned base to final, on dogleg, I began the descent on glidepath before intercepting the localizer and called for the gear down and before landing check. With the final configuration and checklist complete, I asked the Captain if he wanted the landing since we were an emergency, he took control of the plane with the autopilot on while I briefed him of the FMAs. Landing was uneventful. We taxied clear onto taxiway XX and waited for the fire truck's inspection. With the all clear (no fire), we terminated the emergency and taxied to parking.Engine compressor stall.Some missteps between the crew while successfully resolving an engine compressor stall. Better crew coordination would simplify resolution. Alerted that Aircraft X might be returning to ZZZ due to problem with #1 Engine. I immediately contacted ZZZ Tower. I was told, right after flight was wheels up controllers in tower saw sparks/flames coming from left engine and also heard 3 to 4 loud booms. Flight returned to airport and landed without issue on Runway XX. I talked to the Captain. He said that right after takeoff, there was compressor stall #1 Engine. They advised ATC and returned to ZZZ. The aircraft was met by the Fire Department. The Captain said he did not know what caused the loss of the #1 Engine. He also said the maintenance told him there was damage to the engine.
ASRS:1773986.s: Pilots of Aircraft X experienced a #1 engine compressor stall with flames shortly after takeoff, despite a prior #3 engine history. The crew returned for an uneventful landing, though the Captain attributed the incident to unknown causes and confirmed engine damage.

ASRS:1773991.n: Air Carrier Ground Agent 1 in ZZZ called coworker and stated that some MISC HAZMAT (hazardous material) had been placed in position 6R. Apparently this had been loaded into this can 2 days prior, and they didn't realize this until the aircraft had already taken off. I then talked to Agent 1 about the situation and had him to send me the HAZMAT paperwork. Called the Director of Operations and informed of the situation, and also informed the crew of what had happened. As showing on the paperwork, it was Class 9, MISC, 804KG - position 6R. The cause was with the holiday, it caused the ramp to lose track of the can where this HAZMAT was and the paperwork that needed to be with the HAZMAT material. I suggest when there is a holiday, the ramp needs to make sure that they are extra careful about where the HAZMAT is and the [related] paperwork is.
ASRS:1773991.s: A ground agent discovered 804kg of Class 9 hazardous material in position 6R after the aircraft departed, having been loaded two days prior. The reporter attributed the error to holiday-related ramp confusion regarding the container and paperwork, prompting notification of operations and the flight crew.

ASRS:1774011.n: Arriving at security at XA:00pm, we found all security check points and KCM [Known Crew Member] closed. We were directed to security for airport employees in another terminal. After setting off the alarm, I was instructed to start removing various articles of clothing. With a line of airport employees behind me, I asked for a private search. I was taken to yet another terminal and told to enter a room the size of an average walk in closest. Two security personnel crammed in behind me. There was poor ventilation and no possibility of distancing ourselves. We all stood within a foot of each other. I would suggest in this time of COVID, TSA like every other organization must adapt procedures and protocols to prevent the spread of COVID-19. Utilizing KCM decreases the time and contact between security personnel and flight crews, two groups exposed to more human interaction than most. Increasing the hours of KCM operation and relaxing constraints within the program to facilitate secure social distancing is a reasonable adaptation to help mitigate the spread of COVID among both essential workers and the public at large.
ASRS:1774011.s: A flight crew member reported that upon arriving at security, all checkpoints and KCM lanes were closed, forcing a search in a crowded, poorly ventilated room with two personnel. The reporter attributed the risk of COVID-19 spread to these conditions and recommended expanding KCM hours to improve social distancing.

ASRS:1774071.n: Upon executing a missed approach, the aircraft was leveled off early. The error was recognized and the aircraft put back into a climb to reach its target altitude for the missed approach. Pilot flying became disoriented after the acceleration and climb on the go-around in IMC. The aircraft was light and the majority of experience was on the Y series. It had been 15 days since the last flight, and 76 days since flying in an X [series] for the pilot flying. The PF reaction to the increased pitch attitude and acceleration was to level the plane prematurely.[Need] Review of SOP procedures for go-around, and mental preparation for pitch attitude changes from the Y to X series on the X type aircraft on takeoff and go-around configurations.
ASRS:1774071.s: The pilot flying, with limited recent experience on the X series aircraft, prematurely leveled off during a missed approach in IMC due to disorientation from pitch and acceleration changes. The error was corrected by resuming the climb, prompting a request to review go-around SOPs and mental preparation for aircraft type differences.

ASRS:1774080.n: On [Date], we operated Aircraft X from ZZZ-ROA and I was the CA (Captain) onboard. It was our Day 3 and Leg 4 of the day. I was the Pilot Flying, while my FO (First Officer) was Pilot Monitoring. Both of us were new to this airport, so we reviewed the 10-7 pages and airport diagram to make sure we selected an adequate runway for landing, because they both were relatively short runways in mountainous terrain surrounding area. Once we were in the air and leveled off at our cruising altitude, we started setting up for the approach and briefed it all. As we got closer to the airport and were with Approach, he descended us to 6,000 ft. We both saw the runway and reported it. The ATC asked us to give him at least 6 mile final and we concurred. We looked at the runway and descended down to 4,500 ft. approaching from the southwest to intercept [Runway] 34 localizer. As we got closer to the intercept point for the localizer, the aircraft annunciated 'Caution terrain' 'Pull up' simultaneously, there was no break in between at all. There was also no terrain data that displayed on the MFD on both of our screens. I disconnected the AP (Autopilot) and added power needed to climb immediately. The 'Pull up' annunciation was only said once and went away. We only climbed 500 ft. to 5,000 ft. and continued to intercept the course to land. We also reported the event to the ATC and they didn't say anything. The 'Master Warning' switch light also didn't go on. This event lasted about 2 seconds and we continued to land at the airport.Both of us were new the airport and should've stayed with ATC until intercepted and then call for visual.This event could've easily been avoided by simply just staying with the Approach Control until established on approach, because it is a very mountainous area. Being an unfamiliar crew flying to this area and going visual to land this runway can put you in this situation, even though being in VMC conditions and having runway in sight. I would also like to suggest a guidance in 10-7 to be added regarding landing in this airport and staying with ATC until cleared of mountains and only going visual once cleared and over the valley. On [Date], my Captain and I operated Aircraft X from ZZZ to ROA. It was Day 3, Leg 4 of our trip. On this leg, I was the Pilot Monitoring, while my CA (Captain) was flying the aircraft. This was the first time either of us operated to Roanoke, so we reviewed the 10-7 pages, and airport diagram to make sure we selected an adequate runway for landing, since they both were relatively short runways in a mountainous area. Once in cruise flight at our final altitude, we started setting up for the approach and briefed it as necessary. The plan was to set up for the visual backed up by the ILS for Runway 34. As we got closer to the airport and were with Approach, the controller descended us to 6,000 ft. We both saw the runway and reported it. ATC then cleared us for the visual, but asked us to give him at least 6 mile final and we concurred. We looked at the runway, surrounding terrain, and approach plate, and decided to descend down to 4,500 ft. approaching from the southwest to intercept the Runway 34 localizer. We figured this was a correct altitude, as the highest obstacle on the plate was 3,508 ft. As we got closer to the intercept point for the localizer, the aircraft annunciated 'Caution terrain' 'Pull up' simultaneously, there was no break in between at all. There was also no terrain data that displayed on the MFD on both of our screens. My Captain immediately disconnected the AP (Autopilot) and added power as necessary. The 'Pull up' annunciation and all other GPWS alerts were only said once and went away as soon as we started the climb. We only climbed 500 ft. to 5,000 ft. and continued to intercept the course to land. The event was reported to ATC as well, and they acknowledged. This event lasted about 2 seconds and we continued to land at the airport.This was the first time either of us have operated to this particular airport, and should have either stayed above the approach's MSA of 5,700 ft., or even stayed with the Approach Controller, making him give us headings and altitudes rather than calling the airport in sight and getting cleared for the visual.This event could have easily been avoided by staying with the Approach Controller until established on the approach, rather than calling the airport in sight and getting cleared for the visual. A crew flying to this area that is unfamiliar with the surrounding terrain and conducting a visual approach to this runway can end up in this situation, even with VMC conditions and having the runway in sight. I would also like to suggest some guidance in the 10-7 pages to be added regarding landing at this airport and staying with ATC until cleared of the mountains and only going visual once cleared and over the valley. Something similar to the 10-7 pages for ZZZ regarding the GPWS events would be helpful to other crews in avoiding a similar situation.
ASRS:1774080.s: The Captain and First Officer of Aircraft X received a simultaneous "Caution terrain" and "Pull up" alert at 4,500 ft while conducting a visual approach to Runway 34 at ROA. The crew attributed the event to descending below the Minimum Safe Altitude in mountainous terrain before establishing on the localizer, though they climbed 500 ft and landed safely.

ASRS:1774081.n: Being vectored onto the final approach course 26R, we had a brief encounter with a wake turbulence. And then again during the landing flare to the point where it was becoming a problem to maintain a stabilized approach path above the runway in ground effect. Did not have time to notify air traffic control that this happened. I don't know if we were behind a heavy previous arrival. But we were getting really close to having to go around from the landing flare. The roll motion was becoming such a problem with keeping the aircraft stabilized, and aligned with the runway. I was actually shocked that we touchdown as smooth as we did. I asked the pilot flying if he thought that was a bit unusual his statement was 'I was just one more jolt away from going around'. Wake turbulence encounters in Atlanta are becoming an every week problem, more like almost every inbound leg into Atlanta problem. Also it seems there is little consideration given to the fact that we may be departing behind something that might be a threat as well. I'm beginning to think that there's nothing much going to be done about it until something serious happens. Often the wake encounter threats are not much of a problem if there's sufficient crosswind push the wake away from trailing aircraft, from my experience it does not take much to all. However I've learned that this is still a problem at some point on the arrival or departure procedure. For example a crosswind on the departure runways will clear you of the wake threat for takeoff, but might present a very real problem in trail of a heavy navigating to a point, to the same on that departure or arrival. Especially if it's a direct head, or tailwind now.
ASRS:1774081.s: The crew encountered wake turbulence while vectored for final approach to runway 26R in Atlanta, causing significant roll and destabilizing the landing flare. The pilot flying stated they were nearly forced to go around, though the aircraft touched down smoothly without notifying air traffic control.

ASRS:1774086.n: The aircraft was late arriving. There were fumes and a very strong smell coming out of door 1L from the sanitizing spray while we were standing out on the jetway. The training that all FAs are required to complete, states we must wait at least XX minutes before entering the aircraft after spraying is completed. The agents started boarding while we were still on jetway and the customers told the agents. So the gate agents came down to ask what the problem was and we stated the fumes are too strong for us to board. We were pressured to start boarding as to not cause a delay!
ASRS:1774086.s: Cabin crew reported strong sanitizing fumes at door 1L while standing on the jetway, violating required wait times. Gate agents pressured the crew to begin boarding despite the hazardous conditions to avoid delaying the late arrival.

ASRS:1774093.n: As Passenger A boarded our flight, I asked her to please make sure that her mask was on over both her mouth and nose. She did not comply. Then while in the cabin during boarding, I noticed Passenger A was still not wearing her mask properly. I again asked for her to please fix it as it was required. She informed me that her mask was too large. I then went and retrieved a mask from the inflight kit and brought it to her. Passenger A told me that she did not want our mask and that she was not going to change it...I gave her our required paperwork, informed the Captain and asked the gate agent to speak with her. We decided to continue with her on our flight. In flight, she was asked multiple times to comply with our policy again to no avail. I asked for a Supervisor to meet the aircraft. The Customer Service supervisors met the flight. Passenger A continued to disregard the safety of everyone on board.
ASRS:1774093.s: Cabin crew reported that Passenger A refused to wear a mask properly during boarding and flight despite being offered a replacement and informed of policy. The crew notified the Captain and supervisors, but the flight continued with the passenger disregarding safety requirements.

ASRS:1774099.n: As we were taking off from ZZZ and climbing, a very strong burning odor was coming into the cabin. FA (Flight Attendant) A called the flight deck immediately to notify the pilots. They told her this aircraft just got a new engine and they will monitor it. The smell went away shortly there after. As soon as we took off in ZZZ and were still climbing, a very strong burning oil/ engine odor occurred.I immediately called the flight deck and was told that the aircraft had a new engine and the smell was because of that new engine, the pilots said they'd monitor it and to call if it got worse and didn't go away.Smell went away after ten minutes and didn't return.
ASRS:1774099.s: During climb after takeoff from ZZZ, a flight attendant reported a strong burning oil odor to the pilots. The crew attributed the smell to a newly installed engine, monitored the situation, and the odor dissipated within ten minutes without recurrence.

ASRS:1774101.n: Passenger A would not comply with our mask policy. He was first informed to place his mask on over his nose and mouth and then when I passed by a few minutes later collecting trash, I also noticed he had removed his mask and I reminded him that he needed to place his mask on. He then covered his face with his hoodie and I then handed him one of our masks on board. He then showed me he had one already and I asked him to place it over his mouth and nose, which he didn't when we were in final descent. During deplaning when he walked to the front of the aircraft he still didn't have a mask on, and chose to ignore us again when I told him he needs to have a mask on.We did not serve him a warning because this occurred during initial and final descent.A notice should be placed on his reservation regarding him not complying with the company's face mask policy.
ASRS:1774101.s: A cabin crew member reported that a passenger refused to wear a face mask during initial and final descent and while deplaning, despite multiple reminders and being offered a spare mask. The crew did not issue a warning due to the flight phase but recommended a notice be placed on the passenger's reservation for non-compliance.

ASRS:1774103.n: There were some mask compliance issues with passengers in XX1 and XX3 as well as YY1 and YY2. Both separate parties did later comply. Row XX complied after I informed them I'd be issuing a warning if they continued to not comply. I told them that they will be banned from our airline if it continued.That was my 3rd time telling them and they complied. All parties eventually complied.
ASRS:1774103.s: Cabin crew reported mask compliance issues with passengers in rows XX1, XX3, YY1, and YY2. After issuing warnings of potential bans, all parties eventually complied with the mask policy.

ASRS:1774104.n: Passenger A in [seat] X3 did not have his mask on properly when I took his beverage order. I asked him to please cover his nose. As soon as I turned around to do the next row of service he turned his head where I couldn't see and pulled the mask below his nose. I picked up garbage and he again/still did not want to comply with our COVID mask policy and had it down. I asked him again. He'd pull it up then pull it down again being non-compliant.I let our Flight Attendant (FA) D know. Flight Attendants A, B, D and F were doing two trash pick-ups and told him twice to comply. I walked up doing trash and he had it down under his nose again. I told him that we had asked him for compliance multiple times and we would have to take further steps of compliance wasn't reached. He muttered something I could [not] hear. I let FA A know and she said she'd keep an eye on him. We saw that he and his father in [seat] X1 were traveling on to ZZZ. I guarantee he will cause issues on his next flight.We all agreed that if he didn't comply again we would issue a warning. We actually gave him more warnings than we should have as he kept pulling the face mask down after we would walk away. I walked by doing visas and Passenger A again was non component with his mask under his nose. I told our FA A to have a chat with him. He should have been issued a warning but due to bumps on descent we didn't have time and it wasn't safe. Again I know he will be non-compliant on his next leg. He repeatedly did not follow our request to wear his mask properly. He was non-compliant to our COVID safety mask policy. Though a warning wasn't issued I think it should have. Any crew in the future will have problems getting compliance.
ASRS:1774104.s: Cabin crew reported that Passenger A repeatedly violated the COVID mask policy by pulling his mask below his nose during the descent phase. Although the crew issued multiple verbal warnings, they could not issue a formal warning due to turbulence, and the passenger remained non-compliant throughout the flight.

ASRS:1774107.n: We had an issue with a family in regards to our mask policy. After we did the demo I walked back to compliance and saw that the mother, in [seat] XX4, the face mask was below her nose and when I got closer she pulled it up. The three kids in [seats] XX 123 pulled their masks up and kept them on. I turned to the mother and said that 'I need your mask to stay over your nose at all times.' As I'm saying this she has it pinched between her finger pulled away from her face. She snapped back, 'It's there or it's covering' something along those lines and dismissively continued her conversation with the woman across from her. When I walked to the front of the plane before the demo I told the woman in XX3 to follow the mask policy so XX4 knew we were enforcing it. After my first encounter I informed the crew that I already talked to her and received attitude back and for them to keep an eye out.My second encounter was shortly after that when I went to pass out the [snacks] to the family next to her. As I walked up the mask again was down below her nose and when she saw me there she moved it up. I told her I really need her to keep the mask up and she snapped that it was up. I said it wasn't a moment ago and that I didn't want to have any issues on this long flight. Her responses to that was did I know that the politicians didn't believe in masks and I told her that this wasn't political, it was me doing my job to enforce our policy. She continued to give me attitude and talking about it was political. I went to the back and informed Flight Attendant (FA) C and D how my second encounter went and that she would be an issue the remainder of the flight and I strongly believe we should give her the Warning. They both offered to be the one to talk and give it to her. Flight Attendant C took care of that.While passing out the snack mix, I got to the row the husband was in. He asked for the wife's snack and his mask was down and FA D asked him to make sure his mask was up. XX4 had some kind of response that I missed but FA D told her not to have attitude towards us when we were just doing our job. Then she responded as a victim, saying she's been yelled at the whole flight and that she has been talking to us respectfully and not yelling at us. Which is not the truth because my encounters with her were very unpleasant, disrespectful and had the intent to belittle me and the policy.The remainder of the flight the entire family didn't comply with the mask policy. Their son rarely had the mask on when I passed, the daughters below their nose and the husband as well even though he would pull it up as we passed by. We all spoke to the family at one point and most of us multiple times. The mother was constantly having the mask below her nose or pulling the mask away from her face as she spoke to her kids and the woman across from her. I also was informed that another guest moved his seat because he was so uncomfortable sitting in front of them. I was told after everyone was off that they didn't have their mask on properly while deplaning either.
ASRS:1774107.s: A flight attendant reported that a family, specifically the mother in seat XX4, repeatedly violated the mask policy by wearing masks below their noses or removing them during the flight. Despite multiple warnings and a formal warning issued by another crew member, the family remained non-compliant throughout the flight and deplaning, causing discomfort to other passengers.

ASRS:1774109.n: Upon boarding a passenger assigned seat XX1 was walking up the aisle with her mask pulled down. I asked her to cover her nose and mouth with her mask. She does not comply. She asks 'does this plane have oxygen? I can't wear this mask.' I ask her if she is telling me she has a condition that requires oxygen during the flight then she needs to bring an approved Oxygen Canister on the flight. Meanwhile the passenger in [seat] YY1 sits down, mask below nose, and will not comply with many requests from me to pull her mask to cover her nose. I call the Captain to have him contact a Supervisor to remove these passengers and to let him know the passenger who sat in ZZ1 was demanding that I administer oxygen. Now a young man is trying to sit in ZZ2. I ask if that is his assigned seat. He was assigned [seat] XX2 I ask him to sit in his assigned seat. He complies. Then a passenger shows up in [seat] YY2. He gets inside my personal space and is belly to belly with me saying he doesn't like how I am talking to these passengers. [Passenger in seat] ZZ1 is asking me what was I going to do. And I told them that I had called the Captain to get someone to take them off because everyone has to properly wear a mask. I was hemmed in by passenger [in seat] YY2. I finally got past him and went up front. At that point Paramedics came and took the passenger in [seat] ZZ1 off in an aisle chair. The station manager finally shows up and I tell her removal for mask compliance of passenger in [seat] YY1 and passenger in [seat] YY2 [is necessary] for interference of crew member duties. All said and done the whole party was removed from the flight.
ASRS:1774109.s: Cabin crew reported multiple passengers refused mask compliance and interfered with duties during boarding. Paramedics removed one passenger for medical reasons, while the station manager removed the entire group for non-compliance and crew interference.

ASRS:1774126.n: Upon stepping aboard Aircraft X, I immediately detected an odor that had a burnt wire smell. The other FA's also made comments such as, 'What is that smell? It smells like something is burning' as they stepped onboard. I was the D FA and began checking my safety equipment. I looked in the galley to see if any circuit breakers had popped and also looked in the oven to determine if the odor was from a forgotten burnt meal. All circuits were in proper place and there was no food in oven. I then walked down the aisle to determine if the burnt-wire smell was coming from the aft galley. I stopped at Row 21, aircraft right and stepped up on Seat 21 D as the odor was very strong above the OH bin. I could not visibly see any sign of smoke but the odor was quite strong. I then walked back up to fwd galley as I saw that the Captain was beginning a briefing. Captain stated that this aircraft had just come out of 'mothballs' and had just cleared a major inspection in State X. He stated that it had just arrived to ZZZ and the Captain of that flight informed him that a smoke alarm for the aft cabin activated upon landing. Captain stated that this happens from time to time and poses no threat of fire. All of us 4 FAs told him that we smelled a burnt wire odor in the cabin. A male individual, name unknown, representing Maintenance stated that we 'probably were smelling new carpet glue'. Captain waited for the Maintenance personnel member to step off of the aircraft and then told us FA's that if we were not comfortable with the odor that he backed us and would insist that we fly a different aircraft to ZZZ1 or return to hotel if aircraft was not available. All 4 of us FA's unanimously and instantly stated that we did not feel comfortable on this aircraft and we wanted to change aircraft in the interest of Safety First. I then told the Captain that I noticed the odor was particularly strong by OH compartment of 21D. We then walked to that row and Captain also noticed that it had a strong odor of either 'heated dust' or 'hot wire' on the lighting ballast. He then asked me if I personally felt safe taking this aircraft. I told him that I am very safety minded and the odor was not normal or usual to me. We all stayed in the first class seating area and continued personal conversations among us. The Captain was not present as he was talking to Operations. After approximately 15 minutes of remaining in the first class seating area, the other FAs noticed that my voice was getting hoarse and that I was beginning to lose my voice. To the best of my recollection, I believe that C FA, and B FA, both stated that their throats felt scratchy.After approximately another 15 minutes of staying and waiting for a decision onboard, in the first class seating area, we were told by [the] Captain that we were changing into different aircraft for our flight back to ZZZ1. We then deplaned the aircraft and walked to the other waiting aircraft. My voice remained coarse for an additional 30 minutes and I developed a migraine during the boarding process. I had the migraine the entire flight to ZZZ1, and it continued until early afternoon of date. Additionally, I awoke on the morning of date with a sore and scratchy throat. Both my migraine and scratchy throat subsided around 1400 hours on date. I have had a continuous low-grade headache since date through present date. I did not seek any medical attention as I 'normally' suffer from low grade sinus headaches regularly and use an OTC nasal spray along with Tylenol.I commend our Captain, for valuing and backing our decision to prioritize safety first.I would hope that Aircraft X was ferried back to ZZZ without full crew and guests in the pursuit of safety. Upon crew boarding aircraft for return ZZZ-ZZZ1, [flight attendants] smelled what seemed like an electrical burning smell. It was not possible to find a fresh place of air on the plane, but the smell did seem worse as we walked further back. Our Pilots were met by that aircraft's ferrying pilots who also explained an aft lav smoke alarm went off while they were flying/descending after couple hours flight.The aircraft had just completed its mechanical run through after being 'unparked' from its holding location where it had been for 5 months. Unsure what that smell was, and given the circumstances of the aft lav smoke detector going off just previous to our boarding, our crew was offered another aircraft to take back to ZZZ1 which we accepted.At that point we had sat on the plane for likely about 30-45 minutes waiting for the phone calls and approvals and aircraft delay or swap or grounding decisions to be made. The flight attendants were in the cabin the whole time. Pilots came and left to discuss in jetway. Agents boarded for a couple of minutes and concurred on the smell immediately.Crew spoke of headaches, sore throat, and itchy/stuffy nose afterwards. Just concerned for aircraft returning to operation after long time [of being] parked.
ASRS:1774126.s: Flight attendants and pilots detected a strong burnt wire odor on Aircraft X after it was removed from long-term storage, noting a prior aft lav smoke alarm activation. The crew refused to fly due to safety concerns and physical symptoms like headaches and sore throats, resulting in the aircraft being swapped for a replacement.

ASRS:1774129.n: I was the B FA (Flight Attendant) on Aircraft X. We had finished boarding. I was near the aft section of the cabin. I heard a passenger ask 'is that normal?'. There was then smoke coming from the back rows air vents. Smoke was quickly filling the cabin and the fumes were extremely strong. It was burning my nose and throat. I called the A and told him what was going on and to notify the pilots. It was getting harder to breathe and see. We decided to have passengers get off the aircraft for safety. I was getting very light headed, I went back to get the C FA and make sure no passengers were left behind. After everyone got off, the C and I did not feel well at all. We asked to have an EMT look at us. My heart rate was extremely high and blood pressure was high from my normal. We received oxygen. A supervisor met up with us and said she could smell the fumes coming off from us because it was so strong. We still felt very dizzy, lightheaded, my throat was sore and I felt pressure in the back of my head. We decided it wasn't safe for us to continue with our trip due to the exposure. I got further medical attention later at a hospital due to my throat feeling worse. Earlier our water lines were frozen. The mechanics were attempting to fix the frozen line and this all occurred.We also have a video that can prove how thick the smoke was
ASRS:1774129.s: The B FA reported smoke and strong fumes from aft vents on Aircraft X after boarding, caused by mechanics fixing frozen water lines. Passengers evacuated, and the crew required medical attention for respiratory distress and high blood pressure, forcing them to cancel the trip.

ASRS:1774130.n: I was the D Flight Attendant sitting in seat X4 (assigned jump seat). There was a [reward system passenger] sitting behind me in [seat] Y4 and his traveling partner in [seat] Y6. This was my first flight back after a COVID exposure from the plane. During boarding I asked Y6 to make sure her mask stayed over her nose. She said it kept falling down. I offered one of ours but she declined. During the safety demo I once again asked her to pull up her mask. As soon as we took off they both removed their masks. Multiple times I asked them to put their masks on. When we were cleaning up for landing the passenger in Y4 started shouting at me asking for my name. He said because he had a drink in front of him he didn't need to put on his mask. I once again explained our policy was that it was only supposed to be removed briefly. He said he had been on 7 different flights and nobody had asked him to put on his mask. I was the first one. I called the B Flight Attendant to join the conversation. She reiterated our policy. After talking to him for a while he said he was extremely frustrated with the inconsistency of mask policy enforcement. He calmed down when we all agreed there should be more consistency with enforcing or explaining our mask policy.Just wanted to write this up as a safety issue. He also said he would be writing in to Airline. As a [person in the reward system] not sure if he knew better and just didn't want to wear the mask or if nobody on other flights has actually enforced our mask policy. But as someone who travels as often as he does. He clearly needs some clarification.
ASRS:1774130.s: The D Flight Attendant reported that two passengers removed their masks shortly after takeoff and refused to comply with policy during the flight. The situation escalated when one passenger shouted at the crew, citing inconsistent enforcement on previous flights, but de-escalated after the crew explained the rules and agreed on the need for consistency.

ASRS:1774139.n: I was assigned to work Aircraft X while contract vendor was working on the RH wing fuel tanks and fuel tank panels were open. Myself and Crew Member informed our Manager and Supervisor of many safety concerns we had on the work being performed by the vendor. Example of [these] concerns are: Fuel tank pre-entry check list was never filled out by vendor or Supervisor, no fuel-gas concentration readings were recorded. Per A320 fleet AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) 28-10-00-910-002-A. Aircraft supposed to have a rope barrier around the entire perimeter of Aircraft and warning sign on four areas per fig. sheet 1 per AMM. The fuel vendor only roped just one section of Aircraft while having open fuel tank covers. Supervisor and Manager ignored our safety concerns of the vendor improper maintenance procedures and directed us to work next to the open fuel tank areas ( L/H pack Bay ). I felt that Management was making me work under unsafe work environment. Contract vendor not following safety procedures per AMM.Contract vendors and Management need to follow all safety precautions and not ignore them. I was assigned to work Aircraft X while contract vendor was working on the RH wing fuel tanks and fuel tank panels were open. Myself and Crew Member informed our Manager and Supervisor of many safety concerns we had on the work being performed by the vendor. Example of [these] concerns are: Fuel tank pre-entry check list was never filled out by vendor or Supervisor, no fuel-gas concentration readings were recorded. Per A320 fleet AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) 28-10-00-910-002-A. Aircraft supposed to have a rope barrier around the entire perimeter of Aircraft and warning sign on four areas per fig. sheet 1 per AMM. The fuel vendor only roped just one section of Aircraft while having open fuel tank covers. Supervisor and Manager ignored our safety concerns of the vendor improper maintenance procedures and directed us to work next to the open fuel tank areas ( L/H pack Bay ). I feel like the company ignored our safety concerns and put pressure and directed us in working on an unsafe work environment per Aircraft AMM.Contract vendor was not following safety procedures per aircraft maintenance manuals.Contract vendors are required to follow each steps on AMM including completing all documentation of all maintenance performed on Aircraft.
ASRS:1774139.s: A mechanic and crew member reported that a contract vendor ignored A320 AMM safety procedures, including missing fuel tank checklists and inadequate barriers, while working on open RH wing fuel tanks. Management disregarded these concerns and directed the crew to work in the unsafe L/H pack bay area.

ASRS:1774160.n: I have X years of experience flying helicopters both IFR and VFR in the area. I know the area well. I know the rhythm of sporting TFRs and where to find the information (usually ForeFlight). Unfortunately, COVID in 2020 has effectively eliminated almost all of the normal sporting events. I actually thought that since fans couldn't go to sporting events that there would not be any active sporting event TFR's at all since they wouldn't meet the people density standard. Tonight, while en-route to ZZZ1 from ZZZ2, I learned that is not the case.While following my normal routing from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 following Interstate-number Southbound and asking for a ZZZ transition over the south field to ZZZZZ, I called ZZZ Tower to ask for the transition when the Controller asked me if I knew that I was in a TFR. I apologized and informed the Controller that I didn't and that I didn't see the TFR on my Garmin GTN nor on ForeFlight. Another pilot chimed in on freq and also said that he didn't see the TFR. The Controller simply said copy and gave me the transition without mentioning the issue further.I then saw that I did not have the TFR layer on my iPad (ForeFlight) turned on. As soon as I landed in ZZZ2 I turned on the layer and sure enough there was the TFR. I must have clipped the edge of it on my track inbound just north of ZZZ.This issue really stems from unacceptable complacency to sporting event TFR's during the COVID year and also the fact that they don't populate to my Garmin GTN via XM like normal TFRs do. I really wish they would standardize the delivery of TFRs so that we can see then across all services.Regardless, it was unacceptable to not have fully reviewed the flight path for all TFRs prior to departing ZZZ1. ...a mistake I won't be making again.
ASRS:1774160.s: A helicopter pilot en route from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 inadvertently entered a sporting event TFR due to complacency and a disabled ForeFlight layer, noting that the TFR did not populate on the Garmin GTN. The pilot received a transition clearance from ZZZ Tower after admitting the oversight and confirmed the TFR upon landing.

ASRS:1774163.n: I file this report for two reasons: to note a particular pilot's decision-making, and to talk about a larger potentially dangerous airport-environment situation. Here is the relevant data:- The airport in question is Montgomery County Airpark, in Gaithersburg, Maryland, GAI. It is a very busy *uncontrolled* airport. It is within the DC SFRA, so pilots must obtain a discrete transponder code from Potomac Approach before taking off, and before re-entering the SFRA from outside. - The airport's only runway is 32/14, about 4000 feet long. The airport ATIS specifies that Runway 14 is preferred in calm-wind conditions. Also, the only approach to GAI is an RNAV/LPV approach to Runway 14. - There is a very, very active primary-training type airport. Nearly all of its students are [from] overseas, and the frequency of their flight means that the traffic-pattern at the airport is usually 'full.'
