It is typical to have one plane doing a runup, another taking off, another on downwind turning to base, and two or three others approaching from the north, all at the same time.- On the morning of this incident, winds had been in the 5 kt range--but from the north. So traffic through the morning had been all on Runway 32. - Now, the time in question. It was about XA:00 local EST. I was approaching from the north, and I received a code for entering the SFRA from Potomac Approach. As is usual practice, when I was about 12 miles north of GAI, I told Potomac, 'Gaithersburg in sight;' and they gave the formulaic response: 'Stay on discrete transponder code until landing, remain outside Class Bravo, switch to local frequency approved.' So I switched to the local UNICOM, 123.075.-I heard on the frequency what I also saw on my ADS-B display: That the pattern was, as usual, 'busy;' with three or four planes at various points in the circuit. And all of them were using Runway 32. (The winds at that moment were reporting calm on ATIS, but the pattern had been in steady use all day, on 32.)-Over the next eight minutes or so, between first radio contact and landing, I noticed two recurrent phenomena. One was many planes reporting their progress and position in a pattern for Runway 32. I made calls, beginning at 8 miles out, with intentions to follow the established local practice. ('Forty-five to join right downwind for Runway 32.') The other notable entry was one airplane (Airplane X) that reported it was to the west, and 'straight in landing, Runway 14.'-A plane reports 'downwind 32.' Aircraft X says, 'straight in, Runway 14.' Another plane says, 'Aircraft X, we are using 32, please circle to land.' Aircraft pilot says, 'Straight in Runway 14.' At least twice, and I think three times, flight instructors say 'Aircraft X, PLEASE circle to land 32. We are all using 32.' Aircraft X replies, 'Straight in, 14.'-I kept reporting my own position, and said at one point 'Aircraft X, I am turning base to final for landing 32.' At that point I could see him descending to 14 -- i.e., head on. The distances were such that it was clear to me that I could land safely and normally, and get off the runway, before he got too close. And I proceeded to land. I turned off the runway halfway down, while he was still probably a mile out on opposite-direction final. All the other planes in the Runway 32 pattern extended their downwind etc., to land. -The two planes landed at XA:07 pm EST, but in opposite directions.-Later, I saw someone who I assumed to be the Aircraft X pilot. He was, and I asked him: 'Why did you do that?' His answer was that he was fine-tuning the coupled-autopilot and wanted to fly an approach all the way down. -Note: I have been in this situation myself too, wanting to check out autopilots. But I choose airports where I can do so in keeping with the local traffic flow. -The main problem in this scenario was the Aircraft X pilot, who insisted on plowing ahead despite repeated requests on the frequency to switch to join the busy local traffic flow. I realize this is not an 'enforcement' forum, and I mention it just FYI.-The larger point is that the Gaithersburg airport has become unsustainably busy, for its uncontrolled status. I have landed there probably X times over the past XX years. I *always* view the most challenging part of any trip to be the final 10 minutes of trying to fit into the uncontrolled but increasingly busy traffic pattern there. With many primary students in training, they're often doing unexpected things in the pattern, or are uncertain in radio calls. Suggestion / request: Sooner or later there is going to be some safety incident at this airport, coming from too much traffic with too little control. A tower controller would *never* have allowed the situation I'm reporting to emerge. This is a problem waiting to happen at this airport.
ASRS:1774163.s: A pilot reported a near-midair conflict at uncontrolled Montgomery County Airpark (GAI) while landing Runway 32 against Aircraft X, which insisted on a straight-in approach to Runway 14 to test its coupled autopilot. Despite repeated radio requests from other pilots to join the established Runway 32 pattern, Aircraft X proceeded, forcing the reporter to exit the runway early to avoid a head-on collision.

ASRS:1774172.n: Day 1 of the cycle I was arriving in ZZZ to meet up with my First Officer (FO) for flights that afternoon. I came on duty and was scheduled to land in ZZZ this afternoon. I was in contact with my original FO who was home on standby in the morning and was coming to the airport this afternoon for our flights. When I landed in ZZZ, Flights Operations informed me my original FO had been taken off of the flight-line due to COVID. Flight Operations informed me I had another FO coming in to replace him and I should be able to maintain my original departure time out of ZZZ. I was texting my new FO asking when he would be at the airport and he said around XA30. In the meantime I got the airplane ready, so that we could depart as soon as he arrived. When he arrived we called Flight Operations to confirm our flights and then we took off. The next day, Flight Operations reached out to my FO and told him that we had taken off while he was in FAR rest period. I had no idea he was still in rest, I was under the impression he was already on duty as home standby and had been called in for the flight. Upon finding this out I called the Chief Pilot's Office and explained the situation.Looking forward, I'm going to confirm the FO's duty start time so that we are all on the same page and staying legal within flight duty.
ASRS:1774172.s: The Captain and a replacement First Officer departed from ZZZ after the original crew member was removed due to COVID. Flight Operations later reported the replacement First Officer was still in a FAR rest period, as the Captain mistakenly believed he was already on duty.

ASRS:1774180.n: While flying [my aircraft], I experienced an engine failure approximately 15 NM prior to the destination runway while flying at approximately 2,300 feet. I had been experiencing extreme headwinds since a refueling stop and the leg had taken me longer than I'd planned. Because of the added flight time, I was thinking about fuel, but I thought I had enough fuel to make the intended destination with minimum reserves. The engine failure was accompanied by a lack of fuel pressure that was not remedied by turning on an electric fuel pump. I firmly believe it was due to fuel exhaustion. With no airports within gliding distance, I angled the plane towards the interstate, and eventually lined up on a dark area parallel to the highway and attempted a landing onto an area about 100 yards from the highway. As I approached the field, I flared, and initially landed the main wheels successfully and rolled for a couple of seconds, probably 20 yards, but as soon as the nose wheel touched the recently plowed soft dirt, it dug in. I did not suffer any serious injuries that I'm aware of and the plane had surprisingly minor damage. Upon checking the fuel tanks after exiting the plane, they were indeed empty.
ASRS:1774180.s: The pilot experienced an engine failure due to fuel exhaustion at 2,300 feet while 15 NM from the destination. After attempting a forced landing on soft dirt near a highway, the nose wheel dug in, resulting in minor aircraft damage but no serious injuries.

ASRS:1774182.n: I was returning to BED from the West. It was dark. I tuned in the ATIS. The current ATIS was broadcasting that BED was 'landing and departing Runway 23.' After copying the ATIS, I called BED Tower and reported my position as near Minuteman Airport (6B6) and informed the Tower that I was inbound landing with ATIS. The Tower Controller initially cleared me to enter a right downwind for Runway 29. This confused me because the ATIS had stated that BED was 'landing and departing Runway 23.' I asked the Controller for confirmation of the runway assignment and he acknowledged that he had 'made a mistake' and told me to enter a right downwind for Runway 23. After I entered the control space, and near the airport, I noticed the high intensity runway lights and landing traffic was on Runway 29, while runway 23 had their lights on 'dim'. Since the ATIS had not mentioned simultaneous operations to intersecting runways, I became disoriented. I mistook Runway 29 for Runway 23. I was so concerned that I even called the Tower and asked the Controller: 'Is the Aircraft Y lined up with the right runway?'The Tower Controller realized that something was not right and called me and asked me to confirm that I was setting up for right downwind 23 and offered me a clearance to enter a right downwind for Runway 29. I told him that I thought I could still correct, but I ended up flying through the final for Runway 23 and ended up on a left downwind for 23. At about this time, another aircraft, which I later learned was Aircraft Z arriving from the west had also turned inbound to Runway 23 from the north. The Tower Controller told me to turn 20 degrees further right which I did to widen out my downwind leg. Thanks to the Controller, the Aircraft Z was able to land safely and so was I.I now realize that several other factors contributed to my confusion. I was more tired than I realized. I had a very long work week, yet this night was an opportunity to start flying more night flights, after being absent from this experience for over 16 months. The pandemic means hazard [but not] if I bring an instructor to help me re-acquaint to night flying. I allowed myself to be fooled by the warm weather, the light winds and the great visibility into thinking that it would be a good night to re-acquaint myself to cross-country night flying. Tonight, with the lights dimmed in the cockpit, and the high intensity lights on Runway 29, a plane landing on 29, the lights dimmed on Runway 23, and my lack of night flying practice did this happen.I now realize that I had vastly underestimated the combined effects of fatigue, distraction and 'rust.' Added to that, my confusion resulting from the initial mistaken clearance to enter a right downwind for 29, the combination of bright runway lighting on a conflicting runway without any warning that such operations were being conducted, and traffic operating in unexpected directions all combined to make for a much more confusing situation than I ever would have expected.The controllers explained to me that even when Runway 23 is the operating runway, they still allow traffic to land and depart Runway 29 because Runway 23 is too short for some aircraft that use the field. Nevertheless, I believe that safety would be greatly improved if, during nighttime operations, the ATIS included the warning concerning operations being conducted simultaneously to conflicting runways. This is especially true at BED where runway alignment issues are already an issue. I believe that such a warning would have eliminated my confusion at seeing traffic landing and departing on Runway 29 and then mistaking it for Runway 23.
ASRS:1774182.s: A fatigued pilot returning to BED at night became disoriented after an initial incorrect clearance for Runway 29 conflicted with ATIS information for Runway 23. The pilot mistakenly identified Runway 29 as 23 due to lighting differences and lack of ATIS warnings about simultaneous operations, but the controller corrected the path to ensure a safe landing.

ASRS:1774183.n: I was doing pattern work at ZZZ between XA:00 and XB:00. The airfield had a large amount of arriving traffic during the hours I was flying. After a touch & go on RWY XX, I was asked to extend the upwind before flying a right pattern. About mid-field on the downwind, tower requested a left-360. After my first 360, I was instructed to extend my downwind. A second plane [Aircraft Y] was approaching the airport from the northwest. Aircraft Y was asked to 'make a right 270, keep it tight and get ready to line up behind a [jet]'ATC then asked me to widen out my downwind and look for Aircraft Y making the right 270. At this point it was at my 11 o clock, 3 miles. About 5 seconds later I was able to identify the aircraft, let tower know that I had them in sight and was preparing to line up behind them. About 15 seconds later, tower called me up again, asking 'Aircraft X - extend it out a little bit, actually just follow behind and I'll call your base you will have to follow a jet behind on final'. I read back and confirmed.About 30 seconds later, tower called me up again, 'Aircraft X just so I don't get you too far from the field, make a left 360'. I read back the instruction and began my left 360. At this point, I was already thinking about Aircraft Y as I was planning on how I would get back on the downwind and line up behind them. I believe Aircraft Y was just about to finish its right 270 as I was about 90 degrees into my 360. I was able to spot and track the plane on Foreflight with Sentry, but since I had to make a 360 I lost visual when I initiated my turn. Tower, likely receiving a traffic alert called the other plane to make them aware of me: 'Aircraft X about a mile south making a left 360 - he has you in sight'. I do not think he asked them to confirm that they had me in sight and I can't tell from the live-ATC recording whether they read it back. The added statement 'he has you in sight' was extremely dangerous and could have been fatal. Yes, I had the traffic in sight when I was heading toward it and planning to get behind them, but once I started my left 360 there was no way of maintaining a visual with the other plane since I was now heading the opposite direction. I immediately recognized the potential conflict and started looking both outside the plane and on Foreflight trying to spot and track the other plane's relative position. The other plane did not make a 270 turn, but instead kept turning toward the airport/runway i.e. cutting into my path.As I was about 270 degrees into my 360 turn tower called 'Aircraft X - as you are coming out of that 360 turn do you still have Aircraft Y in sight?'At this point, I was already banking hard left in a steep turn trying to pull away from the converging traffic that I saw coming closer toward me. Turning right was not an option as it would have put me in the middle of final with jets arriving. I do not think the other plane confirmed whether or not they had me in sight. If they did, they flew way too close to me for my comfort and should have initiated an avoidance maneuver. In response to tower's question I responded 'Aircraft X unable' because I had to focus on flying the airplane away from the other traffic. We then passed by each other with much less separation than I feel comfortable. The other plane heading toward the runway, and me pulling hard left to the North-West, initiating a climb up to gain altitude. It is hard to tell exactly but horizontal distance could have been less than 500 feet Vertical distance was virtually the same. It happened very quickly. If I had not realized the potential conflict and mitigated by tracking on foreflight and pulling hard left this could have been a really really bad situation. The biggest mistake here, in my opinion, was ATC communicating to the other plane that I had them in sight AFTER I started my 360. There is no way one can maintain visual during such a maneuver while also flying safely and ATC shouldunder no circumstances make that statement. I also think that having two planes completing maneuvers in a way where their exit paths can conflict (right 270 and left 360) in close proximity should be prohibited.There were multiple safer options here. Aircraft Y could have flown a proper base rather than cutting it short onto final. I could have been asked to fly west, or I could have been asked to fly another 360 right after the first one. The fact that ATC changed its instructions relative to how I should fly behind/around the other traffic 3 times in a minute indicates to me that they were not planning ahead but rather responding to/running behind.In the future, I will call out if ATC tells other people that I have them in sight when I don't (i.e. after starting my left 360). I am also surprised nobody (tower/the other plane) complained about how close this was. I am glad to be back on the ground. I hope this helps keep other people safe in the future!
ASRS:1774183.s: A pilot conducting pattern work at ZZZ experienced a near-midair conflict with another aircraft after ATC incorrectly stated the pilot had traffic in sight while executing a left 360. The pilot avoided a collision by banking hard left and climbing, attributing the hazard to conflicting ATC instructions and the false visual confirmation.

ASRS:1774184.n: The HND ATIS for Henderson is not receivable by aircraft arriving to Henderson in the Southeast to East quadrant because of the mountain range just 3 miles east of Henderson, NV airport. The antenna for the ATIS for HND must be relocated to the top of the mountain range.You will expect an air traffic accident because aircraft cannot get the information when Las Vegas approach is so busy that they cannot relay all the information to arriving VMC and Flight following aircraft.Please advise the authorities to take action. This is a hazardous situation.
ASRS:1774184.s: The reporter states that aircraft arriving at Henderson (HND) from the southeast to east cannot receive ATIS due to a mountain range 3 miles east of the airport. This lack of information during busy Las Vegas Approach operations is described as a hazardous situation likely to cause an accident unless the antenna is relocated.

ASRS:1774213.n: At the beginning of my rotation I let the company know that my tire was looking bad and needed to be replaced. As PIC I agreed to continue to fly with a worn tire for a few more legs, it was an educated risk as there was still some tread showing and no cord visible from what I'd seen.We departed ZZZ headed to ZZZ1 for maintenance on a variety of items, on departure the ZZZ Tower reported a loud noise and was concerned it was our tire. There was no indication on taxi or takeoff of a bad tire and Tower didn't observe a flat tire.Landing at ZZZ1, the tire popped on landing and the aircraft had a shake to it on roll out. Upon parking, we looked at the tire and it had exploded and thrown pieces at the lower wing surface, flap, and engine cowl, causing some damage.In the future, when a tire is looking like it needs to be replaced soon, I'll have it replaced instead of giving it a few more landings.
ASRS:1774213.s: The PIC elected to fly with a worn tire despite prior concerns, resulting in a tire explosion upon landing at ZZZ1. The failure caused aircraft shake and debris damage to the wing, flap, and engine cowl, prompting the pilot to commit to immediate replacement in the future.

ASRS:1774233.n: Please listen to the Phoenix [P50] TRACON sectors during peak periods. The Controller could not work all of the traffic. The COVID-19 cutback by ATC is dangerous during peak use hours. The controllers are magnificent but need help/more controllers. One Controller is working an area twice to 3 times the reasonable area. Please let them get back to work like it was before the COVID slowdown.I have been actively flying for XX+ years. Please don't blow this off. The environment is dangerous.
ASRS:1774233.s: A pilot reported that Phoenix TRACON controllers could not manage all traffic during peak periods due to COVID-19 staffing cutbacks. The reporter stated that one controller was working two to three times the reasonable area, creating a dangerous environment.

ASRS:1774246.n: Approached ZZZ Runway XX for landing at approximately XA:50 from the south. After monitoring radio communications and no one in the pattern I made the decision to approach for landing straight in. I made a radio call stating my intentions and reporting 3 mile final for runway XX. I reduced throttle and speed to within flap range. I input flaps adjusted trim and further reduced speed. I turned on the runway lighting and adjusted course to the left then made a radio call for a mile final approach to runway XX. I verified my indicated airspeed was 62kts as I approached the runway, aimed for the numbers, and reminded myself the runway is closer than it appears in the dark. I then touched down hard on the runway and the nose of the aircraft bounced high sounding the stall warning. When the nose gear came back down in contact with the runway again it did not support the aircraft and the propeller came in contact with the runway stopping the aircraft on runway XX. My first concern was that I was obstructing the runway and tried to make a radio call. However, the radio was not working, at which point I powered down the aircraft and was attempting to open the canopy when I was approached by bystanders at the airport. They asked if I was okay and moved the aircraft off the runway via [Taxiway] 1A, by holding on to and lowering the tail pulling the aircraft on its main landing gear.
ASRS:1774246.s: A pilot landing at night on Runway XX experienced a hard touchdown, bounce, and stall warning, resulting in nose gear collapse and propeller contact with the runway. The pilot's radio failed, but bystanders later moved the aircraft off the runway via Taxiway 1A.

ASRS:1774272.n: Uncommanded rollback of Number 2 Engine at FL380. Completed appropriate checklists and communicated with company, flight attendants, and passengers. Diverted without incident.We recognized the issue as it occurred and responded accordingly. I should have divided responsibilities better to prevent high task loading. I was PM in cruise at FL380. Uncommanded rollback of Number 2 Engine. Restart attempt was unsuccessful, and the engine was secured. Completed all appropriate checklists. Diverted to ZZZ. Requested rescue equipment to standby upon landing. Briefed flight attendants and ZZZ Ops. Landed without incident.The diversion information on the normal checklist is helpful in managing tasks during a high workload event.
ASRS:1774272.s: The Pilot Monitoring experienced an uncommanded rollback of Engine 2 at FL380, leading to a failed restart and engine securement. The crew diverted to ZZZ and landed without incident, though the pilot noted that better task division could have reduced workload.

ASRS:1774342.n: The First Officer was flying a visual approach to ZZZ Runway XXR with right traffic from ZZZZZ3 arrival. Radar vector to final, cleared to 3,000 feet from 4,000 feet and cleared the visual. First Officer was in vertical speed and I set 3,000 feet in the MCP window. He armed approach mode and captured the localizer. The aircraft leveled at 3,000 feet and did not capture the glide slope as we were too high. Gear was down, flaps 20 and speed was 163. First Officer disconnected the autopilot and dove down to capture the glide slope. I suggested speed brakes, which he used to get down. This rapid descent caused the Tower to issue an altitude warning. I then became very busy stowing speed brakes, landing flaps, checklists, and verifying stable approach parameters. We never did the 1,000 feet call for set M/A altitude and cleared to land check (which we were). The event, although satisfying the stable approach parameters, was highly irregular and borderline go-around scenario. The debrief included mostly what went wrong and why. We discussed and I noted the main errors. The First Officer said not flying for 7 months was the issue.
ASRS:1774342.s: The First Officer, returning after a seven-month absence, executed a rapid descent to capture the glide slope during a visual approach to ZZZ Runway XXR. This maneuver triggered a Tower altitude warning and caused the crew to miss the 1,000-foot callout, resulting in a borderline go-around scenario.

ASRS:1774362.n: I was assigned today to operate SuperTug X, a towbarless aircraft tow tractor, while working at ZZZ. After towing the aircraft to Gate X, after disconnecting the SuperTug and while attempting to maneuver away, I made light contact with the pushback tractor which was parked behind me. At the time, I was feeling rushed, because I knew there were more tows scheduled for us and there was also someone waiting for me to clear the area so he could connect the ground power to the aircraft. While backing up I felt that I had the proper radius in the turn to clear the parked pushback but apparently did not, and made a light inadvertent contact with either the SuperTug hitch or bumper. I did notice that on this and a few other occasions that day, because I was wearing a different than usual but still company issued face mask, my depth perception seemed to be affected as the mask kept creeping up into my peripheral vision. I think this was a factor in my misjudging the turn in what were already very confined conditions. Another issue is that the SuperTug onboard GPU had recently been repaired, and we were using it for the first time in months, with a commensurate disruption to normal workflow. Although I thought I had clearance at the time, in retrospect I should have taken a minute to move the pushback and reduce the risk. There was no pushback parking spot painted at this gate, so it was parked right against the edge of the OSZ [Outer Safety Zone], even there there was approximately 80 additional linear feet of space behind it available to park. Even if I had moved it, I doubt there was a user check performed on it that day, and therefore moving it without doing one myself would technically put me in violation. There are many more things that can be taken into consideration than just the blatantly obvious in a situational dynamic environment like an airport. Because the contact I made felt light, and I know from experience that the equipment is built to take that kind of minor impact, I made the snap decision to continue with the operation. If you take a look at any piece of airport ground equipment, including SuperTugs, it will immediately become apparent that it is literally covered with innumerable scratches and dents or varying severity, and if we would stop to report and investigate each one, the operation would literally grind to a halt. Therefore, it was my decision in this instance, based on my experience, observations, and common sense to continue. There were other factors which came into play in this decision, which I will briefly expand upon. I need to be clear that if this situation had been one in which I had reason to suspect that there was damage to equipment or even the possibility of damage to an aircraft, that I would have stopped and reported it at once. In this instance I deemed that it would be unreasonable to bring it up.Today was the X day back from my vacation of Y days, and when checking my work assignments for the month, this was only my Z day assigned to a SuperTug for the month, and the first assigned to X brand SuperTug. The other days I was at work during this time I was assigned to auxiliary functions. I believe this is significant in that it feels that this period of lack of hands-on experience caused a perception that my skills may have deteriorated or that I had become rusty. To that point, I noticed that I was taking some calculated risks, most notably when maneuvering on the gate areas, especially around stationary ground equipment, while preparing to capture or egressing from the vicinity of aircraft. My reasoning for this, and which I explained to the Supervisor during the course of the day, was that I was attempting to refresh or hone my skills, which I felt may have become dulled. Another way to put it is that I was trying to find my corners, as persons who operate various types of vehicles say when describing how they feel or sense where the vehicle is in relation to the surrounding environment. While doing this I felt that I was on point, secure and aware of myself and tasks at hand. I could say that in fact I was over-zealous or over-confident, too gung ho, and I should have taken a step back at some point and put all this information together, which I only do now after the fact. I would have to say that the primary reason I did not take that step back was workload / task saturation and distraction, described as follows:Because of the substantial number of people who were not able to work, apparently due to the public health crisis yet ongoing, the manpower available was at or just over half of which would normally be on the team on a given shift. There was not a substantial reduction in workload, and we had what I would consider based on precedent to be a moderately but not excessively heavy day. There was therefore an underlying perception of increased pressure to perform, especially in consideration of supporting the needs of the operation because of the diminished staffing during an unusually trying time.I had also noticed multiple issues during the day, which could have been brought to the attention of management or also could have been overlooked and dealt with at a time of less operational urgency. The most notable of those issues were, a broken seat belt in the SuperTug, radios whose display units were not lighted and hence not visible after sunset, and all the fire extinguishers on the SuperTug were missing the inspection placards. Additionally, no less than three sets or portable stairs that we used during the day had operational deficiencies which would have deemed them unsafe or usable, and which I have been seriously doing a report on. For any or all of these reasons or others, I could have stopped the operation. I chose not to so as not to interrupt the operational tempo but more so because these types of inconsistencies are regularly not recognized as such but instead accepted as the norm, and ignored and worked around, regularly and without second thought or concern. For a company that emphasizes a focus safety as the primary value, in actuality the primary focus appears more to be, unless there is a glaring issue present, in many but not all instances, getting the task accomplished with little or no regard given to risk mitigation. This attitude is part of the culture of this workforce, is long going, omnipresent and systemic. Combined with other negative attitudes and attributes it conspires to create a corporation which says one thing, and does another. To an employee who wants to do the right thing because of the recognition of the fact that it is mutually beneficial to do so, working in this environment can be disheartening, frustrating and disappointing. To be frankly honest, I feel quite often that I am being singled out on occasion for attempting to bring these sorts of things to light, and that local management's attitude towards me is becoming that, if you want to hold us accountable then we will do the same towards you, watch you like a hawk and bring to bear any issue or inconsistency in your performance also. This does feel to me to be somewhat unfair, at times. When I decide to bring an issue to light, I give it careful consideration, more than I probably should, and more often than not I keep quiet about it, do my job and let management do theirs. We should be striving to work together, especially in a critical time such as this now is.I do admit that at some point during the day, I should have recognized that the pressure levels were increasing and should have voluntarily and proactively taken a few minutes to step back and regain composure and reintegrate myself appropriately into the operational flow. I did not do so largely because of operational pressure but also due to the distraction caused by various inconsistencies I described, keeping a running mental tally of these while still maintaining a focus on my tasks. Based on my analysis of the events of this situation, I consider that it would be more likely that I take a pause given another encounter of a similar chain of events.
ASRS:1774362.s: A ground crew member operating a SuperTug at Gate X made light contact with a parked pushback tractor while maneuvering away from an aircraft. The reporter attributed the incident to task saturation, reduced depth perception from a face mask, and a lack of recent hands-on experience with the specific equipment.

ASRS:1774374.n: Flight ABC was taxing into Gate X when a baggage tug who was driving on the service road making a right turn from behind Gate Y failed to yield to the aircraft almost causing the aircraft to collide with the tug and baggage carts which would have been fatal for the driver as well as significant damage to the aircraft. Myself and wingwalkers tried to stop the aircraft which eventually slowed down to avoid colliding with the tug and carts. This is a common issue at this station which goes unreported and when it does, no disciplinary action is taken so it keeps on happen.
ASRS:1774374.s: Flight ABC was taxiing to Gate X when a baggage tug failed to yield while turning from Gate Y, nearly causing a collision with the aircraft and carts. The pilot and wingwalkers stopped the aircraft to avoid impact, noting this is a recurring, unaddressed issue at the station.

ASRS:1774376.n: On teaming gates, the lack of push qualified agents has caused some issues with close departure times between two gates. In order to achieve on [time] departures, some have been advised to have a non-push qualified agent sit on the tractor and ask for brake release until a qualified push agent is able to take over.
ASRS:1774376.s: Ground staff at teaming gates faced departure delays due to a shortage of push-qualified agents. To maintain on-time departures, non-qualified agents were instructed to sit on the tractor and request brake release until qualified personnel arrived.

ASRS:1774389.n: Descending into LUK on the LNAV 3R we first received a report from tower of a low altitude alert in between the FAF and the intermediate step down fix (ZUGMI at or above 1480). I had the aircraft in LNAV/VS with a commanded vertical speed mode of -700FPM. I glanced at the altimeter and saw 1550. This is above the step down altitude and above the MDA. The copilot and I both quickly agreed we were above MDA. At this point also I looked out and could see the runway. We briefly leveled off and planned to continue visually. At this point we received a too low PULL UP. Aural warning. Immediately we went around. After getting back level and configuring we talked about the approach and decided to do it again with less vertical speed and just stay a bit higher on the glide path. We got down to out MDA without issue and landed.I never saw any altitude any lower than the step down altitude on the approach. LUK airport is sunk in the valleys between some hills and I think I should've maybe thought to have a gentler vertical speed.Not accept a fairly close to minimums LNAV only approach with a lot of turbulence into Lunken when ZZZ is right around the corner. Fly the instrument profile at lowest possible vertical speed and visual only after VDP. Although we never busted any altitudes I could've made it a much gentler descent to MDA at the VDP since the VDP is 2.4 from the runway and there are lots of hills on the approach prior to the runway.IMC until ragged bases around 800 AGL to 1,000 AGL. Some Visual conditions at time of the event. Runway/PAPI were in sight.
ASRS:1774389.s: The flight crew received a "too low PULL UP" warning during an LNAV 3R approach to LUK while descending at -700 FPM, prompting an immediate go-around. They attributed the alert to a steep descent profile in turbulent conditions and successfully landed on a second attempt using a gentler vertical speed.

ASRS:1774392.n: Captain's Oxygen Mask on Aircraft X was opaque (could not use visually). I wrote up the discrepancy. Maintenance came out to the aircraft and wiped it clear with an alcohol sanitizer wipe. I reminded him that this was not the procedure that I had watched Maintenance perform over 25 times before, but he assured me that this method was correct. Establish Maintenance procedures that are consistent and will not further damage the O2 mask. Change SOP to mandate a visual inspection of O2 mask prior to each flight.
ASRS:1774392.s: The Captain reported an opaque oxygen mask on Aircraft X, which Maintenance cleared using an alcohol wipe instead of the standard procedure. The reporter requested consistent maintenance protocols and a new SOP mandating visual inspections of the mask before each flight.

ASRS:1774427.n: ZZZ-ATL routing was …DAWWN BEORN.Hobbit2 but we put …DAWNN BEORN.Hobbit2 in the FMS by mistake. We caught it after about 5 miles direct to the wrong fix DAWNN and advised ATC. No one asked for a phone number or anything.Typo with the clearance it was kind of an abnormal morning cause we were rushing once we got to the aircraft. We did the clearance verification, but overlooked the typo on DAWNN (DAWWN)..
ASRS:1774427.s: The flight crew entered a typo in the FMS, routing to fix DAWNN instead of the cleared DAWWN, and flew five miles before correcting the error and advising ATC. The incident resulted from rushing during an abnormal morning, causing the crew to overlook the typo despite performing clearance verification.

ASRS:1774443.n: While departing ZZZ Runway X on the RVAV departure, we experienced a wind shear ahead alert shortly after rotation and after the gear was selected up. While climbing through approximately 500 feet AGL, we entered an area of moderate to severe turbulence followed by a gain and loss of 20+ knots of airspeed. Airspeed excisions were brief in nature, and climb rate decreased from near 3,000 FPM to 1,000 FPM and momentarily less while we transited the wind shear. During this time we also experienced multiple quick rolling and yawing moments that required nearly full control deflection to counter. Both myself and my First Officer agreed that the aircraft was at times momentarily out of control. It is my recollection that the maximum intensity of the turbulence occurred from 500 feet AGL to approximately 3,500 feet AGL. Again these excursions were very quick left and right rolling and yawing motions. During the event, the aircraft energy state never decayed to a dangerous level, however, we were in a lightly loaded -700 with max thrust selected for wind shear avoidance. Above 4,000 feet, we experienced continuous moderate turbulence and icing up to 14,000 feet, and only light turbulence above that. There were no injuries reported, and we did not suspect any aircraft damage. The flight attendants and passengers were briefed before takeoff. Before departure, both myself and the First Officer consulted the Airport Wind System reports as well as reviewed the required wind limits for the departure. The ZZZ Tower and Dispatch were contacted to get a better assessment of what they were seeing with the winds as well. At the time of the beginning of the takeoff roll, the Tower reported steady state wind from the south east 28 KT gusting to 38 KT. The Airport Wind System alert was not functioning, however, [other weather station's] wind and the gust 2-6 Airport Wind System was reporting. All wind reports were within limits at the time of takeoff, and had been for most of the morning. The Dispatcher reported the 8 High Airport Wind System Alert was intermittent all morning. Both myself and my First Officer briefed the departure and took steps necessary to mitigate the perceived threats. Wind shear take off procedures and power settings were used during the take off. After level off, myself and the First Officer consulted the FOM and we were in agreement that we experienced a situation where the aircraft was momentarily not in positive control. A pilot report of MOD to SEV turbulence was relayed to ARTCC as well as company. Dispatch was consulted at this time, and a plan was made to divert to ZZZ1 for maintenance inspection as Maintenance did not want the aircraft stuck in ZZZ2. The remainder of the flight was uneventful. Ensuring Airport Wind System has full functionality and wind profiles are working to the greatest extent possible. Preparing for departure from ZZZ we looked at weather reports including the ZZZ Airport Wind System and PIREPS. Nothing indicated that we would encounter anything greater than moderate turbulence as we took off from Runway X. Shortly after liftoff we encountered moderate turbulence and at about 1,000 ft AGL received a 'Windshear Ahead' alert. We then experienced approximately 30 - 45 seconds of severe turbulence. We gave ATC a PIREP and overflew our original destination of ZZZ2 at the request of Dispatch and Maintenance control to get the plane to a maintenance base.
ASRS:1774443.s: Pilots of a lightly loaded -700 departing ZZZ Runway X encountered severe wind shear and turbulence between 500 and 3,500 feet AGL, causing momentary loss of positive control. The crew diverted to ZZZ1 for a maintenance inspection after the event, reporting no injuries or suspected damage.

ASRS:1774463.n: I was the Captain and Pilot Flying (PF) for Aircraft X from ZZZ to Richmond (RIC) on November XX, 2020, and observed the following. During cruise flight my First Officer and Pilot Monitoring (PM) alerted me that the last time (back in July) that she flew into RIC the airplane caught a false localizer signal and turned no where near the centerline of the respective runway. Having reviewed the Weather Briefing Package, I determined that RIC would be landing to the north, and elected to load the Runway 34 ILS approach. I confirmed all the waypoints with my PM and set up accordingly. I hard tuned the localizer frequency of 110.7, set the approach course of 337 degrees, and set the minimums of 370 feet on the Primary Flight Display (PFD). We received a clearance to cross the NEAVL intersection at 11,000 with a speed of 250 knots. We met that restriction, and then got a clearance to proceed to the KAFKA intersection and pilot's discretion to maintain 2,000 feet. That waypoint was loaded and confirmed. We began a descent. About 12 miles from the airport I slowed the aircraft to 210 knots and had selected Flaps 1. We were about 3,000 feet, and I slowed further to 180 knots, with a setting of Flaps 2. We were about 7 miles from the KAFKA waypoint, and confirmed the airport was insight. I began slowing the plane to 160 knots. About 3 miles from KAFKA, and the approach mode in the armed position, the airplane selected the LOC mode on the PFD and began to turn towards Runway 2. I turned the autopilot off, and manually continued to fly towards the KAFKA waypoint to lose more altitude. The airplane was about 2,300 feet, with 1,700 feet selected in the altitude selector. I continued the approach, and we landed safely. My First Officer questioned the Tower as to why this would happen. The Tower stated that both the Runway 34, and Runway 2 localizers were operational. He said that he would inform the staff at the airport.
ASRS:1774463.s: The Captain of Aircraft X experienced an unintended autopilot turn toward Runway 2 while flying the Runway 34 ILS approach to Richmond. The aircraft captured a false localizer signal despite both localizers being operational, requiring manual intervention to complete a safe landing.

ASRS:1774471.n: After doing safety demo and walking through the cabin for the final safety check, my A FA informed me that the passenger seated in XX1 was not wearing her mask and that she informed her that she needed to put it on. A FA then asked me when I was doing my walk thru to see if she was complying with her request and I said sure. On my way back to my galley I observed passenger XX1 sitting with her mask off. Since this was the second time I used the last approach to try to get her to comply. I spoke with her about her mask she said she couldn't wear it because she was drinking coffee I said I understand but as the announcement states if she isn't actively drinking she has to replace her mask. She then pulled her mask up and said this is ridiculous. I walked back to my galley and informed my A FA that I had spoken with her again about her mask because she had removed it again. At that point we had made the decision that once inflight we would have the Captain make another general announcement reminding everyone to wear a mask. When I walked through the cabin for my final compliance check before landing she had her mask on.
ASRS:1774471.s: A flight attendant reported that a passenger in seat XX1 repeatedly removed her mask during the flight, citing coffee consumption as the reason. The crew decided to have the Captain make a general announcement, and the passenger was compliant with mask requirements during the final pre-landing check.

ASRS:1774486.n: Please strongly address the lack of cooperation on the part of some pilots regarding mask wearing. Flight attendants are not comfortable being in a small enclosed area with fellow employees not following the mask mandate. We are not concerned about what they do when we are not doing lavatory breaks, but are requesting that they follow company policy for the short amount of time we are required to be in the cockpit. This is as much for their safety as ours as we are indeed the ones in contact with dozens of individuals in the cabin.
ASRS:1774486.s: Cabin crew reported that some pilots refused to wear masks while flight attendants were in the cockpit for lavatory breaks. The crew stated this lack of cooperation violated company policy and created safety concerns for employees who contact many passengers.

ASRS:1774490.n: Passengers seated X4 -X5, we mentioned 4 times that the mask is required for the entire duration of the flight and they were upset.
ASRS:1774490.s: Cabin crew informed passengers in seats X4 and X5 four times that masks were required for the entire flight. The passengers became upset regarding this requirement.

ASRS:1774496.n: Passenger X was seated in XX3 during this flight. I asked Passenger X three times to wear his face cover (he had a bandanna). The third time I asked I had a face mask and informed him if his bandanna was giving him trouble he could have the face mask. He said no, he will wear the bandanna and he told me to get away from him. This conversation happened during Taxi and after our safety Demo. I informed the Aft FA [and] the Captain. The Captain said he will make an announcement reminding passengers about wearing the mask. After the double chime, the Aft FA informed me that XX3 took off his bandanna again. I called the Flight Deck and informed them that I was [giving Passenger X] the final warning. I explained to Passenger X. Once I finished he was very angry. He said that he is a veteran who is disabled, he breathed in lots of chemicals during the war and the best think he can do is use the bandanna to cover his mouth. He said he hopes that is enough to keep people from freaking out. I thanked him for his services to our country and empathy for his disabilities. Then he told me aggressively to leave him alone, he said he has not slept for 3 days and that I better not come back and wake him up again. I informed the Captain of everything that was said between Passenger X and I and he said that a CSR will meet us at the gate. I did not approach Passenger X again and he did leave his mask off for the remainder of the flight. I told the CSR everything when he pulled the Jet bridge up to the gate. During the Deplaning process he apologized for how he spoke to me. He said he hadn't sleep for 3 days and it is getting to him and he did have his bandanna covering his nose and mouth. The gate agent spoke to him after he deplaned.
ASRS:1774496.s: A flight attendant reported a passenger in seat XX3 refused to wear a proper face mask during taxi and flight, citing disability and sleep deprivation. The Captain arranged for a CSR to meet the aircraft at the gate, where the passenger apologized after deplaning while still wearing a bandanna.

ASRS:1774498.n: As we were boarding, Passenger X came onboard with her face mask not covering her nose. I politely asked her if she could please cover her nose and mouth with her face mask before entering the aircraft. Passenger X complied and went to her assigned seat. I had to inform Passenger X two other times during a trash walk-through and after I closed the main cabin door to place her face mask over her nose and mouth because she completely took it off both times. Around the fourth time I caught Passenger X with her face mask completely off her face, I politely asked her to comply with Airline's face mask policy. Also, I asked my coworker to double check to see if Passenger X was complying with Airline's face mask policy during another trash walk-through, to which Passenger X wasn't complying with. Passenger X would place her face mask on when we asked her to comply with the face mask policy, but as soon as we walked away she would take it off again. I informed the Captain about Passenger X's non-compliance issues with wearing her face mask. The captain gave me permission to give her the final notice. When I [told] Passenger X the final notice: she pulled her face mask completely down and rolled her eyes at me. I informed the Captain and asked him to call for a CSR to meet us at the gate in ZZZ.When we made it to the gate in ZZZ, the CSR was there waiting. The CSR came on and I told her Passenger X was the one who was having face mask compliance issues. The CSR asked me what happened and I briefly explained. However, the CSR ended up letting Passenger X race right pass her and let her get away. The CSR ask me What am I supposed to do now?' I was at a loss for words. I explained to the CSR that you'll have to go after her because it's not like I could have walked off the aircraft because we were deplaning with an aircraft full of passengers onboard. I pointed Passenger X out to the CSR."
ASRS:1774498.s: Cabin crew reported a passenger repeatedly removing her face mask during boarding and deplaning, prompting the Captain to authorize a final notice and request Customer Service Representative (CSR) assistance at gate ZZZ. The CSR arrived but allowed the passenger to leave the aircraft without intervention, leaving the crew unable to enforce the policy while deplaning.

ASRS:1774515.n: On approach to landing at my home lake I observed traffic parallel to my position. The traffic, a larger single engine float plane, was also visible on my FIS-B. I was over water and the other seaplane was over land. As I descended I noted the airplane turned to the east at low altitude away from the lake and over an adjoining swamp. Since other seaplanes commonly land on the lake I decided to land into the light wind close to the undeveloped shoreline. This would permit the other seaplane unobstructed access to the main body of the lake. As I landed on the water and was in step taxi mode the other seaplane suddenly appeared out of a slough on the water and on a collision course. I immediately turned to avoid the aircraft and the other pilot applied power, continued straight ahead, and departed the lake. The two aircraft were within 100 ft of each other on the water at high speed taxi and in direct conflict. It had not occurred to me that the larger float plane would use the short, narrow slough to land on the water. The slough is a posted waterway prohibiting entry due to the presence of endangered species. Further, the slough is on a local canoe route in common use, particularly on a weekend. It is a tight area for a large float plane to operate in. When I contacted the local seaplane operator he indicated it probably wasn't his aircraft involved, though he did say that the slough was sometimes used because it is 'scenic'. I explained that landing there is prohibited by Florida statute and it is posted. He said he was unfamiliar and would not use it in the future.
ASRS:1774515.s: A pilot landing a seaplane on a lake encountered a collision course with a larger float plane emerging from a prohibited slough. The pilot avoided impact by turning while the other aircraft departed, resulting in a 100-foot separation at high speed due to the unexpected use of the restricted waterway.

ASRS:1774526.n: During a clear day, and after long taxi, we conducted a standard engine Run Up and the aircraft performed flawlessly with strong power output. We were eventually cleared for takeoff and after an uneventful takeoff from Runway XX. Runway XY was CLOSED at ZZZ. Approximately 7 miles north I began to notice that the engine was performing slightly lower than usual. Within moments I saw the RPM drop to 2100 and the engine was 'rumbling'. I executed the emergency checklists at this time, mixture rich, carburetor heat on and power forward and it provided only slightly better performance but not much. I immediately called the Tower and advised them of the engine problem. The tower immediately acknowledged and I continued to bring the aircraft to best glide speed and trouble shoot. I know my aircraft usually likes to run lean so I tried leaning the mixture and it got worse so I immediately enriched the mixture and held it full forward as much as possible and the engine was performing better. In addition I saw that carburetor heat was producing no result so I turned off the carburetor heat and with Throttle, Mixture full forward and carburetor heat off, I was able to sustain over 2300 RPM without any engine shaking. I did a quick scan of the area, and calculation of winds aloft and looked back and saw that indeed I could likely make the ZZZ airport and at worst would have to land on XZ or runway XY, the closed runway but which was mostly vacant. I also calculated and knew, that the winds aloft were quite strong over 3000 ft. so I used full power to climb, catch the southerly winds and return immediately for the airport. I advised ZZZ of my intentions and they said that they would clear the area for me. At all times I was able to climb and if I touched the power controls to reduce them, there would be a decrease in power with more vibration, but at full power I was able to sustain good engine power. My climb worked and stronger winter winds aloft indeed pushed me back into downwind, albeit well above pattern altitude. Nonetheless, I determined that altitude would be the safest option since it would ensure ability to glide to the airport. I was cleared to land and the tower reiterated that the airport would be cleared for me.It is possible during this climb I may have slightly penetrated Class B area above ZZZ but it is not likely as the FlightAware and my handheld GPS did not indicate I reached that altitude. During the process I was always in contact with ZZZ and they had positive ID of my aircraft, so I did not squawk 7700 as I was concerned about moving my hands from the console. Eventually, when I was on a close downwind with landing assured and the only way to slow down to VFE would be to point the nose up as I did not want to risk pulling power and not regaining it. This technique worked and I safely deployed the flaps within operating limitations. I turned base and then final as I eventually deployed additional flaps and cut power. I advised the tower I would be landing and doing some S turns to descend. Landing was uneventful, on the runway just after the numbers. I was able to taxi under my own power however, my mechanic told me he was later unable to restart the engine, most likely due to engine failure. I believe the tower did an amazing job. I also did not hesitate to tell them my intentions. If at any time I thought I would not be able to circle back to Runway XX, I would have easily made Runway XZ or Runway XY if necessary. I do not believe that there were any deviations whether it be owner/operator/pilot related, or mechanical or ATC. It is my belief that everyone did what they had to. My mechanic did run compression checks and other diagnostic tests which are still in progress and the most likely issue was fuel starvation caused by the carburetor. I have acquired a refurbished one recently which will be inspected and installed and, once installed a complete diagnostic will be done once again to determine whether there were other issues.
ASRS:1774526.s: The pilot experienced engine power loss and vibration shortly after takeoff, likely due to carburetor-induced fuel starvation. By adjusting mixture and throttle settings, the pilot maintained sufficient power to return to the airport and land safely, though the engine subsequently failed to restart.

ASRS:1774534.n: While doing a flight over downtown City X, a large static noise came out of my headset and the GPS/Radios started flickering. I then looked at my alternator charge to see it at around 10 volts, well below the 14 volts needed to charge the battery. I decided to make a landing at ZZZ airport. While on short final, I told the Tower Controller that I just suffered an alternator failure and needed to land asap. He then asked if I was declaring an emergency which I replied 'No.' I landed without further incident.
ASRS:1774534.s: The pilot experienced alternator failure and radio interference during a flight over City X, resulting in low voltage. After informing the tower of the issue without declaring an emergency, the pilot landed safely at ZZZ airport.

ASRS:1774558.n: I issued an approach clearance to cross a fix at or above 11,000 ft. until established on the localizer, cleared ILS approach. The aircraft went through the localizer and was correcting back to the localizer and began a descent into a 10,900 ft. MVA. I was giving a relief briefing and looking at the checklist. When I looked back at the screen the aircraft was at approximately 10,700 ft. and already correcting back to the localizer and exiting the 10,900 ft. MVA into a 9,000 ft. MVA. No low altitude alert went off and I didn't issue a low altitude alert as it seemed unnecessary leaving the higher MVA and by the time I would have issued it the aircraft would have been in the lower MVA. My recommendation would be for the pilot to have complied with instruction to maintain 11,000 ft. until established on the localizer prior to beginning descent.
ASRS:1774558.s: An air traffic controller issued an approach clearance to maintain 11,000 ft until established on the localizer, but the aircraft descended into a 10,900 ft MVA before correcting. The controller did not issue a low altitude alert, recommending the pilot had complied with the instruction to hold altitude until established.

ASRS:1774568.n: Upon initial radio call to Ground Control requesting to taxi for deicing, Ground cleared us to taxi to 'CDF Deice pad' via K, E2. We taxied via Taxiway K, then made the 45deg left turn onto Taxiway E2 and saw the numerous deice spots there. We then contacted Iceman, and he told us to come to the 'CDF Deice Pad.' It turns out there is another deice pad further east on the easternmost part of Taxiway E2. This is not depicted on the 10-9 pages.We taxied further east to the easternmost part of Taxiway E2 without further incident.
ASRS:1774568.s: The flight crew taxied to the CDF Deice Pad via Taxiways K and E2 after Ground Control clearance. They discovered an additional deice pad at the eastern end of E2 not depicted on the 10-9 pages but reached it without incident.

ASRS:1774570.n: We were on final for Runway 25L when we noticed what we believed to be a drone flying in opposite direction and towards us.I took the airplane and applied positive input to roll the airplane into 30-35 degrees of bank to the left. We cleared a now-identified cluster of about 20 balloons.I have encountered and reported drones on final in the past, and I admit I am sensitive to the subject.The maneuver was not very much more than an S-turn except for the rate of bank.
ASRS:1774570.s: The pilot on final for Runway 25L executed a 30-35 degree left bank to avoid what was initially believed to be a drone. The maneuver successfully cleared a cluster of approximately 20 balloons, which the pilot noted was an S-turn with a higher rate of bank.

ASRS:1774577.n: At BNA, the ILS Hold Short line for Runway 31 is depicted on the airport diagram as being located on Taxiway L, east of Taxiway L7. This puts it pretty close to the runway, however, it is actually located on Taxiway L, west of (prior to) Taxiway T6. This means you're past the ILS Hold Short before you even start looking for it, and you'd be beyond it already if you came out of the ramp area on Taxiway T6. We talked to Tower about it, and they told us that the line had been moved many months ago.
ASRS:1774577.s: Pilots at BNA reported that the ILS Hold Short line for Runway 31 is incorrectly depicted on the airport diagram as being east of Taxiway L7, when it is actually located west of Taxiway T6. Tower confirmed the line was moved months ago, creating a discrepancy where aircraft could cross the hold short before locating it.

ASRS:1774578.n: Passenger in seat XX1 would not comply with the Company Face Mask Policy, pre-departure and in cruise. PAs were made from the flight deck addressing the face mask policy. Flight attendants requested numerous times for the passenger to comply. The passenger was verbally abusive during one of the requests. Personnel met the flight in ZZZ. The passenger might have been under the influence per conversations with the lead Flight Attendant.
ASRS:1774578.s: A passenger in seat XX1 refused to comply with the face mask policy pre-departure and in cruise, becoming verbally abusive despite flight deck announcements and crew requests. Ground personnel met the flight in ZZZ, where the lead Flight Attendant suspected the passenger might have been under the influence.

ASRS:1774613.n: I was the PM, CA was flying. At about 7,100 MSL while being vectored on the NE side of CLT airport for Runway 36R (cross side runway) we noticed a drone off our right side about 1-2 O'clock position, passing by off our right side. It was close enough to distinguish it was a 4 propeller drone. It was hard to determine exactly how far away the drone was but my guess would be within a few hundred feet. As we passed by in our descent we appeared to be slightly below it as we passed. We notified ATC and continued the approach to landing uneventfully.At first I thought it was a bird until I quickly realized it was a drone. I kept my eyes on it as long as I could as we passed by. There is no doubt that it was a drone. Cause was drone flying in Class Bravo airspace near CLT at an altitude high enough to be in the way of commercial airline traffic. We were being vectored from the NW to the NE side of Charlotte airport for Runway 36R. I notified the CA when I first saw something, and he too saw the drone. We did not make any altitude or course changes as it happened too quickly and the drone was not in our immediate flight path.
ASRS:1774613.s: The PM and CA observed a four-propeller drone within a few hundred feet while being vectored at 7,100 MSL near CLT for Runway 36R. The drone was flying in Class Bravo airspace, but no altitude or course changes were made as it was not in the immediate flight path, and the approach continued uneventfully.

ASRS:1774629.n: As I was flying to ZZZ, right about over MHT [VOR], I encountered continues moderate turbulence at 6,000 feet, I requested to climb to 8,000 feet, as I was climbing ATC advised me that larger airplanes had reported moderate turbulence between 6,000 and 8,000 then, when I got out of the clouds at 8,000 feet, for a brief moment it got a little better, but, when I got in the clouds again, it got very aggressive turbulent again, the airplane made abrupt movements, life jackets coming loose and over the cabin, safety briefing card flying around and the passenger getting shacked back there, immediately I requested descent to 6,000 and then to 5,000, then at 5,000 I saw ZZZ airport, requested and got the visual approach and landed.
ASRS:1774629.s: The pilot encountered severe turbulence between 6,000 and 8,000 feet while en route to ZZZ, causing life jackets to loosen and passengers to be shaken. After descending to 5,000 feet, the pilot established visual contact with ZZZ airport and completed a safe landing.

ASRS:1774635.n: While preflighting a stub flight we received an amended flight plan from Dispatch. The Dispatcher said that there was a bend in the flight plan and that he wanted to remove that. Because this was a stub flight our application struggled to upload the correct flight plan. It kept wanting to upload our original flight plan. The PACOTS east routing (Pacific Organized Track System) for that day was our original flight plan which had us departing the 130W longitude for DACEM onward to pick up the IRNMN arrival into LAX. However the Dispatcher rerouted us to fly from 140W bypassing 130W to begin an arrival using the RYDER arrival. This confused not only us but departure Area Control who had our original flight plan in their system. We departed the gate with the correct uploaded ATC flight plan but possessed on our iPads the amended flight plan from Dispatch... in addition our FO (First Officer) refused to coordinate with Dispatch to revise our our flight plan to its original format which resulted in erroneous flight progress forms from ACARS. To be clear the flight plan only deviated towards the latter end of the flight with the confusion resulting from the Dispatcher uploading an erroneous flight plan to remove a bend in the flight however that was not loaded to the PACOTS east routing for the day. Our FO contacted SFO radio to confirm our routing was correct with our FMS but neglected to inform Dispatch who thought we were still flying the amended route he had given us. It would be helpful if the company would provide guidance regarding how procedurally they would prefer crews coordinate changes to flight plans with ATC. Do they prefer we coordinate with ATC directly or would they prefer that we contact Dispatch and ask that they upload the correct route and that we check it with ATC. It would seem there is a loophole in regards to keeping Dispatch up to speed on changes to flight plans. I believe there is language in the FOM regarding any changes to the flight plan to notify Dispatch of those changes. In this case the changes were minimal however the arrival time differed by about 6-8 minutes from the original flight plan and the amended one from Dispatch. Dispatch was unaware that this stub flight was not flying the amended flight plan they sent us. When I, as the relief pilot, arrived from my break on the flight deck I noticed the erroneous flight progress forms and notified Dispatch who then sent us the revised flight plan. Dispatch was unaware that we were back on our original PACOTS routing. This was accomplished 2+45 into the flight. However if I had not done this it would not have gotten done as the FO refused to contact Dispatch to clear up the confusion. please advise. The First Officer refused input from both the Captain and myself, the relief pilot, to contact Dispatch and get them in the loop regarding discrepancies from filed flights from amended ones. Stub flights caused more confusion than necessary. Clear guidance is needed from company on how they prefer the crew to remedy route discrepancies from Dispatch versus filed. Do they prefer the crew to contact ATC and fix the problem ourselves or do they prefer Dispatch to get involved and fix the discrepancy. Just prior to pushback, we received a message from Dispatch with regards to a change in our flight planned route. We delayed pushback until receiving new flight plan. Only change was to end of route after waypoint at 140W. We then called Clearance Delivery and did a full route verification. They still only had the original, unchanged route. Since the only discrepancy between the flight plans was at the end of the flight, we opted to depart. After departure, we received the flight progress report that showed the modified route (after 140W). During flight, after checking in with San Francisco ARINC, we asked for a verification of our cleared routed. ARINC verified it was the original flight planned route. We then sent a message to Dispatch with our cleared route and received an update. Dispatch believed we requested a look at modifying our route to remove a 'dog leg' segment from our route which we hadn't. We were a STUB flight and that might have been a factor as the original flight was near to the arrival time. The change to our flight plan wasn't requested and wasn't essential to safety. Unless critical to flight safety, last minute changes to flight plans (especially international) can cause miscommunications and errors in navigation and should be avoided.
ASRS:1774635.s: A crew on a stub flight experienced routing confusion after Dispatch amended the plan to remove a bend, conflicting with the original PACOTS east routing filed with ATC. The First Officer refused to coordinate the discrepancy with Dispatch, causing erroneous flight progress forms until a relief pilot corrected the situation 2 hours and 45 minutes into the flight.

ASRS:1774636.n: During climbout on a heading of east on the ZZZZZ2 SID while passing 8,000 feet between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 we got a TCAS TA regarding traffic descending off ZZZZZ3 on the ZZZZZ4 flowing south at 1 o'clock, 3-5 miles ahead that was no factor. This is something we see every day on climb out or descent in and out of ZZZ due to climb and descent rates. ATC then called traffic at our '10-11 O'clock 3 miles descending to one one (11) thousand I called 'traffic in site no factor, they're passing above and behind us.' ATC then asked our Altitude. I replied 'level 10,000 feet.He asked our altitude again, I replied 'Level 10,000 feet, he said he saw us at 10,500 feet and gave us an updated Altimeter setting, and cleared us to climb to 17,000 feet. Passing 12,000 feet he asked us what altitude we were passing. I replied '12,000 feet.' He then replied 'That's what we show as well. For some reason I had you at 10,500 feet back there. I have a phone number to copy when you are ready.' We took the number down, and he said 'Call us when you get to your destination to discuss a possible pilot deviation.'The Captain called when we got to ZZZ1. The Controller Supervisor who answered said he had just sat down, had no idea what we were talking about, said he would do some research and call us back. 5 minutes later he called us back and said, 'After review, the previous Controller showed you slightly high and stopped traffic on the arrival at 12,000 feet (which I thought was at 11,000 based on his advisory call). Then showed our altitude correct in the climb after he inquired again passing 12,000 feet. Said there was no conflicts or loss of separation, not a big deal, and that he would just file it as an RA report and close It out, however, we had no known RA's, nor any TA/RA indications for the potential conflicting traffic passing above and behind us? The ATC Supervisor didn't take any further action or questions, and wished us a safe rest of our day and left It at that. We thought It would behoove of us to fill out this report regardless.Wrong altimeter setting. We had a lot of distractions from multiple visitors on the flight deck at the gate while setting up cockpit and during the before start checklist (flight attendants, gate agents, deadheading crew and commuting pilots who we knew who stopped by to visit). Flight attendants held off boarding passengers who were held up at the door, until catering, who arrived at the aircraft late, had cleared the forward galley and aisle, and got them their snack/sanitary packages set up to hand out. So this backlogged the jet bridge, had the flight attendants coming in and out of the cockpit along with the commuting pilots, and gave us a lot of distractions. This back log seemed to frustrate the agent, for It was the flight attendants who were keeping the passengers out of the way until they were ready for them. For that, the gate agent was rushing to close the flight (We still pushed 10 min early). The FA A seemed rushed, and just closed the flight deck door before verifying if we were ready or saying 'seated and stowed;' which was nonstandard. These multiple interruptions (which seem to happen every flight these days) just added up, we had the current ATIS printed off, but when back tracked to get caught up, we missed the altimeter settings, which must have been set from a flight a day or two prior due to the difference in what It actually was at the time.Verify, Verify, Verify, Trap the Errors, Don't let the distractions of the daily operations knock you off your game. It was a beautiful cold VFR morning, flying with a Captain I had enjoyed flying with in the past, so I felt we were both comfortable and familiar with how each other operates within the SOP's and as a person. The Aircraft had sat overnight. I would like to see more operational (non-flying) related distraction/awareness incorporated into training. The day prior on a separate flight we had a passenger removed by law enforcement for non-compliance/and possible criminal related activity. Gate agents are constantly under stress to get flights out on time or early. To top It all off, everyone has been under stress of the pandemic, furlough related, or state of the airline related issues.-"
ASRS:1774636.s: During climbout on the ZZZZZ2 SID, the crew received conflicting altitude data from ATC due to an incorrect altimeter setting caused by flight deck distractions. The controller initially suspected a pilot deviation, but a supervisor later confirmed no separation loss occurred and closed the incident as an RA report.

ASRS:1774644.n: Maintenance placarded potable water in lavatory LX inoperative per MEL. I asked the Maintenance Technician who brought logbook up to cockpit to confirm compliance with correction requiring the entire lavatory be placarded inoperative due to COVID precautions. He said he understood that placarding the sink was sufficient to comply with MEL. My interpretation was different, and out of an abundance of caution I asked him to place a 'lavatory inop' placard on the affected lavatory door. We advised FA A, and did not use that lavatory. During cruise, after additional review of the maintenance text, I contacted Maintenance Control. They confirmed that to comply with the correction, the entire lavatory should have been placarded and requested I make a Logbook entry to that effect before arrival into ZZZ.
ASRS:1774644.s: The pilot and a maintenance technician disagreed on placarding an inoperative lavatory sink versus the entire unit. Maintenance Control later confirmed the entire lavatory required placarding, prompting a logbook entry before arrival.

ASRS:1774646.n: Traveling in level cruise at FL370, smooth air, Mach .80 we experienced an aircraft Mach speed exceedence. With no noticeable wind change the aircraft accelerated, uncommanded, up to Mach .84. The A/T system made minimal, if any, changes to the cruise power setting. The Captain (PF) immediately spun the Mach speed way back and extended full speed brakes. This was the point at which the A/T finally brought the power back. We stabilized the aircraft, configured the automation and continued to the destination with no other abnormalities.We possibly could have reacted more aggressively and sooner, but we fully expected the A/T system to respond correctly to the speed increase and reduce power accordingly. Aside from that, I cannot see anything else that could have prevented the situation.I don't know what we could change to prevent this situation again.
ASRS:1774646.s: During level cruise at FL370, the aircraft experienced an uncommanded acceleration to Mach .84 while the autothrottle failed to reduce power. The Captain manually reduced speed and deployed speed brakes to stabilize the aircraft, which then continued to the destination without further abnormalities.

ASRS:1774648.n: While turning into Gate X during daytime OPS at ZZZ, 3-4 tugs crossed directly in front of the aircraft forcing me (Captain) to quickly bring the 767 to a stop to avoid a potential collision. After blocking in, I talked to maintenance and found out the problem. ZZZ OPS is short of people to marshal the aircraft in. No wing walkers are present. Maintenance marshalled us into parking. Tug drivers are used to Wing Walkers and without the presence of them are driving in front of aircraft pulling into the gates. Maintenance said this is not an uncommon problem. This is caused because of a need to change of habit pattern due to lack of Wing Walkers. Captain suggest ZZZ tug drivers, etc. Need to immediately be informed that Wing Walkers may not be present when aircraft are pulling into the gate. This lack of Wing Walkers (due to a shortage of people) has taken away a primary cue that tug/ramp personnel had used previously. Tell tug drivers to look for a marshaller with their wands raised and/or the aircraft turning into the gate. What happened today was not good.
ASRS:1774648.s: During daytime gate entry at ZZZ, three to four tugs crossed in front of a 767, forcing the Captain to stop to avoid a collision. The incident occurred because a shortage of wing walkers removed a primary visual cue for tug drivers, who were accustomed to their presence.

ASRS:1774655.n: On approach to ZZZ, the ATIS was obtained with reported winds of 340 @ 15 G 28. The airport was configured to land east, utilizing Runways XL and XXC. The First Officer (FO) and I discussed how this was odd and not desirable as the tailwind component with gusts was at our 10 knot limitation. Additionally, the ATIS stated there were wind shear advisories in the area. On final approach inside the FAF, maintaining target airspeed within Vref +10 was extremely difficult due to the high wind gusts, shifting winds, and shear. As pilot flying, my airspeed was hovering at +10 with occasional jumps up to +20. The wind vector on the MFD was showing winds at 030 between 20-35 knots until 100 feet or so, where the winds sheared to 340 at an unknown speed. I touched down within the touchdown zone but off centerline by approximately 10 feet. Taxi to the hanger was uneventful and no damage was noted. During the debrief, the FO and I agreed a go-around with a request to land on a Westerly direction should have been made. The cause of this event were gusty winds, poor traffic flow decision by ATC, and undesirable speed control by the Pilot Flying due to windshear. ATC decision to land to the east with reported winds of 340 @ 15 G 28. This decision by ATC caused an unsafe tailwind condition when coupled with very strong and gusty crosswinds. Additionally, myself or the FO should have requested a landing to the west. However, the First Officer and I determined that any request would be denied as ZZZ has a reputation for not accommodating these types of request in order to maintain efficient traffic flows. There is pressure to land with the prevailing flow of traffic at a major airport like ZZZ when the crew sees other aircraft landing in the existing conditions, even if the crew would prefer an alternate runway. I strongly believe ATC created an unsafe situation that may have inadvertently pressured pilots into landing with a tailwind in gusty conditions. When I made the decision to conduct the approach, a go around would have been the correct action when the wind sheared at 100 feet.
ASRS:1774655.s: The flight crew and ATC were involved during an approach to ZZZ in gusty winds with shear advisories. The crew landed off-centerline due to ATC's east runway assignment creating an unsafe tailwind, though they agreed a go-around was the correct action.
