ASRS:1774668.n: We were told to Taxi C - G cross Runway XX to the gate. We contacted ramp and were given taxi to the gate. Our gate was X2 and we made the mistake of picking the wrong alley and started down the odd gate side. We realized our mistake as well as Ramp Control and we asked to go up the next line over and then to the even numbered side gates. We apologized for this and Ramp was pleasant towards us, told us 'Oh you're good, don't worry' allowing us to turn. It was not a busy time on the ground and we had plenty of room to make our turns to get to our gate. There was no safety issue involved but I feel it to be the correct choice in filing this.Contributing factors: I had not touched an airplane in over 1 month and I had not flown as Captain in well over 1.5 months or been to ZZZ in over 2 months, so I was focusing and not splitting attention accordingly I would say. I had my charts open and just misread.We were delayed all day so there was a time pressure.The gate that I was going to next was on the odd numbered side and I think I was thinking of the odd side due to this.I had been sitting in a crash pad for a few days and I believe that the stress of commuting and not being home for over 6 days may have had a factor on my mental state.Things learned: Slow down and read the charts better as well as make sure to properly look at the gate information displayed on the ACARS. It is always OK to ask for help. Never assume one gate vs the other. Not actively working means focus more on the task at hand for degraded skills.
ASRS:1774668.s: The Captain, returning after a long break, misread charts and taxied to the wrong gate alley due to fatigue and time pressure. Ramp Control allowed a safe correction with no safety issues, though the pilot noted degraded skills from inactivity.

ASRS:1774673.n: The Captain was flying. We got switched from the ZZZZZ to the ZZZZZ1 arrival and told to keep 300 knots. ZZZ was busier than normal since COVID and we got task saturated. They cleared us for the ILS XX approach and direct to ZZZZZ2 to join the final. We were then cleared for the approach and proceeded to descend to 2,300 feet via VNAV before hitting approach mode. Since ZZZ had wanted us at 300 knots we were in manual speeds. We descended below 10,000 feet at 300 knots and noticed it at about 9,300 feet. We leveled off to slow to 250 knots by 9,100 feet and continued as normal. It was a simple and common error caused by task saturation and typical ZZZ switching approaches 3 times and arrivals twice. ATC did not say anything.This is a common issue with ZZZ but also something we should have seen. We were more careful to monitor throughout the rest of the trip. This is also an issue of COVID and not flying much. No pilot is flying the amount that we used to. Especially Captains and First Officers on reserve. That is not an excuse, but an observation. ZZZ was busy like it used to be and none of us have been used to that since before the pandemic.We will be more careful, and I will more closely monitor events as well as prevent task saturation so this doesn't happen again.
ASRS:1774673.s: The Captain and crew descended below 10,000 feet at 300 knots during the ILS XX approach at ZZZ due to task saturation from frequent arrival changes and reduced flight experience. They leveled off to slow to 250 knots by 9,100 feet, noting ATC did not intervene.

ASRS:1774678.n: I was assisting a bathroom break for the flight deck. Both pilots were not wearing masks! The First Officer put the mask on when I went in. It is ridiculous that they are allowed to take off their masks in the cockpit. The Captain wasn't wearing his. I asked him, 'Where's your mask?;' He acted as if he didn't hear me. I was very very uncomfortable. It was like he violated my boundary. I am stunned this is a reality at our company. Since when are they allowed not to wear a mask? I hate to think that flight attendants need to deal with this absolute nonsense. If they are not wearing one before we go in, we are to deal with millions of droplets. It is the end of November. Well into the pandemic, if one doesn't understand the importance of wearing a mask, then why do we have them as company employees? It's a shame this became a political agenda. It never should have been.
ASRS:1774678.s: A flight attendant reported that both pilots were not wearing masks in the cockpit while she assisted with a bathroom break. The First Officer put his mask on upon her entry, but the Captain ignored her request to wear one, causing the attendant significant discomfort regarding safety protocols.

ASRS:1774686.n: I was working from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was working in the AFT position. As I was in the back I watched the passengers as they were boarding, even helped a few out with questions. I noticed Passenger X and Y seated in seat XX3 had her mask under her chin and XX4 did not have on a mask at all. Once everyone was settled and I was able to move toward the front of the cabin I approached the passenger who was seated in seat XX3 and I told her she must put her mask on over her nose and mouth. She has the mask under her chin. I then noticed the child seated in XX4 did not have on a mask at all. I then asked passenger seated in XX3 (the mother) How old is your daughter?' She then responded "She's four (4)' I then told her that the little girl had to wear a mask as well. She immediately told me 'No, she doesn't like that and how do I expect her to breathe?' The little girl was very aggressive towards the mother and began yelling at her and telling her 'No, No, Nooooooooo....' She also pinched and hit at her mother for talking to her in their language about the mask. I politely explained to the mother the company's policy and she then said 'Ok' She pulled out the child's mask from her pocket and placed it on her face. The little girl snatched the mask off, threw it on the floor and yelled out 'NOOOOOOOO!' in her mother's face. I told the Captain what was going on and gave him full details.So once the door closed and we did our safety demo and was sitting waiting to push back both passengers seated in seat XX3 and XX4 had their mask down and off. I went back to her and told her (the mother) that she had to keep her mask on. She looked at me and rolled her eyes and she put the mask back up on her face. I offered to give her another mask (that are provided on the aircraft) she said 'No!' The passenger seated in the exit row seat looked surprised and began shaking their heads at her (the mother & child's behavior) The child was not listening to her mother and she kept screaming at her. The mother was trying to negotiate with the child but she was not paying her any attention. I told the Captain and he told me to go back to the passenger and tell her that they must wear the mask or we will re-open the door and have them removed from the aircraft. She then responded 'Ok, we will keep it on.' So once we get in the air and we get the 10,000 chime I get up to walk toward the galley and I pass seat XX3 and XX4 they both have their mask down and not on at all. It was the same exact thing I spoke to her about on the ground twice. I then had to tell her for the third time to put her mask back on her face covering her nose and mouth.Once service was done and I went to collect the garbage passengers seated in XX3 and XX4 was non-compliant once again. They were the only passengers on the flight who has to be spoken to on several times about the mask. At this point I issued a policy violation to her and as she was reading it she began to challenge me on the wording of the card. She said the violation stated kids two (2) did not have to wear a mask. I was confused because the child was four (4) going on five (5). This passenger was trying to find reason as to why her child should not wear a mask or why she could have her mask under her chin or top lip. After reading it she put the mask on both herself and the child. The child looked up and rolled her eyes at me because her mom said something to her in their language about her wearing the mask. Once we deplaned, I told the Captain that I had to issue the policy violation to her and that I was going to write a report about the incident and he said 'Ok.'"
ASRS:1774686.s: A flight attendant reported that a mother and her four-year-old child repeatedly refused to wear face masks correctly during boarding, pushback, and cruise. After multiple warnings and a threat of removal, the crew issued a policy violation, which the passengers accepted only after challenging the age requirement wording.

ASRS:1774687.n: Was experiencing fatigue, headache and mild nausea, didn't feel well enough to do another two flights after the turn I had already done.Crew was concerned about COVID. Tested my temperature and it was elevated. Crew and I no longer felt it would be safe to keep me on the aircraft.Called in sick on line.
ASRS:1774687.s: A fatigued pilot with headache, nausea, and elevated temperature was removed from duty by concerned crew due to COVID fears. The pilot called in sick before operating two additional flights, deeming it unsafe to continue.

ASRS:1774703.n: Since the new Joplin Tower was built the beacon light was put on the new tower and as a result the visibility to see the light from a distance at night is very poor. I hangar at Joplin and have flown out of the airport for several years and can confirm the before and after the beacon light visibility has definitely been reduced. I have at times found it hard to locate the airport at night when flying into the airport, even using my GPS. I think the beacon light should be elevated higher up and made brighter.
ASRS:1774703.s: A pilot reported that the new Joplin Tower beacon light has poor night visibility, making it difficult to locate the airport even with GPS. The pilot attributes this reduced visibility to the light's current placement and recommends elevating and brightening it.

ASRS:1774706.n: During a night flight to check out a new comm radio I had installed in my experimental aircraft, the canopy opened and broke the plexiglass out. I was approximately 7 miles east of the airport and had just listened to ATIS, switched to Tower frequency and started my decent from 4,500 feet. Before I contacted Tower, the canopy on my aircraft opened and broke the plexiglass out of the frame. I maintained control of the aircraft and was able to keep my headset on. I had a hard time talking to the Tower due to the wind blast in the cockpit. I was able to slow down to help with the wind noise and to see outside better with less wind entering the cockpit. I requested priority handling and was cleared to land. I was able to maintain control of the aircraft and make a safe landing. I was able to taxi to parking.I requested priority handling at the time not knowing how things would progress with the canopy being damaged. Seeing at night with the cold air entering the cockpit was challenging.After considering the age of the aircraft, which was built over 40 years ago, more detailed inspections of latches, hinges and plexiglass would be paramount to continued operation of aging aircraft.
ASRS:1774706.s: During a night descent from 4,500 feet in an experimental aircraft, the pilot's canopy opened and broke the plexiglass. The pilot maintained control, requested priority handling due to wind noise, and made a safe landing, noting the need for detailed inspections on aging airframes.

ASRS:1774722.n: A line of scattered thunderstorms were moving west to east. We spoke with Clearance Delivery and Departure Control regarding the direction to go around these storms. Departure suggested we follow a flight which had just gone westbound to avoid the storms. We agreed. Departure Control said we should be given a turn in a few miles. We were then instructed to contact Center. The frequency was busy and they would not respond to our communications. We were at 23000 ft. and could not get Center to respond. We tried multiple times to check-in and ask for deviations, but no answer. We were using NEXRAD and on board radar. Our path was taking us through two storm cells separated by approximately 30 miles. The radar was showing light to moderate precipitation ahead of us. At no time did it show any red returns ahead of us. Center finally contacted us and told us to climb to 40000 ft. As we initiated the climb, we encountered moderate turbulence with approximately 10 seconds of severe turbulence. As we climbed through 26000 ft. we cleared the clouds and the turbulence abated. We had one passenger on board that was briefed on the expected turbulence and the seat belt sign was on. The passenger was seated with his seat belt on, but did hit his head on the ceiling of the cabin during the turbulence. He did not report any injuries. The cause of the problem was a saturated ATC system that couldn't handle the traffic load. Perhaps more controllers to handle the traffic load could alleviate the situation.
ASRS:1774722.s: Pilots flying at 23,000 feet encountered moderate to severe turbulence while climbing to 40,000 feet after a delayed ATC response due to a saturated system. One belted passenger struck his head on the cabin ceiling but reported no injuries.

ASRS:1774730.n: After checking with Orlando approach to see which restricted areas to the south were active today. I diverted the student to 2RR. We proceeded southbound and remained east of all restricted areas. The student preformed a landing at 2RR. On climb out of 2RR and proceeding due north and remaining east of all restricted areas I called Miami Center for flight following back to ISM. The controller informed me that we were in active restricted airspace. However I confirmed my location via G1000 based avionics and ForeFlight EFB Geo referenced sectional charts to be well east of all restricted area. The air traffic controller then proceeded to describe an airspace that was not depicted on any of our sectionals or chart. He was describing a restricted airspace directly above 2RR which is nowhere depicted on any charts. We proceeded VFR with him and went eastbound out of the airspace that we had no depiction of. We then proceeded northbound. I think that there may be some restricted airspace that is not depicted on sectional charts yet ATC depicts on their chart. This could be a discrepancy and continue to happen. I suggest that the charting of the R2901 restricted airspace around 2RR be investigated and compare the sectional chart to the charting that ATC is using.
ASRS:1774730.s: A flight instructor and student flying a G1000-equipped aircraft from 2RR to ISM were told by Miami Center they were in active restricted airspace, despite the pilot confirming their position was clear via avionics and charts. The controller described an undepicted restricted area above 2RR, leading the pilot to suspect a charting discrepancy regarding R2901.

ASRS:1774734.n: Myself and my student departed ZZZ VFR to the east on [Date] at approximately XA:30 local time for a routine instrument training flight. We took Aircraft X which had been flown twice that day already with no issues. The preflight was normal, and run-up was normal. We found no indication of a potential malfunction. We had been maneuvering for approximately 15 minutes in the east practice area when [Student] began to make an altitude correction from 3,700 ft. MSL to 3,500 ft. MSL. He attempted to take out some power, but when he reduced the throttle towards the idle position there was no RPM change indicated. He stopped reducing the throttle when he noticed it was pulling out farther than he had ever seen it go before. With concern that the throttle may not be secured properly now, I moved the throttle to the full open position, then moved slightly toward the aft position (approx. 1/2 inch reduction). This reduction was successful and the power reduced to 2400 RPM. With power still being available, I took the flight controls via a positive three-way exchange, turned direct ZZZ visually immediately, called the tower, for partial engine failure. We were 10 miles due east of ZZZ at this time. I selected a field for a forced landing in case that became necessary, and as we got closer to ZZZ I verbally selected another field, and then finally a grass strip just [southeast] of ZZZ before I had ZZZ ensured.I requested to stay at 3,500 ft. MSL (or at least high enough to ensure gliding distance to XXL-the runway I wanted and later requested) and enter the pattern possibly that high. I reported two miles east of the field, got cleared to land, and once I had the runway ensured, I began to reduce the throttle. I remember only trying to reduce about 300-400 RPM, but the power went from 2400 RPM to 1300 RPM. I then put the throttle to the fully open position. At full open, the RPM indication was still 1300. I told the tower I was now in a full engine-out situation. I was approximately 1 to 1.5 nm [northeast] of the approach end of [Runway] XXL when the full failure happened. After getting lined up on final, I reduced the throttle to idle (I did not want a resurgence of power at an unexpected time) and did not attempt a restart. I had [Runway] XXL ensured, and I knew the best option was to commit to the forced landing on a large, paved runway rather than risk restarting an engine that may just die again. On final, [Student] opened his door to ensure at least one safe exit. I glided into [Runway] XXL and maintained positive aircraft control with a smooth touchdown. I did have to perform a forward slip with full flaps to ensure touchdown in the first 3rd of the runway- I recommend the flaps be inspected. I had enough energy to roll off on Taxiway Bravo, clear of [Runway] XXL. We then exited the aircraft and waited for a tow. [Student] told me once we were on the ground that he noticed the fuel flow was indicating 0 while I was on short final just after I had declared the full engine out. He said nothing else caught his eye during those seconds. He was trying to study the MVP50 [Electronic Engine Monitor] for any possible explanation as to the cause of the failure while I was flying.
ASRS:1774734.s: An instructor and student in Aircraft X experienced a partial then total engine failure during VFR instrument training near ZZZ. The instructor executed a forced landing on Runway XXL after throttle adjustments failed to restore power, with the student later noting zero fuel flow on the MVP50 monitor.

ASRS:1774741.n: I was on Local Control. Ground Control was combined with Flight Data and Clearance Delivery. There was a stand-alone Controller in Charge.Aircraft X was rundown for an IFR release. The release was granted by ZZZ TRACON and Aircraft X departed from ZZZ to ZZZ1. At the time ZZZ1 had a ground stop [GS] due to COVID cleaning and we did not coordinate a departure time with TMU.Prior to Aircraft X taxiing, there was a strip printed from TMU stating that there was a ground stop to ZZZ1. That strip was placed near the Status Information Area by the Ground Controller.During Aircraft X's departure roll ZZZ TRACON called over on the shout line to advise us of the ground stop and that is when we became aware that Aircraft X should have been delayed on the ground.We as a Tower team did not catch that Aircraft X needed to be delayed and we should have been more observant to the ground stop strip and requested a departure time from TMU for Aircraft X.I recommend that when a GS is in effect that the GS is displayed on the SIA [Systems Information Area] and that a strip is sent to all facilities at the same time. Often we will receive a flight strip with a CFR, GS, GDP...ect., but the information is not displayed on or SIA for several minutes if at all.
ASRS:1774741.s: Local Control and Ground Controllers failed to delay Aircraft X for departure due to a ZZZ1 ground stop, despite a printed strip being available. The aircraft departed before the tower team noticed the restriction, which was later confirmed by ZZZ TRACON.

ASRS:1774746.n: Originating out of ZZZ, my aircraft had frost on its wings. We proceeded normally to the deicing location. Upon completion of deicing the Captain's wing and as the deicing truck started to back up to move around the wingtip, the entire aft end of the truck became engulfed in flames! A raging fire started on the back end of the truck where the deicing fluid was held. We did not complete the Post Deice Checklist prior to moving the aircraft to safety. My concern was the truck exploding close to the aircraft and its passengers. We taxied the aircraft away from the burning vehicle. I thought it was the safest course of action to move the aircraft quickly out of the danger area. Once in a safe location, I stopped the aircraft, set the brakes, and completed the necessary checklists. Rest of flight was uneventful.
ASRS:1774746.s: While deicing at ZZZ, the deicing truck's fluid tank ignited as it backed away from the aircraft. The crew taxied the aircraft to a safe location before completing the Post Deice Checklist, and the remainder of the flight was uneventful.

ASRS:1774748.n: I was the Pilot Flying on this leg. After departing ZZZ1 while climbing through Flight Level 280 on our way up to FL340 Autopilot #1 disconnected and would not reengage. A/P (Autopilot) #2 would engage but after about 30 seconds it also disengaged along with the auto thrust going into THRUST LOCK mode. Then several ECAMs (Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor) appeared including RUD TRIM1 FAULT, YAW DAMPER 1, RUD TRV LIM 1. The First Officer ran the Quick Reference Handbook procedures for each of those problems which included resetting the FACs (Flight Augmentation Computer).We leveled at FL340 and the aircraft was exhibiting a slight Dutch Roll tendency so we descended to FL280 and no more Dutch Roll was observed. Autopilots could be intermittently engaged, flight directors would come and go, autothrust would disengage in THRUST LOCK mode. We consulted with Dispatch and [Maintenance Control] via phone patch. Without further attempting to engage autopilots or autothrust events seemed to stabilize and with consult with Dispatch we planned to continue to destination. We began evaluating along route alternates and asked Dispatch to do the same. Shortly thereafter the flight directors started to come and go repeatedly along with the previously described ECAMS. When each rudder ECAM came and went there was a discernible yaw felt. Other messages would appear momentarily then clear such as 2FD2, and BOTH PFDs (Primary Flight Display) on SINGLE SOURCE (not sure of the wording as it would momentarily flash then disappear).At this time we made the decision to divert and after evaluating the weather decided with dispatch concurrence to divert to ZZZ2. An [urgent situation] was declared with ATC and a clearance to ZZZ2 was obtained and a safe landing was made. ECAMS intermittently continued while enroute.The aircraft was always fully under control. After gate arrival I debriefed with the [Flight Manager] and maintenance log entries were submitted. Briefed local ZZZ2 maintenance personnel.
ASRS:1774748.s: The Pilot Flying reported that after departing ZZZ1, both autopilots and autothrust failed intermittently with multiple rudder and flight director ECAMs while climbing to FL340. The crew diverted to ZZZ2 after symptoms worsened, declaring an urgent situation, but maintained full control and landed safely.

ASRS:1774749.n: Shortly after takeoff, FA (Flight Attendant) called to say door 2R was open. There was no indicator light on. Cabin was not pressurizing. Returned to ZZZ landing uneventfully. Dispatch was notified, no priority handling requested. Aircraft was under landing weight. Was told by FA front edge of door 2R was open 3-4 inches.
ASRS:1774749.s: Shortly after takeoff, a flight attendant reported door 2R was open 3-4 inches with no indicator light, causing a loss of cabin pressurization. The crew returned to ZZZ for an uneventful landing while under landing weight, notifying dispatch without requesting priority handling.

ASRS:1774753.n: This was originally scheduled as [Flt Number, Route] However that flight was cancelled due to the inbound aircraft diverting due to a reported autopilot/ILS (Instrument Landing System) failure during an attempt at a Cat 3 Autoland approach. Flight [Number] was rescheduled as a ferry flight [Number] to ZZZ, using the diverted aircraft.The aircraft had some autopilot maintenance done at ZZZ1, and was signed off cleared for flight. Upon arrival at the gate in ZZZ2, the Captain reported that the problems with the autopilot and the ILS were not fixed. Both he and the First Officer stated that the exact same malfunctions occurred on both of the past two flights. They described the Captain's ILS as erratic--intermittent ident, azimuth and glide slope drifting stop to stop and blanking out. The aircraft did not intercept course or glide slope on a Cat 3 approach. On the inbound leg, they described a 30 degree left final approach course LOC (Localizer) intercept where instead of rolling left, the airplane rolled right and turned away from final approach course, prompting the Captain to take over manually. They continued to fly a visual approach due to improved weather conditions since their earlier attempt. The Captain said he had made several ACARS ELB (Aircraft Communications And Reporting System Electronic Logbook) entries at the gate in ZZZ2, but had not received any acknowledgement printouts. Because of this, he had notified ZZZ2 maintenance via radio. The gate agent asked my FO (First Officer) and me how soon we would be ready to push back for ZZZ. We replied that there were open write ups that first had to be worked out or deferred, then released. Shortly after that, a Station Operations Supervisor arrived at the gate and expressed an expectation that we would quick turn the aircraft and depart for ZZZ. There had been no maintenance on the aircraft, nor any service. A Maintenance Supervisor arrived and stated the jet was ok to fly as is, with no open write ups. It was clear that there had been a breakdown in communication between the previous crew and the ZZZ2 Station in regards to the status of this aircraft. They became pushy about getting us off the gate. I was clear that this could not happen until these known, reported discrepancies were written up and resolved. I asked about aircraft servicing (fuel) and catering (food and water). The Pilot Mobile app showed that we had crew meals on this flight. (Both of us require Special Meals due to dietary restrictions.) The Operations Supervisor then went on a tirade about no catering at ZZZ2 and how everyone knows that. Her vehement response surprised both of us, as there was no context or cause for it. The maintenance supervisor continued to insist the aircraft had been fixed in ZZZ1 and was good to fly. I called Dispatch to see if we could get some help from [Maintenance Control]. The controller noted there were no open ELB write ups and therefore no reason to delay departure. No one seemed to register that the previous crew had reported multiple malfunctions of navigation equipment on an evening where IMC (Instrument Meteorological Conditions) was a huge factor. So I said to [Maintenance Control], with the ZZZ2 Maintenance Supervisor and Operations Supervisor within earshot, that I would have to refuse the aircraft unless they properly documented these discrepancies, and either fixed them or legally deferred them. Meanwhile, the First Officer had called the [Flight Manager]. He recommended that we stand our ground on the maintenance issues, continue to be professional, and if we refused the aircraft to follow protocol. We had showed up at the airport slightly hungry, expecting that our crew meals would be boarded as listed. This was becoming a safety of flight problem, as the airport had few options for food at all, and the ones available were in the process of closing down. It was clear that if we were to have any food and water for the 5+10 red eye flight to ZZZ, we wouldhave to stop what we were doing and go find it. I called Dispatch back and tried again to explain the legal operational aspects of why it was important to document these inbound discrepancies. He got a different [Maintenance Controller] on the line and we had a better discussion. The new controller called the previous Captain for a personal debriefing of the inbound flight. That, in turn, got the requisite ELB documentation generated and the maintenance process started. Troubleshooting revealed the problem was not the autopilot but a failed relay in the localizer antenna switch. Once we were confident that our [Company] procedures had been followed, we began preflighting the aircraft for ferry to ZZZ. We were running a little short of time (appx 1 hr before a CCO (Crew Critical Off) time), but not so much as to cause undue hurry. During this time, several of the ZZZ2 station personnel were hovering around us, looking over our shoulders as though we needed close supervision to do our jobs. It was a distraction and a bit creepy. Before closing the door, the Ops supervisor reappeared in the jetway, blamed me for the delay, berating me for threatening to refuse the aircraft over crew meals and bottled water, and for not knowing there is no catering in ZZZ2. Ironically, even though we pushed back with 30 minute's, cushion, we nearly went over our CCO time while waiting at the hold short for the final weight numbers from Station Operations. We lifted off and had an otherwise uneventful flight to ZZZ.
ASRS:1774753.s: The crew refused to depart a ferry flight due to unlogged autopilot and ILS failures and missing crew meals, despite pressure from station supervisors. After Maintenance Control documented the discrepancies, a failed localizer antenna relay was identified and repaired, allowing the aircraft to depart safely.

ASRS:1774772.n: Upon landing on first leg of flight to pick up [a] COVID-19 patient from sending facility I realized I had not received the approved paper work. After shutting down the aircraft, I immediately sent the manifest and risk for approval. I then called Operations to explain and get into compliance. Once in compliance I called my Supervisor.
ASRS:1774772.s: The pilot landed the aircraft on the first leg to pick up a COVID-19 patient but realized the approved paperwork was missing. After shutting down, the pilot submitted the manifest and risk for approval, contacted Operations to achieve compliance, and then notified the Supervisor.

ASRS:1774773.n: Following two previous approach attempts into ZZZ1 followed by diversions to our Filed Alternates, on [consecutive evening and morning flights] of Aircraft X. I was advised by Dispatch that if the Crew was willing, they would like us to fly back to ZZZ1 and make yet a third attempt. I immediately said I did not feel safe operating the flight as I didn't feel the approach was safe based on the current conditions at the airport, and the weather we had experienced during the last two attempts. I then stated I would not be willing to make another attempt. During the first attempt (Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1) we experienced moderate turbulence, gusty winds, heavy rain, in IMC at night followed by a Windshear Warning and Escape Maneuver at 150 ft. AGL, following this up with a consecutive approach the next morning (Aircraft X ZZZ2-ZZZ1) resulting in an early Go-Around / Diversion to alternate due to Heavy Rain, Moderate to Severe Turbulence on Approach, Strong Crosswinds on Final, Changing (Increasing) Gusting Wind Conditions on the surface and the previous aircraft making a Severe Turbulence Encounter Report on Final with the Controller inquiring as to passenger injuries on board. This led to a phone call from my direct Supervisor, who tried to convince me the operation was safe. I clearly stated to both persons, that our Dispatch Release reads, and I quote.. 'By Signing this Dispatch Release we are affirming our belief that this flight can be made safely'. I was very clear that after my previous two attempts, I did not feel comfortable operating the flight. The Initial Plan was for us to depart in just 30 minutes after refueling, which again I stated I did not feel safe operating the flight. Followed by yet another phone call from my Supervisor who reviewed the weather with me. Explaining things were much better now and we can depart. Again, I expressed my concerns as to the safety of the flight based on recent experience in the storm system, and inaccuracies experienced with the past weather reports that allowed us to dispatch prior. I felt I was being pushed to operate the flight. My Supervisor continued to tell me of other carriers that made it into ZZZ1 today. Once again I explained they didn't deal with what we had to do, and again relayed I was not comfortable making a flight to ZZZ1 today. After some discussion, it seemed my Supervisor was becoming agitated stating that if I didn't fly he would have to. I remained silent as this was not pertinent to my decision. I was again asked to operate - to which I repeated my opinion that I didn't feel it was a safe operation and I would not even go there as a passenger if you asked me to at that time. I was then told I was being pulled from the flight, I was being relieved of all duty pending an investigation and I would hear from someone in the company. The phone call was then disconnected by the other party.I feel this was an attempt to force a flight crew to accept a flight that I had clearly stated I didn't feel it was safe to operate. I feel that this is a violation of the Captain's joint Authority with Dispatch to operate a flight and is in direct conflict with PIC's (Pilot in Command) responsibility and authority. It also seems to me to be in conflict with the creation of a 'Just Culture: required be FAA in implementing a SMS. A pilot should never be coerced to accept a mission he/she feels is unsafe. In this situation, the PIC was being asked to Dispatch into an area where an URGENT PIREP was broadcast via Center Frequencies advising of Moderate to Severe Turbulence reported below 11,000 ft. by an aircraft on Final Approach to ZZZ1. Another aircraft should not be dispatched to fly an approach in Severe Turbulence. The most basic principle is Dispatchers, Managers, and Supervisors need to listen to the people under their charges. Air Carriers need to stress the importance of Safety, by not just stating they have a culture based on Safety, but by actually exercisingone especially when performance metrics may not be met but safety goals will be achieved. As Pilots, I feel we are all mission-oriented, but the need to complete the mission can never exceed operational safety.
ASRS:1774773.s: The Captain of Aircraft X refused a third approach attempt to ZZZ1 after two previous diversions caused by severe weather, turbulence, and windshear. The Captain was relieved of duty following a dispute with a Supervisor who pressured the crew to operate despite the Captain's safety concerns and an urgent PIREP of severe turbulence.

ASRS:1774774.n: During final approach to ZZZ, We were instructed by Approach to descend and maintain 7000 ft. and expect vectors for visual approach Runway XX. When we were crossing approximately 9000 ft. and 235 KIAS PF (Pilot Flying) requested flaps 9. PM (Pilot Monitoring) double checked the airspeed and proceeded to select flaps 9 position. Right after moving the handle to the 9 position, we got the EICAS message FLAP FAIL. PF took the radios and requested ATC to stop the descent at 8000 ft. because we have to run a checklist and ATC cleared us to stay at 8000 ft. PF leveled off and PM took the QRH and started looking for the associated procedure. PF and PM agreed to follow procedure XXX-XX-X FLAP FAILURE and PM started to read every step in the checklist. In that moment PF requested a Hold while we solved the issue but after receiving confusing ATC holding instructions, PF requested a square box flying vectors and [advised ATC] due to Flaps Failure. We followed every step in the checklist, verified the new approach speed, the new required landing distance, Pulled the J7 CB, sent an ACARS msg to company and advised FA (Flight Attendant) of the issue. After double checking that conditions were safe to land and the available runway landing distance was suitable for the situation, we decided to continue with the approach to Runway XX and advised ATC. ATC gave us vectors for the visual approach and a normal landing was performed. Brake temperatures were ok after landing and no further issues were found during the rolling after the touchdown, then we requested a normal taxi to the ramp and a normal deplane process occurred. No injuries were reported. At the gate, captain pulled out the information from maintenance messages and FLAP JAMMING and FLAP LH MOTOR BRAKE FAIL were found. On descent to 7000, we were at speed 220 and I asked for flaps 9. We received EICAS message flaps fail. I asked FO (First Officer) to recycle back to zero. We asked ATC to hold and they had us stop the descent maintain 8000. We leveled off and requested box turns. We ran flap fail checklist. Communicated with Dispatch and FA (Flight Attendant). [Advised ATC], landed with no issue. I [Advised ATC] because at zero flaps, possible long landing with higher approach speed is expected as well as potential for hot brakes. So we wanted to err on the caution side. Great CRM by crew.
ASRS:1774774.s: During final approach to ZZZ, the flight crew encountered a flap failure EICAS message after selecting flaps 9 at 9,000 ft. After executing the QRH checklist and leveling at 8,000 ft, they completed a safe visual approach and landing with no injuries, later identifying flap jamming and motor brake failures.

ASRS:1774783.n: Attempted to de ice as per station procedure for light frost appproximately 10 ft. from the gate. De ice personnel used absolutely no standard phraseology. Sprayed left wing and left for approximately 30 minutes to return for right wing. We were informed by the crew chief that it was for the truck to heat to the required temperature. I asked the crew chief to inspect the left wing. He reported that it was now all ice. The First Officer and I both inspected the wing and it was indeed a significant layer of clear ice. We informed the station manager that the wing and also the right wing would need to be de iced at proper temperature of the fluid. The Crew chief and ramp personnel were extremely diligent. They personally inspected the temperature of the truck ( it was 40 degrees) below the minimum temperature). The crew chief also brought the de ice manual for the truck to the flight deck. We informed the station manger that we could not depart until the truck was verified at the proper temperature ( by the ground crew) and that we would then de ice again and that the FO (First Officer) and I would both visually inspect before leaving the gate area. This entire evolution took 120 minutes. The station managers, gate personnel and especially the ground crew were beyond outstanding. The gist of the episode is that the de icer made the situation much worse by spraying improper temperature fluid and created ice and then informed us that the wing was clear. Had the flight crew and ramp crew not been diligent and inspected it could have been a problem. The de ice crew was improperly trained, completely unaware of procedure and dangerous. The contract de ice company at ZZZ needs to be trained properly in procedure, phraseology and common sense or the contract needs to be awarded to a competent company.
ASRS:1774783.s: Flight crew and ground personnel at ZZZ encountered a de-icing failure where improper fluid temperature caused clear ice to form on the wings. The flight was delayed 120 minutes for re-de-icing after the crew identified the ground team's lack of training and adherence to procedures.

ASRS:1774800.n: Departing during the waning stages of an intense storm. Winds were gusting close to 30 kts.. Windshear advisories were on the ATIS, however a flight landing 10 minutes before our departure reported only moderate turbulence with no mention of Windshear. Decided to let FO be the pilot flying. Climbing through 1,100 ft. MSL in a right turn to our cleared altitude of 4,000 ft., the turbulence got very intense, with large, rapid, +or- 15 kts. fluctuations in airspeed. PF (Pilot Flying) called for flaps one, which I set, and thereafter he announced the autopilot was engaged. I had just changed to departure on the radio and then we were cleared to climb to 10,000 ft., and to continue the right turn to our first navigation fix. PF called for flaps up, I selected the flaps up and then noticed the attitude of the airplane was falling below the horizon and we were starting to descend. I also noticed the PF trying to select 10,000 ft. on the altitude preselect. He was having difficulty setting the altitude selector as it was so turbulent , so I stated: 'fly the airplane, we are descending'. The PF disconnected the autopilot and raised the nose after we reached about 3 degrees nose low attitude. During this time, our altitude dropped to about 1,300 ft. MSL (1,200 ft. AGL) and the GPWS 'Don't Sink' advisory sounded. We started to establish a climbing attitude so I directed my attention to setting the altitude preselect, setting the heading bug to our first fix, and the PF asked to also execute this fix in the FMS. After setting the FMS, I noticed our aircraft attitude was dropping below the horizon again and we were descending through 1,300 ft. MSL. Before I could command a correction, the GPWS 'Don't Sink' advisory sounded again, and the PF raised the nose. As we continued the climb, by this time the airspeed was climbing over 250 kts. and the aircraft attitude was raised to control the speed. The speed increased to approximately 287 kts, before starting to decrease. As the speed started to drop, the PF continued to raise the attitude of the airplane, and as we exceeded 25 degrees nose up I commanded the PF to 'lower the nose, our airspeed is decreasing, establish a pitch of 12 degrees'. By the time the airspeed stopped decreasing, our speed was about 5 kts. below the flaps up maneuvering speed. We accelerated and established a normal climb. From this point on, the rest of the climb was uneventful.
ASRS:1774800.s: During departure in severe turbulence and windshear, the crew experienced two GPWS 'Don't Sink' alerts and an airspeed excursion to 287 kts due to difficulty managing the autopilot and altitude selector. The pilots manually corrected the aircraft's attitude and speed to establish a normal climb after the initial descent and subsequent overspeed.

ASRS:1774832.n: On climb out, aircraft nose pitched up more than normal and I was pushing nose forward and trimming down. I noticed the trim was not moving on the trim tab indicator. I had the First Officer attempt to reset stab and Mach trim. I turned on autopilot to see if the autopilot could trim it out. That resulted in a autopilot Nose Up Trim Caution message and I turned off the autopilot and resumed manually flying the aircraft. The nose up trim condition did not improve. I transferred aircraft control to the First Officer while I referenced the QRH. I read through the stab trim and Mach trim runaway procedures even though we did not get a runaway trim message. Every time we tried to reset stab/Mach trim the trim increased by .4 and would not let us lower the trim value making the aircraft more nose up trimmed. I advised ZZZ Departure and ran the appropriate check lists and returned to the field landing on Runway 28L.I think the main problem was the Mach trim inputs from the aircraft computer system which caused the stab trim indicator to increase every time we disconnected and re engaged the stab/Mach trim system. The pilots went back to the hotel after the flight. I ran into the pilots who bought the aircraft in the night before at the hotel and they said that they had an autopilot nose up trim situation after take off from ZZZ1 and they reset it according to the QRH with no other problems.
ASRS:1774832.s: During climb out, the crew experienced an uncommanded nose-up trim condition caused by faulty Mach trim inputs that prevented lowering the stabilizer. After attempting resets and consulting the QRH, they returned to land on Runway 28L, noting a similar issue occurred on the previous flight.

ASRS:1774833.n: Departing Runway XX Captain was the flying pilot and I was Pilot Monitoring. It was a normal takeoff until the Captain asked for the autopilot. About 3-6 seconds later we got a 'AP Trim is NU' caution message. Since we were only 700 feet above the ground the Captain turned off the autopilot and tried to trim the plane himself. He was putting in nose down trim but nothing was happening. During this time we got direct to ZZZZZ and climb to 7,000 ft. We started the turn and kept the plane climbing. During the turn I tried to put nose down trim to see if it would work on my side. It did not. Since we were not getting any messages on EICAS and the trim was still not working, we disconnected the stab trim and Mach trim and then reconnected. The plane was already in a nose high pitch attitude and once we reconnected, the nose high trim increased by an additional .4 units while the captain was trying to trim down. Once we confirmed that we disconnected the the stab trim and Mach trim at that point the Captain transferred the controls to me and he took the radios and started running the QRH. I started to slow the rate of climb of the aircraft and we asked ATC if we could stop the climb and maintain the altitude we were at. ATC gave us clearance to do so, the altitude was 5,000 feet. We were still heading towards ZZZZZ. Then we advised ATC and ask for delay vectors to return back to ZZZ. The Captain did the checklist for the stab trim caution message and we also did our check lists for landing. We then asked ATC for vectors to land on [Runway] XX. We landed with the trim at 8.8 and took off with a trim setting of around 6.8. During the whole fight we never put trimmed up. It was a successful landing in ZZZ. At we taxied to the gate without incident. The stab trim was not responding to our inputs.
ASRS:1774833.s: During departure, the crew encountered an unresponsive stabilizer trim after engaging the autopilot at 700 feet. They manually managed the nose-high pitch, returned to the airport, and landed safely with the trim stuck at 8.8 units.

ASRS:1774850.n: Third day of OE, first time on reserve. Planning a flight to ZZZ, an unfamiliar airport on an unfamiliar route. Multitasking trying to get all the preflight tasks done, while loading the plane, rushing to go as we were already late. We had two boxes of dry ice for which Hazmat paperwork needed to be completed. Failed to email a copy of Hazmat paperwork to Dispatch prior to takeoff.Recalled not sending an email during the afternoon following the flight.Caused by being new to the route, inexperienced dealing with Hazmat procedures, being rushed to leave.Realized my error and decided to submit a report.I will slow down, not let myself to be rushed by external factors. I will send out the email as soon as the Hazmat paperwork is completed.
ASRS:1774850.s: A new pilot on reserve failed to email Hazmat paperwork for dry ice to Dispatch before departing for an unfamiliar airport. The error resulted from inexperience with Hazmat procedures and rushing due to a late departure, prompting the pilot to commit to slowing down and sending documents immediately upon completion.

ASRS:1774853.n: I received a call from our Chief Safety Officer stating that the aircraft we flew yesterday had an open maintenance write-up which we and 8 other crews had flown with. The day before, I was briefed by my PIC on the information related to our flight that day including weather, NOTAMs, and other applicable concerns. No open write up was mentioned and we continued with our flight per usual. As an SIC I suggest that in the future I should specifically ask the PIC during the pre-flight briefing if there are any maintenance concerns. This would provide an extra layer of safety and redundancy in our processes and would hopefully help mitigate the risk of a situation like this occurring in the future. We were dispatched to fly on commercial flight to pick up the aircraft at the maintenance center. Concerns with COVID exposure while traveling on commercial airlines are aggravating. Upon arrival at the airport we were directed to contact the maintenance base to have their van pick us up. When I called, the base informed me that the van service was discontinued. I put in an on-line request for a taxi ride. The address given did not take us to the service center, and there was much confusion and aggravation dealing with the taxi driver to try to get to the proper location. Upon eventual arrival at the service center the aircraft was ready for us, and I ordered fuel. I talked to maintenance both before leaving and during the trip, verifying that all of the paperwork for the maintenance performed was completed to their satisfaction. While completing pre-flight paperwork I apparently overlooked that the flight crew that had originally ferried the aircraft in had written up the pilot seat as a discrepancy, and that the open write-up had not been dealt with, either by being fixed or MELed. Verifying no open write-ups prior to flight is a company SOP, and one that I feel that I normally do as a matter of course. I can only think that dealing with the major maintenance paperwork on the maintenance issues pushed the possibility of an open write-up not related to that work to the side, and I did not properly review the past flight logs in the flight can, thus missing the write-up. My aggravated mental state at dealing with airlines and COVID concerns, multiplied by the ground transportation snafus, were certainly contributing factors.When non-typical operations are being dealt with, stop and take the time to triple-check every detail.
ASRS:1774853.s: The SIC reported flying an aircraft with an open pilot seat discrepancy because they overlooked the write-up during pre-flight checks. The error was attributed to distraction from complex maintenance paperwork, ground transportation issues, and personal stress regarding COVID exposure.

ASRS:1774860.n: Smell of fumes detected on several occasions including all of last month. Aft smoke detectors go off due to the fumes. Pax (Passengers) complain and makes FAs (Flight Attendants) in the aft sick. We've complained many times and nothing seems to be resolving. Deadhead crew members smell it as well.
ASRS:1774860.s: Crew and passengers detected fumes on multiple occasions, triggering aft smoke detectors and causing illness among flight attendants. Despite repeated complaints, the issue remains unresolved, affecting both revenue and deadhead crew members.

ASRS:1774861.n: [I have concerns with] the COVID pre-takeoff PA, which now instructs passenger that flight attendants will collect trash during safety compliance checks. Topics of concern:1. Would this action not be a direct conflict with FAR 121.391 (d)? It is understood that collecting a few used cleaning wipes and some cups does not present an issue. Some may even consider it like collecting pre-departure beverage cups prior to takeoff. However, managing empty pizza boxes (and similar bulky items) will require flight attendants to unlock carts (and/or trash cart doors) since the openings are too narrow to accept such items (FAR 121.577 (c).2. The Flight Attendant could offer to return later for bigger items, but would that not require a judgement call during an extremely limited period? This adds a new distraction from more critical safety matters (seat-belts, tray tables, etc.). A Flight Attendant is responsible for (depending upon aircraft) checking for more than 20 items during routine pre-takeoff/landing compliance checks.3. The Flight Attendant must now carry a trash bag during compliance checks leaving only one hand free to steady themselves from a fall. It is confirmed that taxi surface movement is a high-risk period for injuries. Also, the revised policy now adds more time (additional duty) before being able to secure in a jumpseat.Knowing first-hand the history of Flight Attendant injuries related to surface movement, I strongly recommend the company reevaluate and consider changing to a more reasonable expectation of trash collection after takeoff.
ASRS:1774861.s: A flight attendant reported that the new pre-takeoff trash collection policy conflicts with FAR 121.391 and 121.577, creating safety risks during taxi. The reporter argues that managing bulky items requires unlocking carts, adds distractions from compliance checks, and increases injury risk by limiting hand use for stability.

ASRS:1774874.n: I was flying with my student in the designated practice area, working on a variety of maneuvers. There were 2 other company traffic in the practice area (both training helicopters), one of which was cleared to operate at 2,000 ft MSL and below. Without this radio-communication approval from the control tower, all helicopters are to remain below 600 ft AGL. I was unaware of this helicopter operating at 2,000 ft and below, as although the Control Tower cleared them into the practice area, I did not hear it, as my student was talking. Most of the time (but not always), the Control Tower will call up all other helicopters in the practice area to inform them of the joining company. This explicit advisory was not issued to my tail number, which in this scenario is why I was not aware of the company traffic. While my student and I were taking off in a normal takeoff configuration, we did not see the other involved aircraft which was entering a practice engine failure directly above us, flying in the same direction as us. It wasn't until about 200 ft AGL on the climb out that I (and not my student) saw the descending aircraft about 100 feet ahead of and above us. I quickly lowered the collective to arrest our rate of climb and decelerated to avoid a collision, and once the company traffic was well clear I proceeded to climb out in a normal profile. When questioning the other pilot and their student after the flight if they saw us, they said that the saw us on the ground, but did not see us take off. They were unaware that the near-miss had occurred. Control Tower not explicit warning us of the company traffic joining us. Not adequately visually clearing the area above me before take off. As per company SOP, this is normally only done when conducting a maximum performance takeoff maneuver. Not adequately listening to the Control Tower frequency. Other pilot not deciding to recover their descent well before 600 ft AGL, knowing that there are two aircraft operating at 600 ft and below. Company policy is recovery by 100 ft. Taking off to the south, despite Runway XX being active. However, it is understood in our standard operating procedures that all takeoffs in the north practice area should be made in the opposite direction when the winds are strong from the west and Runway XX is active, due to obstacle clearance and left crosswind avoidance. As the other pilot corroborated later, he was not able to confidently predict which direction we would be taking off in.
ASRS:1774874.s: A training helicopter pilot and student nearly collided with another training helicopter descending above them during takeoff in a practice area. The reporter attributed the incident to missed tower advisories, inadequate visual scanning, and the other pilot failing to recover their descent below 600 ft AGL as required.

ASRS:1774881.n: I had just landed the Piper PA 28 140 cruiser I have been approved to be flying solo by my CFI I just returned from training maneuvers like a tracking VOR's, slow flight, stalls etc. Then I came in for a landing and then after landing I decided to do a touch and go as I did I had a 90 degree crosswind that was coming at 5 knots which was well within my CFI's logbook approval for me. However after I had given it full throttle for the touch and go there was a gust of wind which lifted my left wing slightly. As I put left rudder in my foot inadvertently hit the break and caused my plane to pull to the left off of the runway at which time my nose gear collapsed which caused the incident with my airplane.
ASRS:1774881.s: A solo student pilot in a Piper PA-28-140 Cruiser experienced a nose gear collapse during a touch-and-go landing in a 5-knot crosswind. The incident occurred when the pilot inadvertently applied the brake while correcting for a gust, causing the aircraft to veer off the runway.

ASRS:1774911.n: It all happened with 20 to 30 minutes of my shift. The position was not too busy when I first sat down but quickly got busy. Multiple aircraft were calling on different frequencies. Aircraft were departing satellite airports looking to pick up an IFR clearance in the air. Other areas and facilities kept calling, and pilots kept stepping on each other. There was also a lot of paperwork to clean up and things to organize when I sat down. I had noticed that the aircraft was going to be a factor for a satellite departure so I took them off the arrival and gave them a 050 heading. Once the traffic was clear I turned the aircraft to a 360 heading and issued 2,000 feet. That is not a normal procedure for me at all and if I do take people off the arrival I usual give 6,000 or 3,000 feet. I have no idea why I issued 2,000 feet.I had already told the others in my area that I was too busy to answer other questions and put them in an uncomfortable position to question the altitude I had issued. I noticed the aircraft was around 2,400 feet at the northern most part of the 2,600 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA) and didn't change anything because by the time the climb would have started they would have been well out of that MVA. There's not much that I could have done to change the situation.
ASRS:1774911.s: An air traffic controller issued an unusual 2,000-foot clearance to a departing aircraft due to high workload and frequency congestion. The controller allowed the aircraft to descend below the 2,600-foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude, reasoning that the climb would occur after exiting the restricted area.

ASRS:1774916.n: ZZZ Approach was closed for staffing reasons due to COVID illness / quarantine on the midnight shift. Sector X (my sector) was in control of the airspace. Sector Y had Aircraft X arriving to ZZZ from the southeast. The pilot dialed up the ATIS at ZZZ which told the pilot to come up on my frequency for a weather update. I read the weather to the pilot then sent them back to sector Y freq. I kept the datablock up on my scope assuming that I would get a hand off soon and clear the Aircraft X for an approach. Since ZZZ is really close to the boundary with [sectors] X / Y, the Controller decided to work the aircraft all the way into ZZZ. I treated it like a point-out as did he although we made no official coordination.At the same time, I had another aircraft (Aircraft Y) about 60 miles north of ZZZ inbound to the field and was asking about runway conditions at ZZZ. I had a number to call the field operations for updates because the TRACON /Tower was closed. When calling from the line, I got a recording staying the 'This line is no longer in service and to hang up and try again.' I asked the second Controller in my area if he knew of an issue with the phone number. He got on the Supervisor's phone and called for an update. The field ops told him about the snow on the runways as well as Runway X Left being closed for snow removal. This was not in our NOTAMs. That Controller then ran down to the other area who was working the Aircraft X and told them what was going on. Luckily the Aircraft X wasn't too low for radio coverage, the Controller issued them present heading and a climb back up to 6,000. The Aircraft X was then put on my frequency where I let them fly out to the west a bit farther and set up for a turn back to the IAF for Runway X Right. The plane then landed safely at ZZZ.There should have been formal coordination between Sector Y and myself on who was working the Aircraft X into ZZZ. It doesn't change the fact that a runway was closed at ZZZ without a NOTAM in our system. The only reason we found out was because of the Aircraft Y inbound from the north asking about updates on the field conditions and the other Controller making the phone call for me. I'm not sure how long it takes for NOTAMs to populate in our system but it's not fast enough. I guess they hit enter on the keyboard and immediately jumped in snowplows and took to the runway. The NOTAM did eventually populate in our system, but it was after this event took place. I was notified of a poorly handled situation on the mid shift. There were several major breakdowns in communication causing a 'swiss cheese' situation that could have ended devastatingly. Likely some minor changes to ZZZZ/ZZZ (ZZZ ATC 0) Contingency Plan. At roughly XA:00 in the morning Sector Y was working Aircraft X, during the enroute/initial descent portion of the flight arriving ZZZ. Keeping in mind ZZZ Approach is ATC 0 and Sector X assumes ALL of their airspace with procedures in place. At some point Aircraft X calls Sector X, likely on a second radio while in communication with Sector Y, to obtain the weather since the ATIS is not updated hourly and instructs pilots to do exactly that for the latest weather and field conditions. Presumably the pilot was then instructed to return to Sector Y frequency since the flight was a little ways out (and no radar contact) where Sector Y proceeded to work the aircraft all the way into the airport with no coordination to Sector X. Sector X Controller proceeded to watch this unfold without attempting to initiate the coordination to Sector Y to say 'radar contact' or even 'point-out approved' since there was no traffic for this aircraft. This was wrong in and of itself for several reasons including questioning the reach of Sector Y frequencies.Sector Y has this aircraft set up for an instrument approach, runway unknown to Sector X. Simultaneously, Sector X is in communication with Aircraft Y, inbound to ZZZ. The pilot of this flight asked us for runway conditions. The Controller working the sector was unable to get a hold of ZZZ airport operations with the line for an unknown reason. The Sector X, A-side called on another phone and after a brief conversation with operations learned that operations had tried calling Sector X on frequency to inform us that Runway XL is closed while they clear the runway of snow. It was also about this time that the NOTAM populated in ERIDS (En-route Information Display System) which is definitely not enough time between NOTAM being received and giving [the] Controller time to see [the] NOTAM relative to the location and phase of flight to Aircraft X arrival, especially if NOTAMs had already been checked and issued at the initial descent per 7110.65. While this phone call was taking place, Aircraft X was on final at approximately 3,500 feet or less. A-side ran to Sector Y and asked what runway the flight is set up for and was told Runway XL and was immediately told to cancel approach clearance and climb aircraft to 6,000 runway heading and place the aircraft on Sector X's frequency. It's amazing that Sector Y's frequency was able to even reach the aircraft. With poor visibility and snow plows kicking up snow, the plows would never have been seen even if the runway had been.Recommendations:1. Airport operations not getting a hold of an actual person to communicate runway closure and in a timely manner.2. Sector Y working an aircraft into airspace that wasn't their own. Breakdown in understanding ownership of ZZZ1 or negligence?3. Sector X Controller not initiating 'radar contact' of this flight.4. Retrain OM's. Many overnight OM's are not properly executing text files at time of ATC 0 placing ZZZ approach airspace at a sector that's adjacent to the actual sector being worked. Sector X is one scope on the mid at Sector Z. ZZZ approach is being opened at Sector X and more often than not, is NOT followed up with a CS message to combine with Sector Z. Until a few years ago, Sector X was the mid scope and text file needs updated. This second step was clear in an email prior to this period of ZZZ, ATC 0 but is being overlooked. Controllers in Sector X assume it's being done correctly by having the airspace next to them and don't speak up about it. So if an aircraft didn't call Sector X for weather, Sector X could potentially be completely unaware of Sector Y working aircraft into ZZZ as 'auto-pop' would happen on the adjacent scope. During this incident, ZZZ Approach was opened at the adjacent scope as I was told. That did not cause this though or factor into it, however.5. Airport operations told to contact ZZZ Center on frequency which was never going to work. Needs to be a phone call to center and nothing done until this takes place.It was discussed this morning after this incident that regardless of the weather, ZZZ (Sector X) shall reach out to airport operations for ALL arrivals to make sure they are clear of the runway. Supposedly one of the operators on the runway had a radio with a dead battery and obviously would not have heard a pilot calling short final or any other calls. Why wouldn't a radio be tested with another handheld and how could it have been unknown that it was dead?Changes to the ATC-0 plan may need to happen to stop this from happening again.
ASRS:1774916.s: Sector Y controllers vectored Aircraft X toward ZZZ without formal coordination with Sector X, unaware that Runway X Left was closed for snow removal due to a delayed NOTAM. Sector X discovered the closure via a separate inbound aircraft, prompting a climb and reroute of Aircraft X to avoid the active snowplows and closed runway.

ASRS:1774923.n: While climbing on the ZZZ4 departure, ATC issued a turn to heading 265 and a climb to 17,000 feet. I read back the climb instructions, and both I and the Captain confirmed the instructions. While climbing through 8,300 feet, Departure asked if we were leveling at 8,000 feet, to which I responded, that our last instructions where to climb to 17,000 feet. Departure then instructed us to descend to 8,000 feet and turn left 30 degrees, at which time we received a TA and we acquired the aircraft visually. After the TA cleared, Departure issued a new climb clearance to 16,000 feet and we continued on to our destination.Conditions at the time were clear skies with low traffic chatter on the frequency, normal workload on climbout, and the Captain hand flew the aircraft to about 16,000 feet and all through the incident.Not sure there is any issue on the flight crew side, but perhaps ATC may have to look into this. I have noticed that the ATC staffing levels have changed since COVID and that they are working more than one frequency per Controller. Not sure if this was the case and was given wrong instructions by mistake. During climbout from ZZZ, we switched to Departure and a received a clearance to turn to the west and a climb to 17,000 feet. FO, who was PM, read back the clearance and set the heading bug and 17,000 feet. This was also the clearance I heard and read back both of the changes to the PM. Approaching 8,000 feet Departure Control queried if we were leveling at 8,000 feet. As the PF I immediately started to correct back to 8,000 feet (highest I saw was 8,600 feet) and began a left turn as directed by ATC. During this time, we received a brief TA alert. As we were rolling out FO saw the traffic and called it out and said it was no factor. Almost immediately after that we received a clearance back to a heading of 270 and a climb to 16,000 feet.
ASRS:1774923.s: During the ZZZ4 departure climb, ATC issued conflicting altitude instructions, causing the flight crew to descend from 8,600 to 8,000 feet and receive a Traffic Advisory. The pilot attributed the near-miss to potential ATC staffing issues and incorrect clearances, noting the crew corrected the error after visual acquisition of the traffic.

ASRS:1774946.n: Company Flights Aircraft X (event flight) and Aircraft Y had all the elements in play for a severe collision during taxi operations at ZZZ airport, had it not been for the keen and alert awareness of the First Officer (FO) on our flight.Other Company Flight Aircraft Y had just landed on Runway XXC, exited onto Taxiway B, and received clearance to back-taxi on Runway XXR full-length and proceed to the gate. Shortly thereafter Aircraft X received taxi clearance to taxi to Runway XXC via Taxiway P, cross Runway XXR, left onto Taxiway G, and join Taxiway EX.Both flights were taxiing toward the intersection of Runway XXR and Taxiway P when it is assumed that Tower saw the potential collision as both aircraft had 'ALL LIGHTS ON' indicating that Aircraft Y was taxiing with clearance on an active runway, and Aircraft X was preparing to cross an active runway with proper clearance. Tower then attempted to modify the taxi clearance for Aircraft X but made an error by initiating the call with Aircraft Y's call sign. The transmission was unfortunately interrupted by a third aircraft trying to transmit as the Tower was attempting to correct the call sign, resulting in the amended clearance transmission being unintelligible to both Flights X and Y.Aircraft X was underway at a nominal taxi speed, and Aircraft Y was observed taxiing at a higher-than-normal speed as they back-taxied toward the turnoff point at the end of Runway XXR. Taxiway P enters at a slight angle preventing the Captain of Aircraft X from clearly seeing any approaching traffic from his right. As the Captain of Aircraft X, we had full intention of entering the intersection as initially cleared. Just prior I initiated a Safety call by saying 'Clear left.' At that point the FO looked right and said, 'Wow, they're moving fast, and don't think they're intending to stop.' Hearing that, I immediately began a full stop of our aircraft prior to crossing the hold short line, followed by turning our lights off, and yielding to Aircraft Y, in case we were the ones in error with the crossing clearance. Startled that we had just avoided a serious collision, we discussed the possibility of us missing a clearance or how that collision seemed inevitable had we not made the final 'Clearing check' prior to crossing the runway. Because of the frequency congestion with Tower working all three frequencies (Clearance, Ground, and Tower) and the fact that we didn't actually cross the hold short line, we held any immediate inquiry as to the miscommunication of the clearance to ourselves.Upon further discussion among ourselves after departure, we were certain that we did not miss any clearances from ATC and that this was a certain potential mishap that needed further investigation to acknowledge the chain of events from going unrecognized in the future. We discovered that both aircraft had the appropriate clearance to be where they were and that there was an attempt by ATC to issue an amended clearance to us. Tower initially called Aircraft Y then quickly attempted to correct to Aircraft X, but the transmission was interrupted by a third aircraft rendering the call sign and amended clearance unintelligible for either aircraft to be warned appropriately about each other.Due to the angle to which Aircraft X was approaching Runway XXR, there wasn't a good line of sight for the Captain to see any approaching traffic back-taxing on Runway XXR until it would have been too late. It was only due to the vigilance and discipline from the FO in effectively communicating the immediate danger that we were we able to avoid a severe collision given the circumstances.It is believed that Tower was operating at reduced staffing levels even though there were a lot of aircraft movements at ZZZ that evening. This was likely due to COVID protocols in place with ATC. The increased workload enabled him to issue clearances to both Flight X and Y to be on Runway XXR at the same time if timing was ideal. In thiscase, an amendment to the clearance was attempted to be issued, however, time was not in our favor for the Tower to initiate the call with the wrong call sign and be interrupted by a third aircraft making the transition intelligible by either flight.
ASRS:1774946.s: The First Officer on Aircraft X prevented a collision with Aircraft Y during taxi operations at ZZZ airport by spotting the fast-approaching aircraft before crossing Runway XXR. The incident resulted from an unintelligible ATC clearance amendment caused by frequency congestion and a wrong call sign, compounded by limited visibility and reduced tower staffing.

ASRS:1774947.n: While trying to clear Runway XL, the Tower Controller told us which taxiway to take. I could not understand him and asked again. I understood the second transmission, and we cleared the runway. Once clear I asked him where he wanted us to go. He gave instructions and then tried to explain why he gave a specific taxiway. We could not understand that transmission nearly at all. I then said, 'Sir, I can't understand what you're saying, your transmission is very muffled.' He then came through perfectly clear and then said, 'it's the mask;' or something to that effect.
ASRS:1774947.s: The pilot and Tower Controller experienced communication difficulties while clearing Runway XL due to the controller's muffled transmissions. The controller later attributed the poor audio quality to his mask, after which his transmissions became clear.

ASRS:1774963.n: At peak times our customers all come at once in masses. They do not follow the social distancing protocol that the CDC, the state, and airline [mandate]. The agglomeration of people is a safety issue. It takes one person to have the virus to [be a] transmitter to others.
ASRS:1774963.s: Cabin crew reported that during peak times, passengers gathered in masses without following mandated social distancing protocols. This agglomeration created a safety issue where a single infected person could transmit the virus to others.

ASRS:1774985.n: Getting radar vectors to intercept the final approach course to Runway 34L RNO, ATC instructed us to fly direct to SPOON at 11,000 ft and intercept the localizer. The direct routing to SPOON took us on a westerly heading approximately 90 degrees to the final approach course. SPOON is defined as a radar fix on the approach chart and is D24.6 from the field. As such, we were reluctant to use the localizer to guide our turn to final and instead used GPS to navigate to SPOON and turn onto final. Upon overflying SPOON, the GPS commanded an aggressive, yet smooth, right turn to final. Once on final, we intercepted the localizer and descended on the glide path while observing the altitude restrictions at APIME, WAGGE, and EPOSE. The FO (First Officer) and I were fully 'dialed in' for this approach as we had briefed the procedure, identified the surrounding terrain, and associated threats. Landed uneventfully. Three days later I was advised ATC identified our airplane as one that lost acceptable separation with terrain during our approach. The FO was making his first trip to RNO and I had only been to RNO a few times in at least a few years. We were initially planning to fly an approach to the south until ATC told us to expect one to Runway 34L. The routing to SPOON put us at (approx.) 90 degrees to the final approach course with (from memory) an unreliable localizer signal at D24.6. That large angle and our reluctance to use the localizer so far from the field forced us into using the GPS which caused an overfly situation, and thus, and overshoot of the final approach course. I think getting a heading to intercept the final approach course inside SPOON and at a lesser angle would alleviate the overshoot possibility and the resulting loss of separation. We were cleared to and were proceeding direct to SPOON at 11,000 ft on a track of approximately 070 when we were cleared to intercept the localizer for the ILS 34L. The Pilot Flying (Captain) and I discussed intercepting the localizer so far from the field (SPOON is 24.6D from the field) and the PF elected to stay in Nav [mode] until we had turned on to the final. We saw the line the nav was going to take and that it was going to fly over SPOON and then turn us onto final with a slight overshoot and the PF verbalized this. We had done an extremely thorough review of the RNO brief and of all of the pages in FD Pro and based on the clear weather and our awareness of the terrain hazards we concluded that this would be an appropriate course of action. We overflew SPOON, 'nav'd' to the final approach course and then selected the approach mode and flew the rest of the approach and landing uneventfully. The extremely steep intercept angle and relatively close proximity to SPOON when we were cleared to intercept the localizer along with the far distance from the field. Emphasize to both ATC and aircrew the ramifications of a steep intercept angle to final.
ASRS:1774985.s: The Captain and First Officer flew an ILS 34L approach at RNO, using GPS to navigate to SPOON at 11,000 ft due to a steep 90-degree intercept angle. ATC later reported a loss of terrain separation caused by the aircraft overshooting the final approach course after overflying SPOON.

ASRS:1775013.n: We were given a taxi instruction from Gate X to Runway XXL via 'Romeo, Yankee, Uniform, Kilo cross [Runway] Y, to XXL' but we taxied Romeo to Yankee, taxied on Y past Uniform (apparently missed it) and crossed [Runway] Y at Yankee. The ZZZ Ground Controller caught our mistake and gave us amended clearance to XXL via 'Victor to Kilo, Kilo to XXL.'I believe I simply misheard the Ground Control clearance, because I briefed the taxi route as I executed it, and I believe the FO repeated it to Ground without anyone questioning it. It was only questioned after we crossed Runway Y, and the Controller realized we were not on K but on Y taxiway. So, either I simply misheard, or I was tired and did not catch the error, and the FO did not catch it either. Either way, my error.This shows how easy it is to get a clearance wrong, especially when you have not flown into a particular hub airport in nearly a year. It points out how we have to stay extra vigilant, especially in these COVID-19 times, because crews are not flying as much, and ATC controllers are handling multiple sectors/tasks, so even if one repeats the clearance the way you believe it is, the ATC Controller may not catch the error.
ASRS:1775013.s: The flight crew misheard a taxi clearance at a hub airport, causing them to cross Runway Y at the wrong taxiway intersection. The ZZZ Ground Controller detected the error and issued an amended clearance after the crew admitted the mistake resulted from fatigue and lack of recent experience.

ASRS:1775014.n: Upon being vectored for the ILS approach to Runway XX at ZZZ, ATC cleared us to descend from 3,000 MSL to 2000 MSL. The PNF was distracted while trying to control the cabin pressure that had been wildly uncontrollable since the beginning of descent from FL410. As the PIC and PF, I set the Altitude Alerter to 2,000 and vertical speed to 700 FPM descent, with autopilot engaged. During the descent to 2,000 MSL, I briefly looked up at the Pressurization Control Panel to monitor the PNF progress in controlling the cabin pressure, I noted the cabin pressure was finally close to the aircraft's actual altitude.
