I directed the PNF to select 'RAM AIR' ON. That action stabilized the cabin for landing. ATC called to confirm our 2,000 feet clearance limit and I realized that the aircraft did not level off at 2,000 feet and the autopilot was not engaged. I acknowledged our clearance to ATC, manually flew the plane from 1,700 feet to 2,000 feet and reengaged to Autopilot. Since the cabin pressure was finally under control, an uneventful approach and landing were completed. Due to the distraction of the cabin pressure control issues, as PF I briefly failed to monitor the aircraft flight profile. Since I had tasked the PNF to attempt to stabilize the cabin pressure, I take full responsibility for failing to continuously monitor the aircraft flight profile.No matter what cockpit distractions occur, it is incumbent upon the PF to continuously monitor the aircraft flight profile. And if using the Autopilot, PF should continuously monitor that it functions as programed and does not inadvertently disconnect. The flight went well up to the time of descent when the cabin pressure started to malfunction. All attempts were made to control the pressurization using ADC 1 & 2 and Manual control. As preparations were made for landing, air traffic control issued further descent to 2,000 feet and the flying pilot was in control of the aircraft with the auto pilot engaged. The aircraft did not capture the 2,000 foot altitude because the autopilot was inadvertently disconnected and the aircraft continued descent to 1,600 feet at which time the deviation was noted and immediately corrected. The aircraft was subsequently vectored onto the final course and the rest of the approach and landing was uneventful. The pilot monitoring should have noticed the altitude deviation as a result of the auto pilot not being engaged while manually controlling the pressurization and the pilot flying should have been aware that the auto pilot was not engaged. It is imperative that the pilot flying concentrates on flying the aircraft while the other attends to the malfunction and refers to the checklists.
ASRS:1775014.s: During an ILS approach to Runway XX, the Pilot Flying descended below the cleared 2,000 feet to 1,600 feet after the autopilot inadvertently disconnected while the crew managed a cabin pressure malfunction. The Pilot Flying manually corrected the altitude deviation, and the aircraft completed an uneventful landing.

ASRS:1775022.n: Day VMC. Conducted initial approach [Runway] XXR. PF (Pilot Flying) called missed approach into ZZZ [Runway] XXR due to windshear with airspeed loss below 500 ft. AFE (Above Field Elevation) with advancement in override thrust. Subsequently received windshear caution. After selecting TOGA and pitch up flew flight director. No windshear escape guidance provided as the windshear was not sustained. Thrust was advanced to GA (Go-Around) RSV as a precaution. Stable in the missed approach maneuver with no caution windshear, PF called Flaps 4 due to flaps full configured. Gear retracted at a safe altitude with positive climb rate. Flew ATC assigned runway heading with missed approach climb profile. Subsequent approach flown to the ILS profile with Flaps 5. Flew the glide slope to RWY [Runway] XXR. No windshear event occurred. Received wind report with gust factor 28 kts. Selected manual speeds to increase approach sped until 4-5 kts. until after passing 500 ft. AFE 'stable' call the target speed was reduced. Maintained visual descent rate with visual cues and instrumentation of the ILS. During round out to flare automation set the aural 'sink rate' message. FO (First Officer) announced correcting due to the aural call and confirmed with a cross check the sink rate was induced by maintaining descent rate with the descent maneuver to coupled round out pitch rate simultaneously for the landing maneuver, not due to windshear as the speed was stable. FO and CA (Captain) on debrief both acknowledged the aural alert at post flight and both agreed with given conditions the approach to landing was stable given the conditions. Touchdown was within LTP (Landing Threshold Point) distance.Second approach with Flaps 5 configuration allowed for a higher approach speed and acknowledging the wind factor with increase in target speed for gusty conditions allowed for less susceptibility for the same condition. Automation with sensor inputs from other automated systems is subject to its own set design limitations and may not reflect positive confirmation of the event with pilot judgment of the same situation monitoring the same event. Such as automation latencies detecting the windshear event prior to the windshear caution, or sink rate alert while the pilot is initiating real time assertive maneuvers in turbulent conditions. Inertial vertical speed descent rates measure acceleration as it filters out noise of turbulence conditions causing a lag as opposed to real time judgment of the flight crew. Approach into ZZZ on our 1st attempt we conducted a missed approach due to wind shear. On the 2nd approach in the flare we briefly went to a sink rate of 1,100 [ft. per minute] the FO (First Officer) was already correcting and we received a 'sink rate' aural tone just prior to touchdown.
ASRS:1775022.s: The flight crew executed a missed approach on the first attempt due to windshear below 500 ft AFE. On the second approach, a brief sink rate of 1,100 fpm triggered an aural alert during the flare, but the crew corrected and landed safely within the threshold.

ASRS:1775027.n: Enroute to ZZZ1 we failed to set altimeters to 29.92 when climbing through 18,000 feet. Due to the very high altimeter setting at our departure field, it lead to us inadvertently leveling off 300 feet below our assigned altitude. ATC queried our altimeter setting and we immediately corrected. Inconsistent scheduling and continued ongoing stress from the organization's uncertain future lead to a flight deck environment prime for small errors such as this one.
ASRS:1775027.s: Pilots en route to ZZZ1 inadvertently leveled off 300 feet below their assigned altitude after failing to set altimeters to 29.92 when climbing through 18,000 feet. The error was corrected after ATC queried the setting, attributed by the crew to organizational stress and inconsistent scheduling.

ASRS:1775038.n: CLT tower cleared us to take off close in trail of an Airbus 321 to allow an aircraft to have adequate spacing to land close in behind us. The current weather report at that time indicated winds 120@5. This is perfect light quartering tailwind to hold wingtip vortexes over the runway for longer than normal amounts of time. Upon liftoff we encountered the [A321's] wake and experienced a moderate buffet and slight roll action at roughly 100-200 feet above the field.While the Airbus 321 isn't considered a 'heavy' jet, given the weather conditions and the comparative weight between our two aircraft, it is still imperative that adequate spacing be given in the interest of safety.
ASRS:1775038.s: The pilot reported encountering wake turbulence from a preceding Airbus A321 during takeoff at CLT while cleared for close-in trail spacing. Moderate buffet and slight roll occurred at 100–200 feet due to light quartering tailwinds holding vortices over the runway longer than normal.

ASRS:1775039.n: On a visual approach to Runway X, the FO was flying, he started the approach a little high but managed to get back on a 3 degree glide to the runway. By the time I noticed we were at 500 feet and his airspeed was still about 20 knots above Vref. The airspeed managed to get down to Vapp with the engines spooled before touchdown. I hadn't flown in a month so my situational awareness was not on a level it should have been and I should have called a go-around.
ASRS:1775039.s: The Captain and First Officer conducted a visual approach where the First Officer flew high and fast, reaching 500 feet with airspeed 20 knots above Vref. The Captain attributed the lack of a go-around call to reduced situational awareness from a month-long absence, though the aircraft landed safely after speed decreased.

ASRS:1775053.n: After completing all required checklist and announcing our taxi out, our intention to takeoff on Runway 4 (twice) the PF (I was the PNF) and I performed a perfectly standard initial takeoff procedure, including (PF) announcing that the final was clear and the (PNF) announcing that the downfield looked clear. During the takeoff we both notice a small bird on our direct takeoff path. The bird passed by the aircraft with no incident or abnormal engine indication. V1 was called and shortly there after the PF announced that he saw an aircraft on the runway and immediately started the aircraft rotation (slightly below Vr). As the PNF I noticed the lower than normal speed and the aircraft on the runway in front of us, so I immediately lowered our flaps to 15 degrees to assist in the required takeoff lift. We passed over the other aircraft, whom never announced their position (there was another aircraft inbound '10 miles out' that we both heard on the radio clearly). We performed a normal climbout and checklists without further incident.
ASRS:1775053.s: The PNF and PF executed a takeoff on Runway 4, passing a bird and an unannounced aircraft on the runway. The PF rotated early due to the obstruction, while the PNF lowered flaps to 15 degrees to assist lift, resulting in a safe climbout with no engine damage.

ASRS:1775105.n: After landing at CBF the airport manager approached and asked about turning on the PCL [Pilot Controlled Lighting] lighting. Airport manager stated that it was very expensive for airport lights to be turned on and asked if local pilots and flight instructors could be coached on not turning the lights on so much during the day and at night when not necessary. It was explained to airport manager that turning on the lights is at the pilots discretion and a potential safety issue and asking them to try to monitor turning runway lights on and off to help airport control their electric expenses seemed as counter to safe operations of aircraft.
ASRS:1775105.s: After landing at CBF, the airport manager requested pilots reduce Pilot Controlled Lighting usage to save costs. The pilot explained that lighting activation is at the pilot's discretion for safety, noting that restricting it to control expenses contradicts safe aircraft operations.

ASRS:1775109.n: When loading Cargo Compartment the Loading Supervisor noticed that there was no DG (Dangerous Goods) info for this ULD (Unit Load Devise) in the Load Platform Program.He contacted the Load Controller who then contacted Cargo for the information and the DG info was then updated in Load Platform Program.
ASRS:1775109.s: The Loading Supervisor identified missing Dangerous Goods information for a ULD in the Load Platform Program during cargo loading. After contacting the Load Controller and Cargo, the missing data was successfully updated in the system.

ASRS:1775115.n: VFR traffic failed to level when instructed by ATC. I had to drop 500 feet and bank had while accelerating to avoid a mid air collision. We only got one small heading change from ATC that made us more of a factor.
ASRS:1775115.s: The pilot reported that VFR traffic failed to level as instructed by ATC, forcing a 500-foot descent and bank while accelerating to avoid a mid-air collision. The pilot stated that a single small heading change from ATC increased the collision risk.

ASRS:1775147.n: Working a slow but steady local session with Supervisor working GC/CD combined. Very low staffing due to COVID. Steady traffic all day, I wouldn't call it too busy though. Very last transmission of my shift was to Aircraft X.Aircraft X called on about a 7 mile final (new pilot). I cleared it to land on Runway XX right and then started my position relief briefing within seconds of my transmission.Finished the brief and my 2 minute overlap, said bye to my fellow coworkers and left. Aircraft X was probably on a 2 mile final by then.I was paged at the bottom of elevator and Supervisor asked 'Did you give Aircraft X Runway XX right or Runway XX left'? I told him I didn't remember.Turned out aircraft landed on Runway XX left instead of Runway XX right. No separation issues luckily.All they said was 'cleared to land' I didn't even realize it at the time.I was distracted, ready for the briefing to be done after a long, busy day with a skeleton crew.Expectation bias all the way, I just assumed they said XX right in their transmission.All controllers tend to get complacent in this job when everything goes right for some time, I need to stay vigilant and listen to every transmission. If I would've just listened to that pilot's readback instead of thinking about getting off position and being done for the day, I would've noticed it and I would've got verification that she was cleared to land on runway XX right and all would've been good.
ASRS:1775147.s: An air traffic controller cleared Aircraft X to land on Runway XX right but failed to hear the pilot's readback for Runway XX left due to distraction and expectation bias during shift relief. The aircraft landed on the wrong runway, though no separation issues occurred.

ASRS:1775153.n: Training on combined sectors, moderate traffic, two practice approach aircraft in satellite airspace all other traffic in departure sectors.Aircraft X came off ZZZ on the published missed approach for the RNAV RWY XX approach, he checked in and was radar identified while in the published left turn towards the missed approach fix, ZZZZZ. The trainee subsequently verified the pilot's previous request to return to ZZZ1 on an IFR clearance. The trainee cleared Aircraft X direct ZZZ and instructed the aircraft to maintain 2,000'. At the time, the aircraft was within a 2,000' MVA [Minimum Vectoring Altitude]. I believe both the trainee and I anticipated that the pilot would make a right turn direct to ZZZ1, not recognizing that a continued left turn may be more appropriate because the aircraft was already in the published left turn on the missed approach. With the anticipation of a right turn in mind and the aircraft in a 2,000' MVA my attention as the OJTI turned to the other departure traffic, which was going to require the trainee to merge and weave multiple departures off multiple airports (ZZZ2/ZZZ3/ZZZ4) to get them on course and through our airspace. This was an area the trainee had shown struggles in in previous sessions as well as earlier in this training session, so I was attempting to stay ahead and have a plan of my own if needed. Upon reviewing the incident, I became aware that in the moments following Aircraft X's clearance I was suggesting an alternative course of action for one of the trainee's departures in an effort to illustrate a way to expedite getting a departure on course which also got them out of the way of succeeding departures quicker. Unfortunately, this conversation kept my focus on the departure traffic as opposed to the continued turn that Aircraft X made into the higher MVA. Aircraft X subsequently continued a left turn towards ZZZ1 and entered a 2,500' MVA at his assigned altitude of 2,000'. The trainee was aware of the incident almost immediately. The trainee issued a climb to 2,500' to Aircraft X when the aircraft was only a third or a half a mile inside the 2,000' MVA. I was not aware of the situation until I heard the trainee issue the climb to Aircraft X. I subsequently requested that we be relieved. The trainee and I debriefed, after which I informed management of the incident when I requested time for myself and the trainee to review the incident and fill out our report. To my knowledge, Aircraft X climbed to the MVA and subsequently landed at ZZZ1 without further incident.Numerous things could have prevented this occurrence. Had the trainee climbed Aircraft X to 3,000' instead of descending them to 2,000' they would have been above the MVA. Had the trainee left the aircraft on the published missed approach for even a few miles they would have climbed above the MVA and a subsequent clearance may have included a more appropriate altitude. Had the aircraft made the anticipated right turn instead of continuing in a left turn they would have remained in the 2,000' MVA. Had the trainee issued the clearance to ZZZ1 via radar vectors, I believe they would have assigned a vector that would have remained within the 2,000' MVA and avoided the situation. Recertification time on [positions] (departures) and Article 67 training on[positions](south satellite). Aircraft X departed ZZZ on the published missed from the RNV runway XX approach. Requested clearance to ZZZ1 airport. I observed Aircraft X in a 2;000ft MVA [Minimum Vectoring Altitude] and told pilot to maintain 2,000' and proceed direct ZZZ1, which is north east of ZZZ. A direct flight path would have kept the aircraft away from the 2500ft MVA east of their position. Pilot was in a left hand turn though, and continued a left hand turn direct ZZZ1. I was expecting a right hand turn direct. The left hand turn put the aircraft 2-3 miles further east than planned and inside the 2;500ft MVA. I climbed the aircraft to 2;500ft and let them continue on course. I, as the controller should have been more aware of the chance the aircraft could have entered higher MVA. I should have climbed Aircraft X to 2;500ft before sending direct ZZZ1 to account for a left or right turn.
ASRS:1775153.s: During training, a trainee controller cleared Aircraft X to maintain 2,000' direct ZZZ1 after a missed approach, but the pilot's continued left turn entered a 2,500' MVA. The trainee issued a climb to 2,500' once the aircraft was inside the higher MVA, and the aircraft subsequently landed safely.
